details: Mārkaṇḍeya introduces the future eighth Manu. Suratha of Caitra’s line loses to hostile kings, returns to his own city and resumes ruling his own territory, then suffers renewed enemy attack. His powerful corrupt ministers seize treasury and army even in his city. Riding away under a hunting pretext, he reaches Medhas’s hermitage yet worries about kingdom, elephant, servants and treasure.
outcome: Suratha remains attached after dispossession.
title: Suratha remains attached after dispossession.

details: Suratha asks the distressed merchant his identity. Samādhi says wife, sons and kinsmen expelled him for wealth; he still worries about their welfare. Suratha questions this affection; Samādhi admits knowledge has not made him unloving.
outcome: Their shared attachment becomes the question.
title: Their shared attachment becomes the question.

details: They approach Medhas respectfully. Suratha asks why discrimination does not end attachment. Medhas cites hungry birds feeding young and explains Mahāmāyā’s power over even knowers; propitiated, she also grants liberating knowledge. Suratha asks her origin, nature and activity.
outcome: Medhas begins Devī’s narratives.
title: Medhas begins Devī’s narratives.

details: Medhas distinguishes eternal Devī from births described when she appears for divine purposes. At cosmic dissolution Viṣṇu sleeps on Śeṣa; Madhu and Kaiṭabha arise from his ear-region and threaten lotus-seated Brahmā.
outcome: Brahmā seeks awakening of Viṣṇu.
title: Brahmā seeks awakening of Viṣṇu.

details: Brahmā praises the goddess as sacrificial utterance, cosmic creation, preservation and dissolution, knowledge, illusion, nature and armed power. He asks her to delude the demons and awaken Viṣṇu to kill them.
outcome: Brahmā’s invocation addresses cosmic sleep.
title: Brahmā’s invocation addresses cosmic sleep.

details: Yoganidrā leaves Viṣṇu’s eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart and breast and appears before Brahmā. Viṣṇu awakens and fights the demons with his arms for five thousand years; deluded and intoxicated with strength, they offer him a boon.
outcome: Demons become boon-offerers.
title: Demons become boon-offerers.

details: Viṣṇu chooses their death at his hands. They stipulate a place where earth is not flooded; he accepts and kills them with his discus. The Sanskrit says jaghane, while Pargiter renders the bodily locus ambiguously; a precise thigh-position is reserved for review.
outcome: Madhu and Kaiṭabha are slain under their stated condition.
title: Madhu and Kaiṭabha are slain under their stated condition.

details: After a hundred-year war Mahiṣa wins Indra’s office and divine jurisdictions; displaced gods roam earth. Led by Brahmā, they tell Śiva and Viṣṇu their defeat and seek a plan to kill him.
outcome: Displaced gods seek deliverance.
title: Displaced gods seek deliverance.

details: Divine energies converge as Devī: Śiva’s face, Yama’s hair, Viṣṇu’s arms, Moon’s breasts, Indra’s waist, Varuṇa’s legs/thighs, Earth’s hips, Brahmā’s feet, Sun’s toes, Vasus’ fingers, Kubera’s nose, Prajāpati’s teeth, Agni’s eyes, twilights’ brows and wind’s ears.
outcome: Gods’ energies manifest as a woman.
title: Gods’ energies manifest as a woman.

details: Śiva gives a trident; Viṣṇu a discus; Varuṇa a conch and noose; Agni a spear; wind a bow and full quivers; Indra a vajra and Airāvata’s bell; Yama a rod; Prajāpati a rosary; Brahmā a water-pot; Sun rays; Kāla sword and shield.
outcome: Devī receives divine equipment.
title: Devī receives divine equipment.

details: Milk Ocean supplies pearl necklace and imperishable garments; ornaments adorn Devī. Viśvakarman gives axe, diverse weapons and impenetrable armor; Ocean lotus garlands and lotus; Himavat lion and gems; Kubera a wine cup; Śeṣa a jeweled serpent necklace.
outcome: Devī is adorned and mounted.
title: Devī is adorned and mounted.

details: Devī’s roar shakes worlds, sea, earth and mountains; gods and sages praise her. Mahiṣa musters armies and approaches its source. Her light, crown, bow sound and thousand arms fill the worlds; Cikṣura and Cāmara enter battle.
outcome: The battle begins.
title: The battle begins.

details: Udagra, Mahāhanu, Asiloman, Bāṣkala, Biḍāla and huge contingents fight with missile and close weapons; Pargiter inserts Ugradarśana from Bombay’s reading where the displayed Sanskrit has no proper name. Mahiṣa leads enormous chariot, elephant and horse forces.
outcome: Named and collective contingents engage.
title: Named and collective contingents engage.

details: Devī cuts enemy missiles effortlessly. Her lion attacks; her breaths create energized troops carrying axes, javelins, swords and halberds, with drums and conchs. Her weapons kill and bind enemies; bell sound confounds them.
outcome: Devī’s breath-born army joins combat.
title: Devī’s breath-born army joins combat.

details: Mutilated demons and armed headless bodies continue fighting or dance to martial music. Fallen forces obstruct the field and blood forms rivers. Devī, lion and emanated troops destroy the host; gods shower flowers.
outcome: Mahiṣa’s army is destroyed.
title: Mahiṣa’s army is destroyed.

details: Cikṣura shoots arrows; Devī cuts them, kills horses and driver, breaks bow and banner and wounds him. His sword strikes lion and Devī’s arm, then breaks. His thrown śūla and his body are shattered by hers.
outcome: Cikṣura is slain.
title: Cikṣura is slain.

details: Elephant-mounted Cāmara hurls a spear; Devī’s huṃ renders it powerless, and arrows cut his next śūla. Lion leaps onto elephant, wrestles Cāmara on the ground, then springs and severs his head with a paw-blow.
outcome: Cāmara is slain.
title: Cāmara is slain.

details: Devī kills Udagra with stones/trees, Karāla with bodily blows, Uddhata with club, Bāṣkala with bhindipāla, Tāmra/Andhaka with arrows, Ugrāsya/Ugravīrya/Mahāhanu with trident, Biḍāla with sword and Durdhara/Durmukha with arrows.
outcome: Named chiefs are slain.
title: Named chiefs are slain.

details: Buffalo-shaped Mahiṣa attacks troops with muzzle, hooves, tail, horns, rush, roar, circling and breath, then attacks lion. His movements shake earth, sea, clouds and mountains.
outcome: Mahiṣa confronts Devī directly.
title: Mahiṣa confronts Devī directly.

details: Devī binds Mahiṣa. He changes buffalo to lion, then armed man as she cuts at him; arrows strike man, sword and shield. Elephant-form seizes lion; she cuts its trunk. He becomes buffalo again.
outcome: Mahiṣa’s successive forms are countered.
title: Mahiṣa’s successive forms are countered.

details: Devī drinks and laughs; arrows break hurled mountains. She tells Mahiṣa his roaring is brief, leaps, presses his neck and strikes with śūla. As he emerges halfway from the buffalo mouth, she beheads him. Gods rejoice; celestial singers and dancers celebrate.
outcome: Mahiṣāsura is slain.
title: Mahiṣāsura is slain.

details: Gods praise Devī’s cosmic power, knowledge, prosperity, protection and mercy in battle, including the claim that slain enemies reach heaven. They ask her gentle and fearsome forms and her weapons to protect every direction.
outcome: Gods worship the victorious Devī.
title: Gods worship the victorious Devī.

details: Gods offer flowers, perfumes and incense. Invited to choose a boon, they ask relief whenever they remember her in calamity and prosperity for mortals singing this hymn. She agrees and disappears; Medhas introduces her later emergence from Gaurī.
outcome: Devī grants remembrance-based protection.
title: Devī grants remembrance-based protection.

details: Śumbha and Niśumbha seize the three worlds, divine jurisdictions and sacrificial portions. Dispossessed gods recall Devī’s earlier promise, go to Himavat and invoke her as Viṣṇu’s māyā.
outcome: Gods invoke the previous boon.
title: Gods invoke the previous boon.

details: Their hymn salutes Devī in auspicious and fierce modes and as consciousness, intellect, sleep, hunger, shadow, power, thirst, patience, class, modesty, peace, faith, beauty, fortune, activity, memory, mercy, contentment, mother, error, sense-governance and pervading awareness.
outcome: The hymn asks immediate deliverance.
title: The hymn asks immediate deliverance.

details: Pārvatī arrives to bathe and asks whom gods praise. Ambikā emerges from her bodily sheath and answers that the hymn addresses her; she is named Kauśikī. Pārvatī turns dark and is called Kālikā. Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa see Ambikā.
outcome: Kauśikī manifests and is seen by the scouts.
title: Kauśikī manifests and is seen by the scouts.

details: Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa commend her beauty and urge seizure alongside Śumbha’s treasures: Airāvata, Pārijāta, Uccaiḥśravas, Brahmā’s vehicle, Mahāpadma, Ocean’s garland, Varuṇa’s umbrella, Prajāpati’s chariot, Utkrāntidā, Varuṇa’s noose held by Niśumbha, sea-gems and Agni’s garments.
outcome: Scouts urge Śumbha to acquire her.
title: Scouts urge Śumbha to acquire her.

details: Śumbha sends Sugrīva to secure willing arrival. The envoy claims Śumbha’s rule, sacrifices and treasures, offers marriage to him or younger Niśumbha and promises incomparable sovereignty.
outcome: The envoy delivers the marriage demand.
title: The envoy delivers the marriage demand.

details: Devī replies that her former vow requires a husband who defeats her in battle, removes her pride and equals her strength. Sugrīva mocks a lone woman’s chance and threatens dragging her by her hair; she repeats the vow and asks him to report it.
outcome: Devī makes battle her marriage condition.
title: Devī makes battle her marriage condition.

details: Sugrīva reports her response. Angry Śumbha orders Dhūmralocana to drag her by the hair and kill any rescuer, god, Yakṣa or Gandharva. He arrives with sixty thousand Asuras and threatens forcible capture.
outcome: Dhūmralocana attempts seizure.
title: Dhūmralocana attempts seizure.

details: Devī asks what she can do if one sent by the Asura king, strong and with an army, takes her by force. When he charges, her huṃ reduces him to ashes. His army showers arrows, śakti spears and axes; her lion kills with paws, jaws and claws, tears bodies and drinks blood, destroying the host.
outcome: Dhūmralocana and his force are destroyed.
title: Dhūmralocana and his force are destroyed.

details: Śumbha orders Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa to bring her bound or dragged by hair; if capture is doubtful, all troops should kill her and the lion, then seize her.
outcome: Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa are dispatched.
title: Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa are dispatched.

details: Fourfold forces approach smiling lion-seated Devī on a golden peak. Her angry face darkens; Kālī emerges from her frowning forehead with sword, noose, khaṭvāṅga, skull garland, tiger skin, gaunt body, wide mouth, tongue and sunken red eyes.
outcome: Kālī manifests against the attackers.
title: Kālī manifests against the attackers.

details: Kālī devours elephants with crews and bells, horses with fighters, chariots with drivers and enemy weapons; she crushes foes bodily and kills with sword, staff and teeth.
outcome: Kālī destroys the army.
title: Kālī destroys the army.

details: Caṇḍa charges, and Muṇḍa showers arrows and discuses. Kālī laughs, seizes Caṇḍa’s hair and cuts his head, then kills Muṇḍa. Survivors flee. Presenting their heads to Caṇḍikā, she reserves Śumbha/Niśumbha for her; Caṇḍikā names her Cāmuṇḍā.
outcome: Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa die; Kālī receives a name.
title: Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa die; Kālī receives a name.

details: Śumbha musters eighty-six Daityas, eighty-four Kambūs, fifty valiant families, one hundred Dhaumra families, Kālakas, Daurhṛdas, Mauryas and Kālakeyas, and marches. Devī’s bow, bell, lion and Kālī’s cries resound; armies surround them.
outcome: Śumbha’s whole force mobilizes.
title: Śumbha’s whole force mobilizes.

details: Divine Śaktis arrive: Brahmāṇī with swans, rosary and pot; Māheśvarī on bull with trident, snakes and moon; Kaumārī on peacock with spear; Vaiṣṇavī on Garuḍa with conch, discus, club, Śārṅga and sword; boar Vārāhī, lion-form Nārasiṃhī and thousand-eyed elephant-riding Aindrī with vajra.
outcome: Divine Śaktis join Caṇḍikā.
title: Divine Śaktis join Caṇḍikā.

details: Caṇḍikā’s fierce Śakti emerges with a hundred-jackal cry and appoints Śiva envoy: restore Indra’s worlds and divine sacrifice portions, retreat to Pātāla to live, or fight and feed her jackals. Hence Śivadūtī’s name. The Asuras reject the ultimatum and attack.
outcome: Śivadūtī’s ultimatum is rejected.
title: Śivadūtī’s ultimatum is rejected.

details: Devī cuts missiles. Kālī strikes with śūla and staff; Brahmāṇī’s water weakens courage and force. Māheśvarī uses trident, Vaiṣṇavī discus, Kaumārī spear, Aindrī vajra; Vārāhī snout, tusks and discus; Nārasiṃhī claws/devouring; Śivadūtī laughter/devouring. Asuras flee the Mothers.
outcome: Mātṛkās rout the enemy.
title: Mātṛkās rout the enemy.

details: Raktabīja advances with club. Each blood-drop falling to earth produces an equal in size and strength. Aindrī’s vajra and club, Vaiṣṇavī’s discus and other Mothers’ weapons cause multiplying blood-born fighters; he clubs them individually. Gods fear the proliferating army.
outcome: Blood-replication defeats ordinary attacks.
title: Blood-replication defeats ordinary attacks.

details: Caṇḍikā directs Cāmuṇḍā to catch the blood and devour generated Asuras. As Devī wounds Raktabīja, Kālī drinks every flow, including fighters generated in her mouth. His club causes Devī no pain; multi-weapon blows drain him bloodless. Gods rejoice and Mothers dance.
outcome: Raktabīja dies when replication is intercepted.
title: Raktabīja dies when replication is intercepted.

details: Suratha asks what followed Raktabīja’s death. Medhas narrates the brothers’ fury: Niśumbha and Śumbha advance with their armies and shower arrows; Caṇḍikā cuts their arrows and wounds them.
outcome: Brothers enter the battle.
title: Brothers enter the battle.

details: Niśumbha strikes lion with sword. Devī’s kṣurapra cuts sword and eight-moon shield; discus cuts spear, fist shatters śūla, trident burns his club to ash, and arrows fell his axe-bearing advance.
outcome: Niśumbha first falls unconscious.
title: Niśumbha first falls unconscious.

details: Eight-armed Śumbha advances. Conch, bow, bell, lion, Kālī’s hand-strikes and Śivadūtī’s laugh terrify forces; Devī challenges him. A great firebrand counters his flaming spear. After reciprocal arrow-cutting, Caṇḍikā’s śūla fells him unconscious.
outcome: Śumbha is temporarily incapacitated.
title: Śumbha is temporarily incapacitated.

details: Niśumbha revives and shoots Devī, Kālī and lion. Ten thousand arms throw discuses; Devī cuts these and arrows. She cuts his club with sword and pierces his heart with śūla; another strong man emerges challenging her and is beheaded.
outcome: Niśumbha and the heart-born warrior are slain.
title: Niśumbha and the heart-born warrior are slain.

details: Lion, Kālī and Śivadūtī devour troops; Kaumārī’s spear, Brahmāṇī’s mantra-purified water, Māheśvarī’s trident, Vārāhī’s snout, Vaiṣṇavī’s discus and Aindrī’s vajra destroy or repel them. Some die, some flee, some are eaten.
outcome: Remaining forces are routed.
title: Remaining forces are routed.

details: Śumbha grieving his brother accuses Durgā of relying on other goddesses. She states that they are her manifestations, absorbs them into herself and stands alone; the apparent plurality is withdrawn before the duel.
outcome: Devī accepts solitary combat.
title: Devī accepts solitary combat.

details: Each counters divine missiles; Devī breaks his with huṃ. Arrows break Śumbha’s bow, discus his spear, arrows his sword, hundred-moon shield and mace. Without horse or driver he punches her breast; her palm-blow fells him.
outcome: Śumbha loses arms and chariot.
title: Śumbha loses arms and chariot.

details: Śumbha rises, seizes Devī and ascends. Unsupported she wrestles him in the sky, whirls and throws him down. He charges again with fist raised; her śūla pierces his chest and kills him, shaking earth and seas.
outcome: Śumbha is slain.
title: Śumbha is slain.

details: The universe clears: fiery portents cease, rivers return to channels, winds and sunlight become auspicious, sacrificial fires burn peacefully, and gods, Gandharvas and Apsarases celebrate.
outcome: Cosmic order is restored.
title: Cosmic order is restored.

details: Agni-led gods sing the Nārāyaṇī hymn: Devī sustains earth and water, deludes and liberates, appears as divine Śaktis, shields suppliants, and guards against enemies and disasters. They ask unceasing protection and pacification for the worlds.
outcome: The gods request continuing protection.
title: The gods request continuing protection.

details: Invited to choose a boon, gods request removal of troubles and foes. Devī predicts other Śumbha and Niśumbha in the twenty-eighth age of Vaivasvata’s manvantara; born of Yaśodā in Nanda’s house and residing at Vindhya, she will kill them.
outcome: A future Vindhya manifestation is promised.
title: A future Vindhya manifestation is promised.

details: Devī predicts a fierce form devouring Vaipracitta Dānavas; their consumption reddens her teeth like pomegranate flowers, producing the name Raktadantikā.
outcome: Raktadantikā is foretold.
title: Raktadantikā is foretold.

details: After a hundred-year drought, remembered by sages, she will appear without womb-birth as hundred-eyed Śatākṣī, nourish the world with vegetables from her body until rain, become Śākambharī, kill Durgama and be named Durgādevī. Sanskrit clarifies wording omitted or mistranscribed in English.
outcome: Śatākṣī, Śākambharī and Durgādevī are foretold.
title: Śatākṣī, Śākambharī and Durgādevī are foretold.

details: Devī predicts taking a terrible form in Himalaya and devouring Rākṣasas to protect sages; their praise establishes Bhīmādevī’s name.
outcome: Bhīmādevī is foretold.
title: Bhīmādevī is foretold.

details: When Aruṇa troubles the three worlds, she will become innumerable bees and kill him, gaining the name Bhrāmarī. She promises repeated manifestations whenever Dānava oppression arises. Pargiter’s main text reads Aruṇākṣa, with Aruṇa noted as variant.
outcome: Bhrāmarī and recurring deliverance are promised.
title: Bhrāmarī and recurring deliverance are promised.

details: Devī promises relief to attentive hymn-praisers and faithful listeners on eighth, ninth and fourteenth lunar days: no sin-born troubles, poverty or separation, and no fear of foes, robbers, rulers, weapons, fire or floods. Regular recitation secures presence in her shrine.
outcome: Hearing and recitation receive stated benefits.
title: Hearing and recitation receive stated benefits.

details: Her exploits should be heard at bali, worship, fire rites and festivals; she accepts knowing or unknowing offerings. Autumn hearing grants freedom from trouble, wealth, grain, children and courage; recitation pacifies portents, bad dreams, planetary afflictions and child-seizure, reconciles broken fellowship and repels harmful beings.
outcome: Ritual settings and further benefits are stated.
title: Ritual settings and further benefits are stated.

details: One hearing wins favor comparable to sustained offerings and gives purification and health; battle narratives remove fear and rebirth, hymns improve understanding. Remembering her exploits delivers from forest fire, isolated roads, robbers, enemies, wild beasts, angry rulers, death sentence, bonds, sea storms, battle and pain.
outcome: Remembrance is promised as rescue.
title: Remembrance is promised as rescue.

details: Devī disappears before the watching gods. They regain offices and sacrificial shares; surviving Daityas go to Pātāla after the brothers’ deaths.
outcome: The third battle cycle concludes.
title: The third battle cycle concludes.

details: Medhas explains eternal Devī’s repeated world-protecting manifestations: creator, deluder, giver of knowledge and prosperity, cosmic destruction, stability, good fortune and ill fortune; worship brings wealth, sons and righteous understanding.
outcome: Medhas explains the story’s theological consequence.
title: Medhas explains the story’s theological consequence.

details: Medhas urges refuge in Devī, giver of enjoyment, heaven and release. Suratha bows and joins Samādhi on a riverbank; they make an earthen image, recite, offer flowers, incense, fire and water, restrict food and give blood-sprinkled offerings for three years.
outcome: Their worship pleases Devī.
title: Their worship pleases Devī.

details: Devī appears and offers their desired gifts. Suratha requests regained rule with enemies defeated now and lasting kingship in another birth; disillusioned Samādhi requests knowledge removing attachment to I and mine.
outcome: The two devotees request different goals.
title: The two devotees request different goals.

details: Devī promises Suratha his kingdom within days after killing enemies, then birth from Vivasvat as Manu Sāvarṇi; she grants Samādhi perfected knowledge. Praised by both, she disappears. Mārkaṇḍeya reiterates Suratha’s future birth as the eighth Manu.
outcome: Both boons are granted; the frame closes.
title: Both boons are granted; the frame closes.

cause: Indra’s attraction during the festival and encounter with Durvasas.
details: Dakṣa requests origins and battles of eight incarnations; Mudgala begins Vakratunda. Indra’s annual accession festival assembles the named gods, sages, attendants and musicians recorded in mud-e-festival-roster. Rambhā’s performance and ball play enthrall Indra, who closes it prematurely. After forest play with Rambhā, seeing Durvāsas makes him leave her and bow; his seed falls on earth. He returns home, repeatedly condemns his distraction and resumes his own dharma. Matsara arises from his seed; Earth nurtures, names and initiates him at five. He studies Vedas with an unnamed teacher, and marries Durbuddhi’s daughter Madakarā.
outcome: Matsara reaches adulthood and marriage.

cause: Matsara decides to conquer the cosmic egg by intense austerity.
details: Matsara obtains the five-syllable formula from Sukra and propitiates Sambhu. He stays in a secluded forest, observes Pasupata initiation, fasts for a thousand divine years, repeats the formula and meditates on Sadasiva. His austerity disturbs gods and beings. Gods and sages seek Sankara’s protection; Sankara comes with Parvati and his attendants. They see Matsara reduced to skin and bones, covered by an anthill.
outcome: Siva reaches the ascetic.

cause: Siva is pleased with Matsara’s austerity.
details: Siva awakens Matsara and invites his wishes. Matsara regains strength on seeing him, bows, worships and offers a hymn. After Siva renews the offer, Matsara asks for universal fearlessness, devotion, immunity from death caused by the five-element and three-guna domain, health with lasting lordship, and sovereignty over the cosmic egg. Although the request astonishes the assembly, Siva grants all of it because of the fierce austerity.
outcome: The requested compound boon is granted.

cause: Matsara has received the boons.
details: Matsara returns home, making friends, his mother and wife glad, and enjoys pleasures. Madakara bears him two sons: the elder Sundarapriya and younger Visayapriya.
outcome: The narrator introduces Matsara’s sons.

cause: Demons gathered at his father-in-law’s house seek conquest with his boon-supported strength.
details: The assembled demons urge Matsara to conquer the gods. He says that he wants this too, but Earth restrains him because Indra is his father and gods deserve honor. The demons counter with their own account of Jalandhara, argue that gods are enemies of demons, and tell Matsara to leave Earth. He accepts this advice, which the narrator calls harmful, abandons Earth and stays with them.
outcome: Matsara abandons Earth’s counsel and resides with the demons; the campaign follows in1.25.

details: The sages ask Suta for a past example of the merit produced by hearing the Purana. He introduces a sage who could not speak.
outcome: A concrete hearing narrative begins.

details: Lomasa reaches Brahmaloka, bows to Brahma and sits with permission. He requests the Ganesa Purana that Brahma had narrated to Vyasa; Brahma invites him to listen carefully.
outcome: Brahma agrees to narrate.

cause: Brahma agrees to the request.
details: Brahma tells the Purana to Lomasa. The speech-impaired sage listens devotedly to the complete recitation. He subsequently speaks fluently, studies and recites the text for others.
outcome: The listener gains speech and becomes a reciter.

cause: The text presents this as the result of devotional hearing.
details: The sage enjoys desired pleasures and gains sons and grandsons. At life’s end he reaches Ganesa’s auspicious abode.
outcome: The bounded example reaches its final outcome.

cause: Saṃvaraṇa seeks a son.
details: The narrator describes Saṃvaraṇa as an Ikṣvāku-line king devoted to sacrifice, giving, study and protecting his subjects. Childless, he performs a putriya sacrifice complete with its prescribed elements, gifts and food distribution. He then hears Harivamsa and rewards the reader and Brahmins; neither brings a son.
outcome: His wish remains unfulfilled.

cause: The sage proficient in Ganesa Purana arrives at the king’s house.
details: Saṃvaraṇa asks the sage to stay, joyfully hears the Purana from him and rewards him with jewels, pearls, garments and golden ornaments. The king gains a son, becomes devoted to Ganesa, enjoys many pleasures and finally attains Ganesa’s highest state.
outcome: The king’s hearing episode concludes.

cause: His sister hears that her brother gained offspring by hearing the Purana.
details: The king’s unnamed sister summons the same sage and listens to the Purana. She gains a brave son, becomes devoted to Ganesa, has sons and grandsons and enjoys pleasures. At life’s end she reaches Ganesa’s own abode.
outcome: The sister’s hearing episode reaches its final outcome.

cause: Gods seek a son of Śiva to overcome Tāraka.
details: After Dākṣāyaṇī’s death, Śiva withdraws; her rebirth serves him. Gods oppressed by Tāraka seek a son of Śiva and send Kāma, recalling Viṣṇu’s earlier gifts. Kāma shoots Śiva, whose recovered composure leads him to burn Kāma with his third eye; Gaurī leaves for penance.
outcome: Kāma is burned; Gaurī begins penance.
temporal_relation: Includes creation-time retrospective speech (11.8–17) before return to Kāma mission.

cause: Citrakarmā acts on Kāma’s surviving ashes and teaches worship.
details: Citrakarmā shapes Kāma’s ashes into a boy; Rudra’s gaze animates him. Addressing him as son, Citrakarmā teaches Śatarudriya worship. Śiva accepts the boy’s requests for half his opponent’s strength and arrow-based neutralization of hostile weapons, additionally granting sixty thousand years of rule. Brahmā’s utterance supplies the name Bhaṇḍa.
outcome: Animated Bhaṇḍa obtains combat powers and a fixed royal term.

cause: Śukra organizes the new asura ruler’s accession.
details: Śukra crowns Bhaṇḍa; Maya rebuilds Śoṇitapura. Royal gifts include Vijaya bow, protective umbrella, disease-averting chowries and indestructible crown. Eight assistants and four wives are listed. The asuras maintain Vedic rites and Śiva worship during sixty thousand years.
outcome: Bhaṇḍa rules with assistants, wives, protections and religious observances.

cause: Viṣṇu observes growing asura strength; Nārada foresees danger after delusion ends.
details: Viṣṇu sends his deluding Māyā with Viśvācī’s companions; Bhaṇḍa neglects worship. Nārada urges Indra to worship Parāśakti. Śukra warns Bhaṇḍa; Śrutavarmā notes the expired reign, while Bhīmakarmā trusts his combat boon and urges disruption.
outcome: Indra worships Parāśakti; Bhaṇḍa chooses to disrupt worship despite warning about his royal term.
temporal_relation: Main progression after60k-year reign; ten-thousand-year delusion and later worship periods stated.

cause: Bhaṇḍa attacks divine worship and repeatedly fails against the wall.
details: Repeated attacks, including Vāyavya, fail against the regenerated divine wall. Indra’s gods offer their own flesh in a great sacrifice. Lalitā emerges with noose, goad, sugarcane bow and five arrows; her glance restores the mutilated gods.
outcome: Sacrificing gods receive Lalitā’s manifestation and bodily restoration.

cause: The restored gods surrender and Indra asks rescue.
details: The gods praise Lalitā’s cosmic identity; Indra requests rescue. She promises personally to defeat Bhaṇḍa and restore the worlds. Devout recitation of this hymn receives blessings of virtue, learning, longevity, health and family prosperity.
outcome: Lalitā promises victory over Bhaṇḍa and conditional hymn benefits.

cause: Brahmā considers coronation and a suitable divine spouse.
details: Gods and attendants arrive; Viśvakarmā builds a city at Brahmā’s command. Considering a suitable coronation and spouse, Brahmā sees Śiva assume a beautiful form and names him Kāmeśvara. Lalitā and Kāmeśvara mutually desire each other; Brahmā requests their joint enthronement.
outcome: Śiva manifests as Kāmeśvara; mutual attraction prepares marriage.

cause: Lalitā sets independence as her marriage condition.
details: Lalitā insists on independence and a compatible husband; her thrown garland selects Kāmeśvara. Brahmā calls Viṣṇu her brother; Viṣṇu performs the marriage. Gods provide weapons and regalia. Brahmā’s Kusumākara chariot resists weapons, travels freely and removes afflictions through its fragrance.
outcome: She selects Kāmeśvara and receives ceremonial gifts at marriage.

cause: Nārada recalls the purpose of her manifestation after imperial festivities.
details: After the procession, Lalitā fulfills the assembly’s desires by her glance; Brahmā names her Kāmākṣī and Kāmeśvarī. Following ten thousand years of imperial life, Nārada recalls Bhaṇḍa’s threat. Gods return to their homes while continuing service through partial manifestations.
outcome: Gods return home while continuing partial service; the campaign follows.

cause: Lalitā resolves to conquer Bhaṇḍa.
details: Lalitā’s campaign begins. Sampatkarī emerges from her goad and leads elephants on Kaṇakolāhala. Atitvaritavikrānti emerges from the noose, rides Aparājita and leads cavalry; her four hands hold noose, goad, cane and bridle. Daṇḍanāthā’s war preparation follows.
outcome: Elephant and cavalry divisions emerge and set out.

cause: Daṇḍanāthā and Mantriṇī marshal their forces.
details: Daṇḍanāthā rides Vajraghoṣa with boar-faced troops. The text gives her twelve names, including Vārāhī, then Śyāmalā’s names, including Mantriṇī. Dhanurveda emerges from Śyāmalā’s parrot and gives Citrajīva and inexhaustible quivers. Yantriṇī and Tantriṇī attend her.
outcome: Divine names, vehicles and Śyāmalā’s bow establish their campaign roles.

cause: Campaign preparations reach the sovereign chariot.
details: Lalitā proceeds on Śrīcakra, armed with goad, noose, sugarcane bow and five arrows, attended by Kāmeśvarī and other eternal powers. Hayagrīva supplies twenty-five epithets and benefits of their recitation.
outcome: Lalitā advances with armed eternal attendants.

cause: Agastya requests the chariot gods’ names and weapons.
details: Hayagrīva describes Lalitā’s Cakrarāja tiers, including Siddhis, eight mothers, Mudrās, successive yoginī groups and fifteen Nityās. Mantriṇī’s seven-tier Geyacakra houses allied powers, Bhairavas, protective deities and guardians; petitions reach Lalitā through Mantriṇī. Alternative maternal iconography is explicitly reported.
outcome: The narrator enumerates deployment and Mantriṇī’s access role.

cause: Hayagrīva extends the army account to Daṇḍanāthā’s chariot.
details: Kiricakra houses Daṇḍanāthā and supporting powers, including Jṛmbhiṇī, Mohinī, Stambhinī, Dhātunāthās, personified plough and pestle, guardians and vehicles. Surāsindhu’s prospective role is to refresh thirsty combatants. The witness calls this a five-step chariot but later mentions a sixth step.
outcome: Kiricakra powers and support roles are introduced.

cause: Portents and the approaching campaign force Bhaṇḍa to deliberate.
details: Omens disturb Śūnyaka. Bhaṇḍa’s younger brothers Viśukra and Viṣaṅga advise him: Viśukra derides female opponents, while Viṣaṅga urges investigation and recalls earlier divine victories. Bhaṇḍa rejects the warning, boasts of his forces and named sons, and orders Kuṭilākṣa to fortify the city and send an advance force.
outcome: He dismisses caution and orders fortification and attack.

cause: Bhaṇḍa sends an initial general while protecting his city.
details: Bhaṇḍa sends Durmada; Kuṭilākṣa deploys Tālajaṅgha, Tālabhuja, Tālagrīva and Tālaketu at city gates. Sampatkarī fights Durmada on Raṇakolāhala. After Durmada strikes a crown jewel, her arrows pierce his chest and kill him; survivors flee.
outcome: Sampatkarī kills Durmada and survivors flee.

cause: Durmada’s elder brother seeks revenge.
details: Kuraṇḍa, Durmada’s elder brother, seeks revenge. The cavalry goddess asks Sampatkarī to yield the fight, then binds his army with multiplying nooses. Kuraṇḍa cuts her bowstring; she kills him with her goad, whose Pūtanās consume his forces. Survivors retreat.
outcome: The cavalry goddess kills Kuraṇḍa after the noose/bowstring exchange.

cause: Bhaṇḍa escalates after the two brothers’ defeat.
details: Five generals deploy Sarpiṇī, whose destroyed snakes multiply while she survives. Lalitā’s palate-born Nakulī rides Garuḍa, creates mongooses from her teeth and dissolves Sarpiṇī with Gāruḍa. Enemy arrows rout her mongooses; Akṣīṇanākula renews the force. Nakulī kills Karaṅka and four colleagues. Śyāmalā makes her a satellite deity; she spares surviving messengers.
outcome: Nakulī defeats regenerative snake magic and the five generals; survivors are released.

cause: Bhaṇḍa sends seven previously victorious solar-boon holders.
details: Kīkasā’s seven sons attack with a Sun-granted gaze that burns and immobilizes seen enemies and weapons. Lalitā summons Tiraskaraṇikā, Daṇḍanāthā’s guard. From Tamolipta she uses Mohana arrows and Andha to blind them; lost sight ends immobilization. She kills all seven, and the Śaktis destroy their army.
outcome: Tiraskaraṇikā’s blinding restores the Śaktis’ weapons; the generals die.
temporal_relation: Includes Sun-boon flashback at24.59–66 during narrated battle.

cause: Narrator introduces the adversary before Agastya asks how he arose.
details: Before the origin account, Hayagrīva previews Bhaṇḍa’s domination: Viśukra emerges from his right shoulder, Viṣaṅga from his left; he also creates sister Dūminī. The three oppose gods, who flee their offices and families.
outcome: Next chapter supplies origin and boons.
temporal_relation: PREVIEW: later reign narrated before chapter11 origin.

cause: Repeated frontal defeats prompt a concealed attack on the queen.
details: After defeats, Bhaṇḍa orders Viṣaṅga and fifteen generals to attack Lalitā’s rear secretly, aiming to destroy the source of her powers. Dark equipment and silence conceal their approach. They reach Cakrarāja’s ninth tier and wound defenders with invisible Vipāṭas.
outcome: The chariot’s lower defensive tier is penetrated.

cause: Two-sided pressure and a hit on royal equipment alarm the Nityās.
details: Kuṭilākṣa prevents the vanguard returning while Viṣaṅga breaks Lalitā’s fan. Nityās obtain her permission to intervene. Vahnivāsinī and Jvālāmālinī illuminate the attackers; the Nityās descend with Prāṇakodaṇḍas and fight for three watches.
outcome: Light removes concealment; direct fighting becomes possible.

cause: Illumination and Nityā counterattack reverse the ambush.
details: The Nityās kill the invading generals. Kāmeśvarī breaks Viṣaṅga’s armour; he escapes near dawn, destined for Daṇḍanāthā’s later attack. The Nityās refuse to pursue a fleeing warrior. Lalitā’s glance heals their wounds.
outcome: Viṣaṅga survives; wounded defenders are restored.

cause: The first night exposes a defensive failure.
details: Daṇḍanāthā routs Kuṭilākṣa’s night force. She and Mantriṇī acknowledge inadequate rear protection and propose a guarded fire enclosure. Lalitā approves defence before offence. Jvālāmālinī becomes the enclosure; Stambhinī guards its opening, with the chariots and cavalry deliberately positioned.
outcome: A fortified camp closes the route for another ordinary ambush.

cause: Fortification provokes a major assault; Bālā hears the princes approaching.
details: Bhaṇḍa sends his sons with two hundred army divisions to capture Lalitā alive. Bālā, Lalitā’s daughter and perpetually nine-year-old martial prodigy, asks to fight as play despite her mother’s tenderness and concern.
outcome: Mother and daughter debate permission to fight.

cause: Bālā’s resolve changes Lalitā’s initial refusal.
details: Bālā persists; Lalitā embraces her, grants permission, armour and weapons, and a swan-drawn palanquin from her bow staff. Mantriṇī and Daṇḍanāthā reluctantly guard her. The single Bālā appears separately to each prince and fights with missiles and countermissiles.
outcome: Bālā enters with maternal equipment and protective escorts.

cause: Princes continue attacking after their army is destroyed.
details: Bālā’s Nārāyaṇa missile burns the princes’ army. Thirty crescent-tipped arrows sever thirty heads simultaneously. Mantriṇī and Daṇḍanāthā embrace her and report her success; Lalitā rejoices.
outcome: All thirty princes die; their father’s grief initiates the next countermeasure.

cause: Loss of princes turns mourning into strategic revenge.
details: Bhaṇḍa grieves his sons and threatens personal revenge; his advisers restrain him. He sends invisible Viśukra to operate Jayavighna. Viśukra inscribes eight tridents and eight presiding powers on a stone slab, consecrates it with mantra and sacrifice, and throws it over the fire wall.
outcome: The consecrated enemy yantra enters the camp.

cause: Yantra’s influence demoralizes the rank and file.
details: Jayavighna produces sleep, disengagement and rejection of the queen’s authority; the soldiers abandon weapons. Viśukra returns after midnight to exploit their apathy. Mantriṇī and Daṇḍanāthā remain unaffected and report the unexplained breakdown to Lalitā.
outcome: Unaffected commanders seek a remedy.

cause: Lalitā responds to commanders’ appeal.
details: Lalitā looks at Kāmeśvara and laughs; elephant-faced Gaṇanātha appears in her smile’s radiance, embraced by Siddhilakṣmī. He pulverizes Jayavighna with tusks, restoring readiness, then creates elephant-faced allies under six Vighnanāyakas.
outcome: Obstruction is removed and allied reinforcements emerge.

cause: Removal of the yantra permits the army to resume fighting.
details: Gaṇanātha’s forces destroy Viśukra’s troops. Viśukra sends Gajāsura, then flees as his strength declines. Mouse-mounted Gaṇeśvara kills Gajāsura and returns. Lalitā rewards him with precedence in worship before other deities.
outcome: Second night ends with victory and a ritual precedence boon.

cause: Viśukra’s prior defeat prompts a combined assault.
details: Bhaṇḍa sends both brothers with Dhūminī’s nephews, whom he has trained. Mantriṇī and Daṇḍanāthā leave a protective reserve. Duels pair Daṇḍanāthā with Viṣaṅga, Śyāmalā with Viśukra, and supporting commanders with nephews.
outcome: Third day opens with paired battles.

cause: Asura army weakens, prompting a mass incapacitation weapon.
details: Viśukra’s Tṛṣāstra incapacitates the Śaktis with thirst. Mantriṇī proposes the ocean on Daṇḍanāthā’s chariot; at command Surāsindhu showers restoring drink. Śyāmalā surrounds her army with arrows to exclude asuras from it. Recovered troops prepare to resume.
outcome: Countermeasure restores strength without aiding the opposing army.

cause: Restored armies resume duels and overwhelm the combined force.
details: Daṇḍanāthā rewards Surāsindhu with sacrificial use after mantra purification and benefits for worshippers. Battle resumes: the nephews die; Śyāmalā destroys Viśukra using Brahmaśiras. Daṇḍanāthā fights Viṣaṅga until midnight, hooks his head with her plough and kills him with an iron-club blow.
outcome: Both Bhaṇḍa brothers die before the fourth day.

cause: Kin losses drive Bhaṇḍa into the final campaign.
details: Grieving brothers and sons, Bhaṇḍa mobilizes his remaining commanders on Ābhila with Ghātaka sword. Lalitā undertakes the duel herself; Jvālāmālinī enlarges the camp exit. After the fourth morning’s army battle, Lalitā’s arrows multiply as they travel and strike.
outcome: Lalitā and Bhaṇḍa enter a sustained missile exchange.

cause: Each harmful missile receives a specifically named opposing remedy.
details: Bhaṇḍa deploys darkness, heresy, blindness, power-loss, death, memory-loss, fear, disease and lost longevity; Lalitā successively counters each. Acyuta, Ananta and Govinda emerge from her three-name missile, burn diseases and receive a continuing healing charge.
outcome: Nine disabling powers are neutralized.

cause: Regenerated adversaries overpower the Śaktis, who seek Lalitā’s protection.
details: Mahāsurāstra regenerates named asuras. Lalitā laughs; Durgā manifests with divine equipment and repeats the victories cited from Caṇḍikāsaptaśatī. Bhaṇḍa’s Mūkāstra meets Mahāvāgvādinī.
outcome: Durgā destroys the manifested asuras and returns to Lalitā.

cause: Bhaṇḍa escalates to regenerated cosmic adversaries.
details: Veda-thieves are repelled from Lalitā’s right thumb nail. Her index-nail tortoise supports drowned Śaktis and drinks the flood; middle-nail boar destroys Hiraṇyākṣas. Ring-finger man-lion protects Prahlāda against eyebrow-born Hiraṇyakaśipus. Little-finger Vāmanas bind Balīndras.
outcome: Successive finger manifestations defeat the generated threats.

cause: Further generated armies continue the missile contest.
details: Left-thumb Bhārgava Rāma kills Haihaya-generated Arjunas. Rāvaṇa emerges from Bhaṇḍa’s huṃkāra with Kumbhakarṇa and Meghanāda; left-index Kodaṇḍarāma and Lakṣmaṇa defeat them. Left-middle Tālāṅka defeats Dvivida’s monkeys; left-ring Viṣṇu’s Caturvyūha destroys Rājāsura kings.
outcome: Generated epic and royal opponents are destroyed by corresponding manifestations.

cause: All successive countermeasures neutralize Bhaṇḍa’s supporting powers.
details: Left-little-finger Kalki defeats Kali’s generated forces; the avatar leaders return to Vaikuṇṭha. Śāmbhava breaks Mahāmoha. Nārāyaṇa destroys the armies, Pāśupata the commanders, and Mahākāmeśvara kills Bhaṇḍa and burns Śūnyaka, including its women, children and stores. Lalitā brings exhausted troops back at sunset.
outcome: Bhaṇḍa and capital are destroyed; the fourth day closes.

cause: Victory permits restoration of those affected by Kāma’s destruction.
details: Lalitā’s healing gaze refreshes her army. Gods praise her cosmic forms, recall Kāma’s failed mission and present grief-stricken Rati, asking his revival to relieve her widowhood and enable Śiva’s marriage.
outcome: Rati’s condition elicits the goddess’s compassion.

cause: Compassion for Rati prompts restoration; Kāma requests employment.
details: Lalitā restores Kāma from her glance. Śyāmalā adorns Rati; sages renew their marriage. Kāma offers service. Lalitā grants effective arrows, multiplied Kāmas and immunity from Śiva’s burning, directs punishment of devotee-tormentors through illicit desire, and fulfilment for respectful worshippers.
outcome: Restored Kāma receives protection and a mission.

cause: The newly protected love deity executes Lalitā’s commission.
details: Kāma’s emanations spread; with Rati, Vasanta, moon and breeze he shoots Śiva, then Pārvatī. Mutual longing grows. Her father prescribes penance: winter immersion and summer fires under the sun. Śiva is pleased; formal marriage and residence at Kailāsa follow.
outcome: Śiva and Gaurī marry after her austerities.

cause: Marriage completes the divine rescue plan initiated in chapter11.
details: Śiva’s seed passes through Pārvatī, earth, fire, Kṛttikās and Gaṅgā to reeds; six-faced Mahāsena is born and nursed by Gaṅgā. His father trains him; he leads the gods, kills Tāraka and marries Indra’s daughter Devasenā. Kāma returns to serve Lalitā in Śrīpura.
outcome: Tāraka’s defeat closes the origin-to-restoration chain; Kāma returns to Lalitā.

cause: Question arising from Śrīpura’s mention at30.107.
details: Agastya asks what Śrīpura is; Hayagrīva recaps manifestation, marriage and Bhaṇḍa’s defeat. At Lalitā’s direction the triad commissions Viśvakarmā and Maya to construct sixteen residences. This starts a new city-description episode after the restored Kāma’s return.
outcome: Boundary confirmed: war/restoration narrative has ended; capital description begins.

cause: Sages request further sacred narratives.
details: At Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice the sages, having heard eighteen Purāṇas, ask Sūta for more. He selects Gaṇeśa Purāṇa among Upapurāṇas and says its teaching passed Brahmā→Vyāsa→Bhṛgu→Somakānta. Gaṇeśa is praised as Oṃ, cause of causes and ruler of creation, preservation, dissolution and cosmic operations; meritorious detached listeners desire hearing.
outcome: Sūta introduces the Somakānta account.

details: Somakānta rules Devanagara in Saurāṣṭra, learned in Veda and dharma, conqueror of kings, sacrificial donor. His retinue numbers10,000 elephants,20,000 horses,6,000 chariot fighters and uncounted infantry with fire-weapons, bows and double quivers. Ministers Rūpavān, Vidyādhīśa, Kṣemaṅkara, Jñānagamya and Subala serve and conquer territories. Sudharmā, his devoted charitable wife, bears Hemakaṇṭha, strong as10,000 elephants. Comparisons name Bṛhaspati, Dhanada, Earth, Ocean, Sun, Moon, Fire, Manobhava, Rati, Rambhā and Tilottamā.
outcome: Prosperous king and family established.

cause: Past karma ripens as disease.
details: Prior karma brings Somakānta suppurating leprosy, bleeding, worms and wasting. He recalls protecting subjects, defeating foes with arrows and worshipping Sadāśiva, questions the karmic cause and rejects his present kingship and appearance. He proposes forest retirement and Hemakaṇṭha’s coronation, then collapses. Ministers and women revive him with wiping, fanning, medicines and mantra procedures.
outcome: King recovers consciousness and hears responses.

cause: Retirement threatens separation.
details: Ministers propose Hemakaṇṭha rule while they accompany the king. Sudharmā says she will serve her husband in the forest and asks ministers to stay with her son; individuals must bear their own past acts. Hemakaṇṭha refuses life, wealth and kingship without his father. Somakānta rejoices at their affection but defines filial duty as obedience, ancestral offerings and rescue of ancestors; he orders his son to rule with ministers and seek leave for the parents’ departure.
outcome: Somakānta insists on his son’s accession.

cause: Father prepares son to govern.
details: Father and son sit in the royal council chamber. Somakānta prescribes rising before dawn, remembering guru and chosen deity, asking Earth pardon for stepping on her, then morning hymns to Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sun and Girijā. Hymns identify Gaṇeśa as giver of dharma, wealth, desire and liberation; Śiva as giver of boons to Nārāyaṇa and Indra, bearing trident, drum, serpents and tiger skin, destroyer of Manobhava and cities.
outcome: Morning worship instructions given.

details: Somakānta details earth selection and ritual cleanliness by class and life-stage, directional rules for excretion, repeated washing counts, tooth-cleaning with a tree-addressed request for strength, brilliance, cattle, intelligence, wealth and spiritual insight, then bathing, sandhyā, recitation, homa, study, libations, deity worship, vaiśvadeva, hospitality, meals with a Brahmin witness, Purāṇa hearing, giving and avoiding slander.
outcome: Daily purity and worship programme prescribed.

details: Advice turns to aid with property, life and speech, truthfulness, parents/gurus/cows, donations to vulnerable people, proportionate punishment after consulting śāstra or experts, distrust of proven enemies, sixfold policy, spies and messengers, restraint toward praise/blame, protection of returning suppliants, secrecy and conquest of six inner enemies. The king must preserve livelihoods, subjects, deities, groves and sacred sites, rescue Brahmins from debt and cows from mud, and respect servants, ministers, Brahmins and gods. Negative wording at25–27 and some policy phrases require collation; no definitive translation of those uncertain clauses is asserted.
outcome: Ethical and royal conduct taught, with textual uncertainties retained.

cause: Succession follows instruction.
details: Somakānta summons Kṣemaṅkara, Rūpavān and Vidyādhīśa, priests, kings and queens, friends, guild leaders and citizens for Hemakaṇṭha’s consecration. Gaṇeśa and chosen deity are worshipped; maternal rites, auspicious ancestral rite, feeding and mantra-consecration follow. He entrusts his son to the three ministers and demands they obey the son as they obeyed him.
outcome: Hemakaṇṭha is consecrated and entrusted to ministers.

cause: Coronation permits retirement.
details: After coronation Somakānta distributes jewels, cattle, animals, textiles including Kashmir cloth, wealth and villages by rank. He leaves; people abandon work to follow. At a cool reservoir after two gavyūtis he asks pardon for government errors, loyalty to his son and leave to retire, attributing disease and separation to his own past karma.
outcome: King requests followers return.

cause: Followers resist departure.
details: Grieving citizens propose accompanying him to a few pilgrimage sites and returning after recovery. He refuses. Hemakaṇṭha again rejects separation; father insists his teaching must be obeyed, citing Jāmadagnya killing his mother on paternal command, Rāma’s forest exile with younger brother, and Lakṣmaṇa abandoning Sītā in the forest. He promises to return if fate restores fortune; son, three ministers and citizens finally salute, circumambulate and turn home with the army.
outcome: Hemakaṇṭha obeys and returns toward city.

cause: Son makes final appeal to mother.
details: Hemakaṇṭha asks his mother to secure permission for him to accompany and serve both parents. Sudharmā answers that the distressed king will not alter his decision and her duty binds her to her husband; she orders son home. He salutes, circumambulates, returns to the decorated capital, dismisses companions with gifts and governs according to his father’s instruction, balancing joy and sorrow.
outcome: New king begins dutiful rule.

details: Sūta resumes after sages ask about the forest. Somakānta travels with Sudharmā, Subala and Jñānagamya, sharing food and hardship. They reach a forest lake, drink, bathe, perform daily rites and eat fruits. King sleeps on sand while wife massages his feet and two ministers fetch roots, fruits and lotus stalks.
outcome: Retired party pauses at lake.

cause: Lake meeting creates opportunity for aid.
details: Sudharmā sees a radiant boy and asks his parents, name and origin. He identifies himself as obedient Cyavana, son of Bhṛgu and Pulomā, fetching water. He asks why the beautiful woman serves a diseased man and whether the disease was known before marriage. She describes her husband’s former rule, later karmic decline, minister companions, frightening forest beings and reversal from luxury to hardship, and begs Cyavana to become their saving boat.
outcome: Cyavana hears plea and identifies family.

cause: Cyavana reports suffering.
details: Cyavana returns late with water, moved by the suffering. Bhṛgu asks why; son recounts the family’s plight, comparing the disease to Indra’s punishment by Gautama. Bhṛgu orders him to bring everyone. Ministers return with food just as Cyavana arrives with invitation. Sudharmā and companions follow him to the peaceful hermitage where natural enemies coexist and weather is mild and responsive to the sage’s will.
outcome: Bhṛgu invites the party into refuge.

cause: King surrenders after failed remedies.
details: Somakānta and companions bow to Bhṛgu. King praises the sage’s sight as purifying and explains that remedies fail despite dutiful worship; he seeks refuge and a remedy. Bhṛgu meditates, promises to explain prior-life sin and relieve distress, then provides oil massage, baths, six-taste food, adornment and soft bedding. They rest as if restored to royal comfort.
outcome: Bhṛgu reassures and hosts them.

details: Sages ask for the remedy and story continuation. Sūta warns that abandoning narration/hearing, mishandling a recited manuscript or withholding teacher-student exchange brings dumbness and deafness. Next morning Bhṛgu performs rites and begins the former-life account before the bathed king, wife and ministers.
outcome: Prior-life narration begins.

cause: Bhṛgu explains king’s earlier karma.
details: Bhṛgu says Somakānta was Kāmanda, late-born only son of wealthy Vaiśya Cidrūpa and charitable Sulocanā at Kolhāra near Vindhya. Parents doted on him and married him to devout Kuṭumbinī; seven sons and five daughters followed. Father died; mother burned with him and went to heaven. Kāmanda squandered inherited wealth with companions, rejected wife’s warning and sold the house; wife went with children to her father.
outcome: Family separates after squandered wealth.

cause: Expulsion follows public oppression.
details: Kāmanda becomes thief, adulterer, gambler, liar and violent oppressor. Citizens obtain royal leave to exile him. In forest he kills weak people and animals but flees stronger foes, gathers thieves and builds a large stone-and-wood house. His frightened father-in-law sends wife and children there; he lives amid family and robbers supported by killings.
outcome: Robber household established in forest.

cause: Robber captures lone traveller.
details: Kāmanda seizes solitary learned Brahmin Guṇavardhana. Victim pleads he is innocent and newly remarried after his first wife’s death for lawful household and ancestral obligations. Saving life would make Kāmanda a father to him; even robbers protect suppliants. Killing would bring a thousand kalpas of hell, while relatives enjoying the loot would not share his sin.
outcome: Guṇavardhana appeals for life; no literal father-son kinship established.

cause: Kāmanda refuses surrender appeal.
details: Kāmanda rejects the appeal, calls it wasted instruction, refuses release and beheads Guṇavardhana with a sharp sword. Bhṛgu declines to count innumerable killings. Old age and illness bring rejection by household, descendants and friends. Through one trusted Brahmin he summons forest sages and offers gifts; they refuse a fallen donor, describing sinful association, then leave to bathe clothed and recite purifying verses.
outcome: Killing is followed in old age by rejection of his proposed gifts.

cause: Rejected gifts provoke remorse and temple restoration.
details: Illness, family neglect and Brahmin rejection lead Kāmanda to remorse. Brahmins identify an ancient Gaṇeśa image in a ruined forest shrine; he spends his wealth rebuilding a four-gated, four-towered decorated temple with groves and reservoirs; wife, sons, friends and kin take the remaining portion of wealth (hṛtam, not a gift). After death Yama’s messengers torture and bring him before Yama and Citragupta. Offered good or evil fruits first, he chooses merit and is reborn as Saurāṣṭra’s king Somakānta, rewarded for temple construction. Bhṛgu explains this by compassion for a suppliant and austerity power.
outcome: Merit-first choice explains royal birth; evil fruits remain.

cause: King doubts prior-birth account.
details: Somakānta doubts Bhṛgu’s account. Multicoloured birds emerge from his body and tear flesh with beaks. He again surrenders, asks why violence occurs in the sage’s peaceful refuge and begs rescue. Bhṛgu identifies doubt as cause, promises that his huṃkāra will remove the birds, and utterance makes them vanish; king, wife and ministers rejoice.
outcome: Surrender and huṃkāra end bird attack.

cause: Sage prescribes hearing and consecrates cleansing water.
details: Bhṛgu prescribes Gaṇeśa Purāṇa hearing, recites108 names and consecrates water, sprinkling Somakānta. A small black-faced being exits king’s nostril and grows to seven palm-trees tall, breathing fire and foul blood/pus. It calls itself Pāpapuruṣa present in embodied beings, says mantra water expelled it and demands food and lodging, threatening to devour worlds and king. Bhṛgu orders it into a dry mango hollow to eat fallen leaves, threatening ashes for disobedience. Its touch burns the tree; fearing sage it dissolves into the ashes.
outcome: Embodied sin is expelled and confined in ashes.

cause: Tree-ash confinement requires accumulated hearing merit.
details: Bhṛgu directs daily deposition of Purāṇa-hearing merit in the tree’s ashes until mango regrows, when king will be sinless. King asks where text and reciter can be found. Sage names Brahmā→Vyāsa→himself transmission, offers recitation and commands bath and hearing resolve. Somakānta bathes at Bhṛgutīrtha; merely resolving to hear makes him disease-free, without blood, worms or wounds by sage’s grace. Seated with renewed radiance he requests the whole Purāṇa.
outcome: Physical disease resolves on vow; tree-regrowth and full hearing remain future.

details: Bhṛgu promises attentive hearing destroys seven births’ sins by Gaṇeśa’s grace, praises ineffable deity, reports Dakṣa heard from Mudgala after sacrifice destruction, restricts teaching to devoted Gaṇeśa worshippers and explains Vyāsa compiled eighteen Purāṇas and as many Upapurāṇas to preserve dharma in Kali.
outcome: Nested teaching is introduced; Somakānta continues listening.

cause: Vyāsa begins composition with pride and omits Gaṇeśa observance.
details: Bhṛgu narrates Vyāsa, son of Parāśara and a Nārāyaṇa portion, dividing the Veda and beginning Purāṇa composition proud of learning. Omitting opening Gaṇeśa praise/worship produces confusion and loss of recall in religious and ordinary affairs. He visits Brahmā in Satyaloka, honours gods and divine sages, receives a seat and asks why his knowledge has failed despite intended dharma instruction, seeking cause and remedy.
outcome: Confused composer seeks Brahmā’s diagnosis.

cause: Brahmā diagnoses neglect of Gaṇeśa.
details: Brahmā advises considered action without pride/envy, citing Garuḍa’s reduced status as vehicle, an Ambikeya’s son losing everything through envy and Rāma’s destruction of kṣatriyas. He identifies omitted Gaṇeśa remembrance as cause: deity removes devotees’ obstacles and creates others’, governs Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Sun, Fire, Varuṇa and Indra. He orders surrender to elephant-faced deity, whose favour grants wishes; without favour even a thousand years will not suffice. Vyāsa asks deity’s identity, form, known manifestations, works and earlier worshippers.
outcome: Vyāsa requests fuller divine history; arc continues.

details: Brahmā distinguishes the single-syllable and six-syllable Gaṇeśa mantras among seven crore Āgama mantras. Devoted practice is said to yield liberation while living, mastery of siddhis, knowledge, free movement and forms. He teaches bathing, clean garments, cloth/skin/kuśa seat, purification, life installation, internal/external letter placements, breath control, mantra-sandhyā, whole-body deity visualization, mental offerings and recitation until Gaṇeśa appears ready to grant.
outcome: Practice method and prospective efficacy explained.

cause: Vyāsa receives initiation.
details: On an auspicious day Brahmā teaches Vyāsa the one-syllable mantra, advising him to ask arriving Gaṇeśa to dwell steadily in his heart; divine knowledge of past/present/future and successful composition are promised. Vyāsa says instruction dispelled confusion and resolves practice. Brahmā prescribes solitude and prohibits transmission to hostile/unfit recipients; improper disclosure condemns teacher and ten earlier/ten later generations. Devotional recitation promises offspring, wealth, pure knowledge, enjoyment and final release. Recipient-quality word niranukrośe at25 requires review.
outcome: Vyāsa resolves practice; actual divine boon to Vyāsa not yet narrated.

cause: Vyāsa asks for demonstrated mantra success.
details: Vyāsa calls Brahmā his guru and asks who previously obtained success by this mantra. Brahmā praises the eager disciple and explains Oṃ-seeded and Oṃ-framed mantras, universal Gaṇeśa worship and the need to remember him for unobstructed activity; he begins an ancient example.
outcome: Brahmā starts cosmic retrospective.

details: At dissolution winds destroy mountains, twelve suns dry waters, great fire burns and Saṃvartaka clouds flood. Gaṇeśa remains subtler than atoms; after long darkness the sounded single syllable reappears, becomes manifest Gajānana with māyā, and produces three qualities and Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Hara. The three seek their progenitor and instructions, searching21 heavens, space and lower worlds, then fasting and reciting for1,000 divine years without sight.
outcome: Cosmic triad continues seeking deity after unsuccessful austerity.

cause: Failed search and radiance overwhelm seekers.
details: The three search forests, waters and mountains, rest by a lake and encounter unbearable radiance. Exhausted and blinded, they withdraw through the sky, blame themselves and fear. Compassionately deity shows a pleasing four-armed elephant form with sword, shield, bow and śakti, single tusk, red dress and jewelled crown; Airāvata is named in comparison. They bow, touch his feet and begin praise.
outcome: Compassionate visible form permits praise.

details: Vyāsa asks how the three praised him. Divine glance grants clear understanding; their hymn praises transcendent Gaṇeśa, guṇa-linked Brahmā/Viṣṇu/Rudra forms, moon and power/world forms, and protection through feet-directed mind. Gaṇeśa names it Stotrarāja and promises pure devoted morning and three-sandhyā reciters sons, prosperity, wishes and final identity with supreme Brahman.
outcome: Hymn receives name and conditional efficacy.

cause: Triad requests devotion and divine task.
details: Offered a boon, Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Hara request unwavering devotion and assignment of duties. Gaṇeśa affirms firm devotion and assigns creation to rajas-born Brahmā, protection to sattva-linked Viṣṇu and dissolution to tamas-born Hara; gifts include Veda/śāstra/Purāṇa and creation skill to Brahmā, free-form yogic capacity to Viṣṇu, one-/six-syllable mantras, Āgamas and destructive capacity to Hara. One knowledge-gift word26 is defective and remains unexpanded.
outcome: Devotion granted and differentiated capacities assigned.

cause: Brahmā needs a creation model.
details: Brahmā fears inability to create an unseen universe or obey correctly. Gaṇeśa gives divine sight and carries him inward by breath. He sees innumerable universes, each with its own divine and living worlds, including another Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Prajāpati, Śaṅkara, Sun, Wind and Varuṇa. Unable to find limit or escape he praises and surrenders; deity releases him, and Hari/Hara are also brought out and rest. Precise nose/ear-route syntax45–46 is pending collation.
outcome: Vision overwhelms him; surrender gains release.

cause: Pride follows divine gifts and cosmic vision.
details: Somakānta asks how Brahmā created after cosmic vision. Bhṛgu explains Brahmā’s pride in knowledge and power: thousands of grotesque obstacles surround, strike, bind, mock, praise and manipulate him until he abandons pride and faints. Remembering Gaṇeśa he pleads for grace; heavenly voice orders austerity and the obstacles vanish.
outcome: Humbling obstacles end when voice orders penance.

details: Without mantra or location Brahmā wanders through water, steadily meditating on jewelled red elephant-faced deity with serpentine sacred cord, belly serpent and forehead moon. A second heavenly voice repeats the instruction to see a banyan, again puzzling him.
outcome: Banyan instruction prepares dream initiation.

cause: Voice leads to instructional dream.
details: In a dream Brahmā finds the surviving banyan amid dissolution waters. On a leaf appears four-armed, single-tusked elephant-faced child with crown, earrings and red dress. Child sprinkles him with trunk water, sits on his lap, rebukes his ignorance and teaches one-syllable mantra: ten lakh recitations by puraścaraṇa will bring personal appearance and creative power. Waking joyful, Brahmā bathes, stands one-footed on lotus, restrains food/senses and practices1,000 divine years; fire from his mouth afflicts beings and steadfast devotion moves Gaṇeśa to appear.
outcome: Mantra and long austerity yield deity’s appearance.

cause: Successful austerity precedes personal boon dialogue.
details: Radiant axe/lotus-bearing Gaṇeśa overwhelms Brahmā’s sight and memory. He reassures Brahmā he is the dream initiator, adopts gentle form and offers boon. Brahmā requests firm devotion, creation ability, removal of obstacles, completion of tasks when remembered, pure knowledge and final stable liberation. Deity affirms, commands manifold creation, says remembrance destroys obstacles and explicitly grants devotion and knowledge.
outcome: Divine affirmation enables fearless creation.

cause: Granted ability supports worship and creative duty.
details: For worship, Brahmā’s thought brings required articles through Gaṇeśa’s favour. At dakṣiṇā two adorned maidens appear, later named Siddhi and Buddhi; he offers them, performs lamp offering, flowers, thousand-name praise and circumambulation. Gaṇeśa accepts both and disappears; Brahmā resumes broad creation by grace. This passage does not explicitly call the maidens biological daughters or narrate a marriage.
outcome: Accepted offering and accomplished creation close penance episode.

details: Somakānta asks the next creation account. Brahmā produces seven mental sons and asks creation help; they choose austerity and reach supreme Brahman. A second seven also refuse creation despite knowledge; Sanaka and others are mentioned. Brahmā creates Brahmins and Fire from mouth, other classes from arms/thighs/feet, Moon from heart, Sun from eyes, Wind and life from ears, space from navel, heaven from head, Earth from feet and directions from ears, then waters, mountains and plants.
outcome: Creation established before new opponent episode.

cause: Ear-born opponents threaten their former boon giver.
details: Madhu and Kaiṭabha emerge from sleeping Viṣṇu’s ears, insult gods/sages/scripture and threaten to eat Brahmā, shaking Earth and Śeṣa with roars. Knowing through Gaṇeśa’s grace that Viṣṇu will kill them, Brahmā praises eye-resident sleep-goddess, addressed as Pārvatī and as creation/protection/dissolution power. He requests awakening, knowledge for Viṣṇu and delusion of opponents, explaining they worshipped him in previous birth and received various boons making them unkillable by him; his conciliatory praise failed.
outcome: Brahmā requests divine awakening and counterstrategy.

cause: Awakening follows Brahmā’s appeal.
details: While Viṣṇu wakes opponents conquer heaven and Indra/Yama/Kubera residences; gods flee. Freed from Nidrā, Viṣṇu reassures gods, carries conch/discus/mace and blows Pāñcajanya. Afraid but eager to fight, opponents claim conquests of earth, lower worlds and21heavens and demand wrestling. Viṣṇu accepts, sets weapons aside and fights body-to-body for5,000 years without victory.
outcome: Long accepted wrestling fails to defeat opponents.

cause: Failed battle leads to changed form and music.
details: Viṣṇu takes a Gandharva form and plays vīṇā in forest, arresting listeners’ tasks. Hearing on Kailāsa, Śiva sends Nikumbha and Puṣpadanta to fetch musician; he honours him. Music pleases Śiva, Skanda, Gaṇeśvara, Pārvatī, gods and sages. Śiva embraces revealed Viṣṇu and offers wishes. Viṣṇu explains earwax-born foes, Brahmā’s appeal, awakening and failed wrestling, and asks a killing method.
outcome: Śiva offers aid; Viṣṇu asks opponent counterstrategy.

cause: Śiva diagnoses failure as omitted worship.
details: Śiva says Viṣṇu entered battle without Vināyaka worship, losing strength. He orders worship: Gaṇeśa will delude foes and subject them, and by Śiva’s favour Viṣṇu will kill them. Asked the method, he distinguishes one-/six-syllable forms, chooses six-syllable after siddhāri-cakra and ṛṇa/dhana calculations, and promises success through observance. Exact technical calculation procedure is not given in these verses.
outcome: Six-syllable initiation sends Viṣṇu to practice.

cause: Six-syllable practice implements Śiva’s advice.
details: Asked by Somakānta, Bhṛgu describes Viṣṇu’s six-syllable practice at future Siddhakṣetra: bāṇa-astra directional sealing, purification, life installation, internal/external letter placements, breathing, mudrās, mental and16offerings, then recitation. After100years Gaṇeśa appears and offers wishes, saying earlier worship would have assured victory. Viṣṇu praises cosmic deity and requests Madhu–Kaiṭabha’s death by himself, victory/fame over other foes and unfailing devotion. Deity affirms requests, strength, renown and freedom from obstacles, then vanishes.
outcome: Personal boon supports renewed battle.

cause: Received boon prompts installation and renewed challenge.
details: Viṣṇu builds a crystal temple with gold spire and four gates, installs Gaṇḍakī-stone image; gods/sages call it Siddhivināyaka and place Siddhakṣetra because he obtained success there. Returning to foes, he rejects their mocking diminishment with examples of small fire/lamp power; they attack his chest and wrestling resumes.
outcome: Renewed wrestling sets up conditional grant.

cause: Deluded opponents reverse boon proposal.
details: Viṣṇu praises opponents’ endurance and proposes giving a boon; māyā-deluded foes instead offer him boons, pleased with wrestling. He chooses that they become killable by him. Seeing water everywhere, they accept death from him, praise death with his remembrance as liberating and require a place not water-covered. He holds them on his thighs and cuts both heads with razor-edged discus; gods celebrate with flowers.
outcome: Conditional grant permits thigh-supported decapitation.

cause: Opponent defeat restores divine order.
details: Gandharvas dance and apsarases sing. Viṣṇu reports to Brahmā his Śiva initiation, Gaṇeśa boon and resulting victory; gods/sages praise Gaṇeśa and the triad and return home. Regular hearing of this greatness is promised freedom from fear and fulfilment. Verse printed14 between40 and42 is treated as41 by sequence and colophon total45, with transcription variant exposed.
outcome: Celebration, report and return close opponent arc.

cause: Childlessness drives forest departure.
details: Vyāsa requests more after Siddhakṣetra. Brahmā narrates Bhīma of Vidarbha’s Kauṇḍinya, a powerful donor supported by tributary kings and vast army. His devout wife Cāruhāsinī is childless; he deems all fortune futile without a son, appoints learned ministers Manorañjana and Sumantu to keep kingdom for his return or divide it if he never returns, gives gifts and leaves with wife. At one gavyūti he sends citizens and unwilling ministers home, assuring their protection.
outcome: King entrusts kingdom and seeks aid.

cause: Seeking son brings couple to sage.
details: Bhīma and wife find lake and peaceful hermitage of Viśvāmitra with studying disciples. Sage promises a virtuous famous son and asks identity. Bhīma recounts failed austerities, giving and vows, trusts blessing, and asks prior fault/remedy. Viśvāmitra diagnoses proud abandonment of ancestral Gaṇeśa worship: deity’s anger prevents offspring. He begins why Gaṇeśa became their family deity.
outcome: Ancestral exemplum begins before remedy.

cause: Ancestral family context explains present Bhīma.
details: Viśvāmitra recalls ancestor Vallabha, described as seventh earlier person from Bhīma. After long delay a son is born mute, deaf, hunchbacked and suppurating. Mother Kamalā laments childlessness would be better and wishes death. Vallabha comforts her through karma and proposes gems, mantra, medicines, penance, recitation, deity worship and pilgrimage; she bathes child and celebrates birth with Brahmin gifts.
outcome: Ill child retained and remedies begin.

cause: Long failed remedies lead to exile.
details: Vallabha consults and rewards priests, names child Dakṣa and undertakes remedies and12years of austerity for his health and offspring prosperity. Failing, he angrily drives mother and son out. Kamalā carries child, begs village to village and is robbed of clothes/jewels. At another settlement she places him in Śiva shrine while begging; breeze from a devoted Brahmin’s body restores divine form, sight, hearing and speech through Lambodara’s favour. Mother rejoices; citizens feed and clothe them, and child asks mother family details before answering an inquirer.
outcome: Devotee-body breeze unexpectedly restores child.

cause: Miraculous recovery motivates devoted austerity.
details: Dakṣa reports father Vallabha of Bhānunagara in Karṇāṭa and mother Kamalā; healing follows exile and bodily breeze. A compassionate Brahmin teaches both Gaṇeśa worship. Mother and son stand on one great toe, live on air, emaciate and recite eight-syllable deity-name/dative mantra framed by Oṃ. Gaṇeśa appears four-armed, single-tusked, with belly serpent, yellow silks and crown, then adopts Brahmin form and offers desired boon.
outcome: Deity personally appears and offers boon.

cause: Praise precedes unexpected refusal.
details: Dakṣa praises elephant and Brahmin manifestations as supreme cause, witness, cosmic deities/elements, time, knowledge, social forms and emotions. Gaṇeśa says he is pleased and eager to give yet will not grant, lest his devotee be angry: Mudgala, whose bodily breeze healed Dakṣa, will give all wishes and appear when remembered. God vanishes; Dakṣa laments, falls and searches.
outcome: Boon deferred to Mudgala; seeker grieves.

cause: Deferred boon drives search.
details: Distraught Dakṣa questions travellers and trees about Gaṇeśa, collapses and dreams a Brahmin saying Mudgala has given what he earlier requested. A passing Brahmin directs him to Mudgala’s refuge hermitage; he finds learned radiant yogi worshipping four-armed, three-eyed Gaṇeśa image with16offerings, prostrates and is asked identity and suffering.
outcome: Dream and directions bring seeker to Mudgala.

details: Dakṣa recounts Bhānunagara parentage, congenital disabilities, citizens’ rejection, father’s12year failure and expulsion, mother’s arrival at Kauṇḍinya and healing breeze from Mudgala. Comparing Ahalyā’s recovery by Raghunātha’s feet, he vows to preserve body only upon seeing healer. He says both practiced until Gaṇeśa appeared and Kamalā obtained desired wishes.
outcome: Healing and mother’s fulfilment recounted as Dakṣa’s speech.

cause: Dakṣa explains devotional vision and requested wishes.
details: Dakṣa recounts Brahmin manifestation, elephant form with axe, lotus, rosary and modakas, referral to Mudgala and disappearance. Remembering the offer after fainting, he says he asked enduring household wealth and firm devotion; heavenly voice answered given. He interprets Mudgala and Gaṇeśa as identical. This report differs in elaboration/order from chapter20, whose immediate boon refusal is retained separately.
outcome: Speech reports explicit wealth/devotion request and heavenly grant.

cause: Devotional meeting establishes initiation.
details: Mudgala praises Dakṣa’s devotion, saying his own1,000years’ austerity never produced such sight, and bows to the devotee. Both bow and embrace as guru-related friends. Mudgala teaches one-syllable mantra with recitation and meditation, orders daily practice and warns abandonment brings complete ruin; enduring devotion promises subjection of Indra’s guardians, enjoyment and final liberation.
outcome: Daily mantra practice with explicit abandonment consequence prescribed.

cause: Question about prior cause opens another past-life account.
details: Bhīma asks Viśvāmitra why healing and sight came to Dakṣa despite Mudgala’s long austerity, and who he was before. Sage narrates Vaiśya Kalyāṇa of Pallī in Sindhu, devout donor, and wife Indumatī, whose son Ballāla grows devoted. With other boys he bathes and installs a beautiful stone as Gaṇeśa, worships with dūrvā/leaves, meditation, name-recitation, song, dance, forest shelters, flowers, lamps and offerings, and recites Purāṇa/dharma teaching.
outcome: Children’s intense worship established.

cause: Parents complain about children’s absence.
details: Boys forget hunger/thirst; parents blame Ballāla for daily absence and wasting, threaten binding/beating and Kalyāṇa’s expulsion through town ruler. Angry father takes a large club, smashes worship shelter, scatters boys, beats unmoving Ballāla bloody, throws image away and binds son to tree with vine nooses. He taunts that god must feed/release him and threatens death if he returns home.
outcome: Devotee remains bound and injured after shrine destruction.

cause: Abuse evokes curse and complete surrender.
details: Ballāla laments apparent failure of obstacle-removing deity and invokes unchanging natural duties of Śeṣa, Sun, Moon and Fire. He curses shrine-destroying father to blindness, deafness, hunchback and muteness if his devotion is true, declares faith cannot be bound and surrenders life. Gaṇeśa appears as Brahmin; radiance loosens bonds and body becomes whole without wounds/blood, with pure knowledge.
outcome: Divine appearance releases and heals devotee.

cause: Restored devotee praises and requests continuing protection.
details: Ballāla praises deity as universal parent/cause; Gaṇeśa embraces him and confirms shrine destroyer’s hell and bodily curse including bleeding, followed by father expelling him with mother in next embodiment. Ballāla asks firm devotion and deity’s lasting protection at this site. Grant names Ballālavināyaka, affirms steadfast mind/devotion and promises wishes to Pallī pilgrims on Bhādrapada bright fourth. God vanishes; Ballāla installs image and builds temple with Brahmins. Hearing this account is said to remove sins and fulfil wishes.
outcome: Devotion, site manifestation and temple installation granted; family aftermath continues23.

cause: Father’s manifested curse alarms mother.
details: Bhīma asks Kalyāṇa’s fate. Viśvāmitra says Ballāla’s curse immediately produces bleeding wounds, foulness, muteness, blindness and deafness in Kalyāṇa. Indumatī initially laments apparently blameless devout husband, then hears son’s binding and goes with townspeople. Seeing Ballāla whole and worshipping restored shrine, she rebukes misleading reports; astonished people acknowledge devotion and mother embraces son joyfully.
outcome: Mother sees healed son and temple.

cause: Mother appeals to competing filial duty.
details: Indumatī asks son home to cure suffering father, defending paternal discipline and filial obedience, feeding/protection and remedial medicines/mantra/prayer. Ballāla answers Gaṇeśa is universal mother/father, all kinship incidental and karmic fruits deserved; he surrendered life and received life/knowledge. Seeing fallen shrine-destroyer is harmful; mother should release attachment and serve husband. She begs curse relief through compassion.
outcome: Immediate healing refused; mother seeks relief terms.

cause: Mother begs relief rather than disputing curse.
details: Ballāla predicts Kalyāṇa becomes kṣatriya Vallabha, Indumatī becomes Kamalā and the afflicted man becomes her son Dakṣa. Vallabha’s12years fail; mother/son are exiled, then Gaṇeśa-devoted Brahmin touch heals son and deity vision grants divine form. This is named curse-relief cause; mother leaves with mixed sorrow/hope.
