Reflection gives fivefoldness; māyā differentiates Brahmā/Viṣṇu/Śiva as rajas/sattva/tamas, Sun as their ahaṃkāra and Śakti as delusion to accomplish three guṇas. He is here an aṃśa Vakratunda, Bindu-Brahman expressing distinction, with fourth Guṇapa/Buddhi right and five-deity play/Siddhi left. Devotees’ crooked obstacles are destroyed with trunk, explaining Vakratunda name.

Gaṇeśa explains Bindu-form supports gods’ acts/play; forgetting him brings māyā-delusion, so constant inward remembrance and first worship in divine/ancestral rites bring siddhi. He vanishes. Śiva tells Pārvatī this is his own heart meditation, that Brahmā creates, Viṣṇu preserves through manifestations at Gaṇeśa’s order, he destroys, she gives delight and Sun drives actions by time. Her Himācala-daughter birth caused forgotten knowledge; she must recover it and see heart Gaṇeśa as Mahāmāyā.

Śiva lists eight Gaṇarāja avatāras and Brahman correspondences: Vakratunda tvam; Ekadanta tat; Mahodara asi; Gajānana Sāṃkhya; Lambodara Brahman in Śakti; Vikaṭa sat/Sun; Vighnarāja sama/Viṣṇu; Dhūmravarṇa unmanifest neti/Śambhu. They are kalā forms governing eight Brahmans, supported by self-experienced Brahman; ayoga has no play, Svānanda does; full yoga transcends both. Śiva calls Gaṇeśa family deity, daily worships Cintāmaṇi/Vināyaka as light of five mental activities and shows jeweled elephant-faced household image and secluded meditation place to astonished Pārvatī.

Pārvatī asks how universal deluding Śakti became wife of partial/tamasic Śiva. He recounts seeing her power in five-deity rivalry; after Gaṇeśa instruction he propitiated her100 years. She appeared, invited boon, accepted hymn and request to be his wife, granted and vanished. Her left limb emitted Lakṣmī beloved of Nārāyaṇa, right Sāvitrī beloved of Brahmā, heart Saṃjñā wife of Sun. Śiva urges recovered Gaṇeśa yoga; Pārvatī privately practices, gains peace quickly through former impressions and returns to him. Mudgala tells Dakṣa wholehearted Gaṇeśa worship will remove obstacles/grief and make him honored yoga lord.

Śaunaka asks further Gaṇeśa accounts. Sūta resumes Dakṣa asking Mudgala why Brahman-formed Gaṇeśa incarnates and for the eight forms’ stories. Dakṣa praises sages who purify by sight, touch and speech. Mudgala praises patient, equal-minded and helpful questioners, contrasts sinners/nāstikas/dāmbhikas lacking desire for sacred narrative, and first offers his own earlier experience before the avatāra accounts.

Mudgala recounts śiloñcha gleaning and Dvādaśī fast-breaking after a fortnight, gathering a droṇa of food and performing five yajñas. Gods fear his tapas seeks their Indra/Brahmā/Viṣṇu/Śiva offices and send angry Durvāsas to test him. At fast-breaking the sage arrives naked, like a madman, asks alms and is not recognized. Mudgala gives all food; Durvāsas eats the droṇa, smears leftovers on his body and leaves. Mudgala rejoices in feeding the guest and continues fasting. The same guest consumes all food at six fast-breakings; after three months of fasting Mudgala remains unmoved, attributed to prior merit.

Pleased with pure-hearted tapas, Durvāsas reveals his yoga form and declares Mudgala pure, entitled to enjoy the conquered, imperishable heavenly worlds; he returns to his own hermitage. At once a heavenly vimāna arrives. Its ornamented messenger descends and receives Mudgala’s hospitality, says Indra with Bṛhaspati has sent him and awaits Mudgala, and invites him aboard to heavenly enjoyments.

Before accepting, Mudgala asks heavenly virtues and defects. The messenger distinguishes earthly karma-ground from heavenly enjoyment-ground: desired pleasures, youth, no fatigue/sweat/heat/cold, apsaras and desired-form movement, with enjoyment proportionate to prior karma. He admits three defects: no fresh karmic fruit there and worry about expiry; familiar gods/friends expel one without affection when merit is consumed, creating fear of falling; and envy/heart-torment on seeing those with greater merit enjoying more. Despite those defects he again invites Mudgala.

Mudgala asks for a defect-free world. Messenger says desireless karma gains Brahmaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Śiva/Solar/Śakti worlds, yet they too have defects; Brahman-state alone is faultless and attained on earth, the karma-ground, with dharma/artha/kāma/mokṣa. Mudgala rejects heaven’s heart-torment and fall, choosing Brahman. Messenger calls him unfortunate, ignorant and foolish for refusing what tapas/yajña/dāna earns. Mudgala answers bodily heaven cannot liberate a body-bound person; asks him to convey salutation and refusal to Indra with Bṛhaspati, bows, enters his fire-hall. Messenger returns as he came.

Considering the diverse Vedic descriptions of Brahman and uncertain practice, Mudgala decides to approach Aṅgiras, expert in word-Brahman and highest Brahman, his lineage’s root ancestor. He enters the peaceful hermitage: no heat/cold, anger/desire/envy, drought/excess rain, premature death, planetary harm or rākṣasa fear; Vedic pupils and agnihotras, flowering trees, bird-filled lakes and normally hostile animals coexist without enmity. Aṅgiras sits radiant on kuśa with yogins, siddhas, sages and pupils learning Brahmavidyā. Mudgala bows and identifies himself as of Aṅgiras’s gotra.

Aṅgiras addresses Mudgala affectionately as vatsa/tāta/suta, praises his tapas and lineage honor, seats him close, and later asks his purpose. Mudgala asks the sure path to defect-free Brahman, avoiding bodily pleasures. Aṅgiras praises the future Purāṇa teacher and mantra-maker, says Vedas offer diverse Brahman descriptions successively for attainment, and begins the explanation. Affectionate son address is not treated as evidence of an immediate biological father.

Aṅgiras maps anna/prāṇa/manas/vijñāna/ānanda Brahman to their kośas; caitanya to mahākāraṇa, bindu to knowledge-body, cit to so’ham, bodha to self-utthāna, Sāṃkhya to videha, karma/jñāna to their natures, sama to delight, avyakta/sahaja to neti, Śakti to asat, Sun to self, Viṣṇu to both, Śiva to nirmoha, Svānanda to saṃyoga and nirvṛtti to ayoga. All descriptions are true in their settings, but qualifications such as self/cit delimit them. Brahman as Brahman is gained through yoga; karma/jñāna is churned toward it. Brahmaṇaspati is Brahman of Brahmans; external/internal groups, such as kinds of food, are gaṇas; Gaṇeśa is their lord. His avatāra bodies are designated knowledge etc. Brahmans; worship him for Brahman-state.

Mudgala requests avatāra greatness to worship successively for Brahman-state. Aṅgiras says Gaṇeśa’s avatāras are infinite, beyond his telling even in hundreds of years, then lists eight principal forms: Vakratunda/deha-Brahman/Matṣara/lion; Ekadanta/dehī-Brahman/Mada/mouse; Mahodara/jñāna-Brahman/Moha/mouse; Gajānana/Sāṃkhya siddhi/Loma (digital spelling)/mouse; Lambodara/Śakti-Brahman/Krodha/mouse; Vikaṭa/Solar-Brahman/Kāma/peacock; Vighnarāja/Viṣṇu-Brahman/Mamatā/Śeṣa; Dhūmravarṇa/Śiva-nature/Abhimāna/mouse. They give their respective Brahmans by worship. Destroyer/enemy words are attributed list-descriptions, not newly read battles or death outcomes.

Aṅgiras says the eight obstacle-removing forms merge in Svānanda worship, māyā also merges, and saṃyoga gives silence-samādhi. Ayoga Gaṇarāja worship ends māyā-distinction and gives supreme nirvṛtti. Yoga Gaṇeśa/Brahmaṇaspati is the peace of all forms of peace, with no higher Brahman; he urges wholehearted worship. These are doctrinal instructions, not claims of a new bodily battle.

Aṅgiras recounts complete Gaṇeśa tapas and a desired boon granted through pleased devotion: his lineage will have Gaṇeśa devotees, especially Mudgala, an unmatched past/future sovereign devotee. Beings will be uplifted by Mudgala’s bow, touch, speech, sight and wind-contact. After granting, Gaṇeśa vanished. Aṅgiras identifies the present Mudgala as this ornament of his lineage. Exact initial requested words are not separately quoted in this recollection.

Aṅgiras predicts Mudgala’s great Gaṇapatya yoga, ritually teaches the one-syllable great mantra and sends him to a forest for Gaṇeśa’s vision. Mudgala bows, leaves and performs complete exclusive tapas by that mantra’s full procedure. After1000 divine years Gaṇeśa appears: mouse-mounted, four arms, Siddhi/Buddhi, Pramoda/Āmoda entourage, elephant face, large belly, one tusk, three eyes, four weapons, Cintāmaṇi jewel at heart. Pleased by the one-syllable rite he offers a desired boon. Mudgala worships/prostrates, weeps with joy, says birth, age, knowledge, tapas, tīrthas and lineage are fulfilled by sight and even earth/trees/animals fortunate, then begins a hymn.

Śaunaka asks how Mudgala hymned Gaṇeśa; Sūta repeats it. Mudgala admits the Vedas, Brahmā and yogins cannot adequately hymn him, but Gaṇeśa’s sight/grace gives the power to praise. He salutes the supreme beyond Vedas, māyā-maker, deluder of māyā-makers, without beginning/middle/end, praised by Purāṇas and Śiva/gods.

Mudgala hymns Gaṇeśa through earth/water/light/wind, waking-gross/rajas, dreaming-subtle, causal-sleep/equanimity, caitanya/Guṇeśa/nāda/time, bindu/Vakra/deha and cit/so’ham/dehī, Ekadanta enemy of Mada, knowledge/Sāṃkhya, self-experienced silence-samādhi, Śakti/asat, Sun/sat/immortality, Viṣṇu/sama, Śambhu/neti/Dhūmravarṇa, union of four, karma/jñāna/sama/sahaja, Heramba, ayoga/nirvṛtti/yoga-peace/Jyeṣṭharāja, Brahmā creation/rajas, Viṣṇu preservation/sattva, destruction/tamas/Kailāsa/Lambodara, Sun/time/action, Śakti/delusion, Moon/nourishment/nectar/stars, Kāma/Kāmāri, praised by Hari/Indra, Śuka sages and Jaleśa/Indra/Śeṣa. Paired qualified and unqualified salutations remain hymn theology, not literal mutually contradictory incarnational biographies.

The hymn salutes Gaṇeśa as Kāśyapa, Kāpila, Vareṇya’s son, Pārāśara, Śambhu’s son, Pārśva’s child and Mādhava’s woman’s son, then universal mother/father/son/self. These are source-listed hymn designations; no birth episode or exclusive biological genealogy is narrated here. Exact Kāśyapa/Kāpila/Pārāśara contextual identities are not merged with remembered narratives.

Hymn describes noose, tusk and sṛṇi/goad, grants sons/grandsons/kingdom, enjoyment/liberation, infinite powers and names Mayūreśa/Yogeśa/Māyeśa; supports gods and all selves. It maps deha to tvam, trunk to tat, united body to asi, with Siddhi/māyā left and Buddhi right, and a neither-male-nor-female asi nature. These are explicit hymn correspondences rather than a separately narrated battle equipment change.

Hymn says hearing the three-syllable Gaṇeśa name gives joy, and those uttering it once have no birth/death. Worshippers become Brahman and give Brahman by contact, honored by Indra/gods as Gaṇeśa-formed. These are hymn efficacy claims, not independently narrated outcomes.

After the hymn Mudgala goes silent, falls prostrate and holds Gaṇeśa’s feet. Gaṇeśa raises and embraces him, names it Stotrottama, and grants its praising user enjoyment/liberation, firm devotion, freedom from distress/disease, progeny, wealth and grain. Reading21 times for21 days ends māraṇa/uccāṭana etc.; prison afflictions also end and wished ends are attained. He asks Mudgala to request boons, saying none equals his understanding/devotion and he is always under Mudgala’s control.

Mudgala bows joyfully and asks why Gaṇeśa tempts him: he desires nothing, but at the deity’s insistence asks complete firm uninterrupted Gaṇeśa devotion everywhere. Gaṇeśa marvels he asks devotion alone, grants complete unwavering devotion and incomparable fortune. He says devotion has nine forms bringing rasa in mind, with no tenth: śravaṇa,kīrtana,smaraṇa,pādasevana,arcana,vandana,dāsya,sakhya,dehanivedana; he explains their signs for others to attain devotion.

Śravaṇa hears Gaṇeśa qualities, reflects, acts accordingly and experiences exclusive joy until other hearing gives no pleasure; then he abides in the ears. Kīrtana exclusively delights in singing his qualities, not other praise; then he abides on the tongue-tip. Smaraṇa does not forget his duties and attends timely vows/worship; then he abides in memory to enjoy devotion.

Pādasevana knows his feet true and other things false, tirelessly serves them and is idle toward other pursuits; then he abides steadily in the tireless body. Arcana performs his acts with all principal/accessory parts while allowing other acts to be as they are; he abides in this completeness. Vandana considers Vedic teaching that none equals him, holds his superiority and bows most highly; he abides in that highestness and removes highestness elsewhere. Digital23 reads vadanajā, retained as an anomaly;7 explicitly enumerates vandana and22/24 supply the bow/superiority description.

Dāsya follows scriptural Gaṇeśa worship, takes Gaṇapatya character/identity and exclusive devotion; he abides in that nature. Sakhya shares all as friends without outer/inner secret or hypocrisy, considers omniscient Gaṇeśa knows whatever is held in mind anywhere and worships exclusively with reverence/fear; he abides in friendship and is charmed by acts. Nivedana leaves five mental grounds and ego, offers self with the conviction I am Gaṇeśa; he abides in ego-free devotion without separation.

One whose ninefold devotion has such rasa that the mind cannot bear a moment without it is complete devotee. Gaṇeśa says he stays there always, cannot abandon even a moment because bound by devotion, protects always through ninefold mind and is bound in the devotee’s heart; nothing pleases him equally.

All nine forms may coexist but the most abundant rasa determines the leading form. Gaṇeśa lists sovereign exemplars: Kārttikeya/hearing, Sun/chant, Rāmacandra/remembrance, Pārvatī/foot-service, Mahāviṣṇu/arcana, Śaṅkara/vandana, Rāma son of Jamadagni/dāsya, four-faced Brahmā/friendship, Śuka Vaiyāsaki/self-offering. They worship without obstacles and are Brahman-formed. Distinct Rāmacandra and Jamadagni’s Rāma are preserved; patronymic Vaiyāsaki is source kinship designation, not a narrated birth mechanism.

Gaṇeśa makes Mudgala king over these devotees, preeminent in all nine forms, unmatched past/present/future and in direct control of him. Bodily-wind contact and sight etc. purify beings and give Brahman understanding. He disappears; from then Mudgala is honored by all. Whoever faithfully hears/reads Mudgala’s account or tells it to faithful listeners attains all aims, worldly pleasures then Brahman, and sovereign Vighneśa-devotee status.

Pārvatī asks her father who practiced the vow, who taught whom and what results followed. She praises the questioner, speaker and listener of Gaṇeśa stories as gaining piety and a fruitful life, birth, knowledge and action. Himavat announces an ancient history: at Kailāsa, Skanda bows and praises his father Śiva, who sits among gods, Gandharvas and sages, then prepares to question him.
outcome: Himavat opens an embedded Śiva–Skanda teaching.

details: Skanda asks for a vow through which Varada’s favour places siddhis at hand. Śiva calls it Vināyaka’s favourite, yielding the four goals, increasing sons and grandsons, quickly subduing a king, prince or minister, removing great and minor sins amassed over births and making its practitioner a vessel of siddhis. Verse 14 expressly praises attainment without yajña, dāna, japa or homa; the subsequent teaching nevertheless prescribes japa, homa and gifts. Skanda asks its month, procedure and previous practitioners.
outcome: Vow benefits and the no-ritual praise are stated; Skanda requests the procedure.

details: On Nabhas bright fourth, bathe and visit the guru. Honour him with foot-water, drinking water, clothing and ornaments, then begin with his permission. Address him as Śrī Gaṇeśa and request the wish-yielding vow. After instruction, go with him to the Gaṅgā bank, a tank or a deity-made pond; bathe with white mustard, sesame paste and dhātrī, finish daily rites and return home. Worship from a clean seat by the guru’s method. Make an earthen image on Śrāvaṇa fourth and worship daily until Bhādra fourth, observing brahmacarya with fasting, one-meal, night-meal or unasked-food alternatives.
outcome: Guru permission and instruction, month limits and observance options are prescribed.

details: The teacher prescribes a caturthakāla havisyānna meal and the printed akṣaraṃ madhuraṃ bhuñjan food clause; their exact interval and food meanings remain unresolved. Mantra classes include six letters, the printed dvi-catur expression, one, ten and twelve letters. Daily niyuta or ayuta japa, a half or further-half expression and one-tenth homa accompany unwearied day-and-night Gaṇeśa meditation. A fourth-DAY or alkali-free interpretation is not supplied without collation.
outcome: Raw food and numerical terms are retained; precise meanings remain open.

details: On Proṣṭhapada fourth, make a gold image of one pala or the stated successive half alternatives, choosing a peacock OR mouse mount. Prepare a pavilion and grain mound, a gold/silver/copper kalaśa and plate, a cloth pair, five leaves and five gems. Worship the seat, place the image and invoke through root, Vedic or previously stated mantras. Offer seating and waters, jewels, pañcāmṛta and fragrant baths, red clothes and sacred thread, ornaments, scents, rice, incense, lamps and food including vaṭaka, apūpa, laḍḍū, rice and pāyasa. Hand-water, fruit, betel, gold fee, parasol, fan, fly-whisk, ārati, mantra-flowers, hymns and thousand-name praise precede Brahmin honour.
outcome: Gold amount, alternative image mounts and the offering sequence are specified.

details: Keep a night vigil with song and dance. After morning bathing and daily rites, worship again and perform homa with varied liquids. Honour the ācārya/guru with cows, land, sesame and gold; give ample fees to other Brahmins. Feed 108 Brahmins, more if able, or 21; give food and pāyasa to poor, blind and needy people, offer fees and receive blessings. Eat silently with friends and kin. Śiva concludes that the taught Varada vow gives enjoyment, liberation and all desired fruits.
outcome: The procedure ends before the Kardama exemplum; its earlier discrepancy remains open.

details: Śiva tells Skanda of righteous king Kardama, who rules to the ocean limits and has gods attending his court. When Bhṛgu visits, the king rises, honours him like a guru, seats and feeds him. Kardama asks his former-birth identity and the merit behind his unmatched, untroubled kingdom, divine honour, Kubera-like wealth and desired objects appearing at home. He wants to repeat that meritorious practice.
outcome: Kardama asks which past practice caused his kingship and how to repeat it.

cause: Failed livelihood and household rebukes drive the former self into the forest.
details: Bhṛgu uses focused contemplation to recount Kardama’s earlier life as a poor, pure kṣatriya. His work does not support the household, and harsh words from his wife and children drive him into the forest without consulting them. He finds Saubhari teaching distress-removing knowledge to disciples among sages, bows, and is welcomed and seated. He asks relief from the verbal wounds of family and friends, heat, cold, hunger and thirst, while admitting he has not become detached from his harsh loved ones.
outcome: Kardama’s former self asks Saubhari for relief; relatives remain unnamed.

details: Compassionate Saubhari considers a remedy and recommends the Varada Gaṇeśa vow, which removes distress and sin and gives the four goals and unsurpassed siddhi. He cites earlier practice by Brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and brahmarṣis. The kṣatriya asks Gaṇeśa’s identity, form, nature, acts and origin. Saubhari calls him eternal, stainless, sorrowless knowledge-Brahman, without beginning, middle or end, boundless and all-pervading, the source of Oṃ, Vedas and the world.
outcome: Saubhari provides the remedy and Gaṇeśa’s doctrinal identity.

details: Saubhari cites Brahmā’s full hundred years of arduous tapas for creation. Brahmā worships the pleased deity with varied services, divine gems and fruits, and gives the two mentally created maidens Siddhi and Buddhi. Gaṇeśa grants the one-syllable vidyā; the booned Brahmā then creates the world. Viṣṇu previously pleased the deity with the six-letter mantra, made an image and practiced the stated vow and rules without defect for one year. He received a boon and preserved the world. Saubhari urges the kṣatriya to worship this universal cause and leave distress.
outcome: Nested divine precedents supply exact austerities, mental-maiden gift and mantra/role grants.

cause: The former self performs Saubhari’s prescribed vow.
details: The kṣatriya asks the time and procedure, promising practice for relief. Saubhari prescribes Śrāvaṇa’s non-dark fourth through Bhādra fourth, daily sixteen-service worship of an earthen image and Brahmin feeding, promising all wishes. Bhṛgu says Kardama’s former self performs it at Saubhari’s hermitage. At completion, Gaṇeśa’s favour transforms his home into a divine household with servants, cattle and Vedic sound; his adorned wife and children await him. After leaving the teacher he does not recognize the grand house and searches for his former home, until his wife’s messengers bring him in. He recognizes Varada’s power. Bhṛgu attributes his present kingship to the vow.
outcome: The past vow transforms his household and is said to cause later kingship.

details: Kardama joyfully repeats Bhṛgu’s prescribed practice, gains knowledge and dispassion, enjoys desired pleasures, places his sons in his office and reaches Gaṇeśa’s abode without return. Śiva urges Skanda to practice and cites Damayantī, Nala, Candraṅgada, gods, asuras, Gandharvas, sages and people as previous practitioners who gained wishes and a divine destination. Himavat closes his embedded history, promises Pārvatī that the vow will obtain Śiva, and explicitly commands her not to publicize it.
outcome: Kardama’s succession and no-return destination close his account; Himavat adds a prospective promise and secrecy command.

details: Pārvatī asks why Nala performed the vow. Himavat describes Niṣadha’s king as Veda-knowing, brave, generous, wealthy and pure, skilled with chariot, sword, arrows, bow, quiver and armour, and able to travel the three worlds. His innumerable cavalry, elephants, chariots, bowmen and weapon/fire-weapon fighters frighten Indra and direction-lords. His wife Damayantī is beautiful, virtuous and adorned; Brahmā fashioned her from selected essence and gave her the beauty of women in the three worlds. Minister Padmahasta is valiant, intelligent like Bṛhaspati, skilled in policy like Aṅgiras.
outcome: The king, wife, minister and capacities are introduced; comparison sages are not teachers.

details: Padmahasta is compared to Meru in height and the ocean in depth. A court with Apsaras dancers, praisers and brahmarṣis receives Gautama. Nala honours and seats him, calling his own birth, kingship, parents, lineage and life fruitful through the visit. Gautama says he wanted to see the king’s wealth, reports praise by Brahmā, Indra, Hari and Śiva, then asks leave. Nala pleads that he stay to remove uncertainty; the sage agrees. The king asks which merit or tapas produced his extraordinary wealth and who he was in a former birth.
outcome: Nala asks Gautama to explain the merit behind his wealth.

cause: Poverty and rebukes prompt departure into the forest.
details: Gautama says Nala was formerly a poor, pure, knowledgeable kṣatriya in Pippala city beyond Gauṇḍadeśa. Harsh words from his wife, children and friends lead him into the forest at night without consulting them. Wandering among woods, animals and lakes, he finds Kaushika’s hermitage resounding with Vedic recitation and bows. The compassionate sage raises him and blesses him with Gaṇeśa’s auspiciousness. The joyful former self asks for a method granting wishes, ending poverty, and giving enjoyment and liberation. The printed numbering repeats 25; the body is uninterrupted.
outcome: Nala’s former self seeks a remedy from Kaushika; duplicate verse numbering leaves no body gap.

details: Kaushika teaches a month-long Gaṇeśa vow: make a pleasing earthen image, perform the previously stated procedure and daily worship, and hear the story, thereby gaining success. The kṣatriya first asks Gaṇeśa’s identity so he can practice with knowledge. Kaushika describes the ineffable Brahman whose differentiated forms appear in the world, the world’s creator, father, mother and teacher, meditated on by Brahmā, Indra, Śiva and Viṣṇu.
outcome: Guru instruction and deity knowledge precede the vow.

cause: The month-long vow is performed with continuing Gaṇeśa remembrance.
details: With Kaushika’s permission the former self returns home and begins the bright Śrāvaṇa-fourth vow, making the taught image. He meditates on Gaṇeśa while standing, speaking, silent, moving, sleeping and eating. The vow gives success and wealth of elephants, chariots, horses, cattle and servants. He donates for divine pleasure and builds a costly Gaṇeśa temple, enjoys pleasures, then dies and is born as Nala in Niṣadha. Gautama attributes Nala’s steady wealth and three-world honour to this and asks leave.
outcome: Actual wealth, donations, temple building, death and Nala’s rebirth are narrated.

details: After Gautama leaves, Nala trusts his account, makes a fine image, practices the vow, hears Gaṇeśa’s story and worships daily with devotion, obtaining all wishes. Himavat concludes that this is Nala’s practice after Gautama’s instruction about his former-birth vow, whose full glory cannot be narrated.
outcome: Nala’s current-life repeated vow fulfils his wishes and closes the account.

details: Himavat tells Pārvatī of the vow practiced by Candraṅgada and his wife Indumatī. The king rules Karṇa city in Mālava, knows Vedas and śāstras, sacrifices and gives generously, and has a brilliant court. Verse 3 prints aṇimādiguṇāpeta: literally free from qualities such as aṇimā. The printed negative qualifier is retained, without emending it to guṇopeta or attributing miraculous perfections. Indumatī is virtuous, serves her husband and parents-in-law, handles household duties and worships gods and guests. Ministers strongly urge the king to abandon the grievously sinful killing involved in hunting.
outcome: Royal family and ministers’ warning introduced; printed absence qualifier preserved literally, with no supernatural perfection granted.

cause: The king hunts despite the ministers’ warning.
details: Indumatī is explicitly named as the king’s faithful wife and a servant of her parents-in-law. The king proceeds hunting despite the ministers’ appeal against killing. On horseback, he wears blue clothing and headcloth, armguard and finger protection, carrying a small weapon, sword, shield, bow and arrows with his retinue. Killing game and sending it to the city, he is observed by Rākṣasas.
outcome: The royal hunt proceeds despite the warning and encounters danger.

details: The king trembles on seeing huge Rākṣasas described with cave-like mouths, pit-like eyes, open jaws and sky-reaching bodies. The retinue flees; some die and some faint. A cruel Rākṣasī desires the beautiful king, embraces and kisses him. The minister clause bhage kṛtvā in verse 15 remains unresolved; devouring the servants is explicit. The king escapes into a lake unseen by her, but Nāga maidens seize him and take him to their lower-world residence.
outcome: Escape from the Rākṣasī leads to Nāga captivity; the minister clause remains open.

details: The Nāga maidens adorn the king and ask his identity and origin. He identifies himself as Candraṅgada, son of Hemāṅgada, resident of Karṇa in Mālava, who fled the Rākṣasī and was brought here by them. He attributes his survival to the lake and says his hunting people were devoured. The maidens ask him to become their husband and promise pleasures. Addressing them as mothers, he refuses because he observes a one-wife vow; this address does not establish biological parentage.
outcome: The king identifies his father and refuses marriage through his one-wife vow.

cause: The king’s one-wife refusal provokes the maidens’ curse and captivity.
details: The king teaches the ethics of Somavaṃśa kings: avoid others’ wealth, harm, wives and slander; study, sacrifice, give and protect refugees; avoid forbidden conduct and perform prescribed duties. He distinguishes three-varṇa duties, Brahmin additional officiation duties and hospitality for all. The rejected maidens angrily curse him to separation from his wife and shackle him. The Rākṣasī drinks the lake water and eats aquatic creatures without satisfaction. A surviving messenger reports the king’s submergence to the queen.
outcome: Curse and physical captivity follow refusal; the queen receives only a disappearance report.

details: The queen hears of the submergence and falls unconscious. Her friends fan and cool her while weeping. Reviving, she beats her breast, head and face and laments her lost husband: where will he eat, sleep and bathe, who will protect subjects and refugees, and where can either find happiness? She sees the directions as empty, throws away ornaments, breaks bangles and faints again. Her grief expresses limited knowledge of his disappearance; the narrator has already described his living captivity.
outcome: The grieving queen collapses, prompting citizens’ counsel.

details: Pārvatī asks what the people did for the fainting queen. Himavat says the citizens wipe their own tears, address her as mother, urge her to focus on her son, and claim mourning tears burn the dead. They teach impermanence and compare bodily change with replacing clothes. They conjecture that her husband may have attained liberation or heaven and may return, proposing consultation with a sage knowing past and future before further action. Briefly consoled, Indumatī dismisses them, abandons auspicious married marks and wastes away.
outcome: Citizens offer conjectures and temporary consolation; the queen lacks the captivity facts.

cause: Nārada’s assurance changes the queen’s understanding of her husband’s fate.
details: After twelve years of grief Nārada visits. Indumatī tells him of the twelve-year distress; he says her husband is alive somewhere and orders blue headcloth, ear ornaments, forehead kuṅkuma, bangles and maṅgalasūtra. Trusting the truthful sage, she immediately restores these marks, invites Brahmins, honours him and them, gives gifts, sends sugar to every household and orders music. She gives clothing and betel, dismisses the people, then bows to Nārada again.
outcome: Nārada’s assurance restores married-status marks before actual reunion.

details: Indumatī asks where and how her husband lives and how she can see him, offering even difficult vow, gift or tapas. Nārada prescribes Nabhas bright fourth: morning tooth-cleaning, intention and bathing in river, tank or well, white clothes, a beautiful four-armed earthen Gaṇeśa image and steady sixteen-service worship. Food options are ekānna (a single-food option), one meal, or fasting until Bhādra fourth; music, dance and Brahmin feeding accompany a festival according to means. He promises reunion with her living husband held in Pātāla by Nāga maidens and asserts the truth of his account.
outcome: Nārada discloses the living husband’s captivity and gives a conditional reunion remedy.

cause: The queen follows Nārada’s disclosed remedy.
details: After Nārada leaves, Nabhas arrives. Indumatī makes the earthen image and offers fragrant clothing, flowers, varied foods, fruit, gold, lamps, flower handfuls, circumambulations, bows and hymns. Name-remembrance, meditation, music, dance and Brahmin feeding please the deity. Living on only one pala of milk, she observes the vow from Nabhas bright fourth through Bhādra fourth to regain her long-lost beloved. The printed verse-number errors do not interrupt the read body.
outcome: The queen actually performs the taught vow with a one-pala milk diet.

cause: Completion of the vow brings divine favour and changes the captors’ decision.
details: At the completion of Indumatī’s vow, Gaṇeśa’s favour changes the Nāga maidens’ minds. They release the king, honour him with clothing, ornaments, gems and wealth, give a mind-swift horse and send him away. He emerges from the lake, ties the horse to a tree and bathes. Citizens question him; when he asks after Indumatī and their son, they recognize and embrace him. They report her recent bath, fasting, emaciation and survival by holding to her son. Other citizens announce his return in the city.
outcome: The captors release the king, give transport and wealth; citizens recognize his return.

details: Trusted news fills the queen with joy. She sends ministers and troops, decorates the city with flags, wets its streets, prepares assemblies and adorns herself. She gives cows, land and gold to Brahmins and arranges ārati for married women, then approaches the lake with music. Ministers greet, bow to and embrace the king, and sit by his order. He asks everyone’s welfare and honours them with betel and clothing.
outcome: The city prepares a welcome and the king greets his ministers.

details: The king goes to Indumatī’s camp and has a Brahmin rite performed; the printed dvādaśābdadṛśairdvijaiḥ clause remains unresolved in its exact ritual and agent nuance. The secure sequence is auspicious-day recitation, Gaṇeśa worship first, Śaṅkara worship and Brahmin fees. He breaks Śrīphala and approaches the queen, whom he sees as like the Moon’s remaining crescent. No universal twelve-year rite is reconstructed from the clause.
outcome: The worship sequence is secure; the twelve-year ritual expression remains unresolved.

details: Married young women perform the king’s ārati and shower parched grain and flowers. The couple wipes joyful tears and recounts the pain of separation, receiving consolation. The king mounts a decorated elephant with four bells, flags and parasol, amid foot escorts. A hundred staff-bearers precede him, with fire-weapon fighters, horse and chariot riders and a printed lakh-elephant formation at the sides. Musicians, dancers and praisers lead the procession into the city; no per-side versus combined elephant total is imposed.
outcome: The couple reunites and enters the city in a royal procession.

details: Army dust obscures the sun and decorated city. The king honours leading citizens again and gives clothing and betel before they go home. He feeds Brahmins and eats with kin. At night the couple again shares their grief; the royal priest consoles them and they sleep happily. Hearing all that his wife experienced through the Vināyaka vow, Candraṅgada decides to practice it himself and does so with a festival in the next Śrāvaṇa.
outcome: The household is restored and Candraṅgada subsequently practices the vow.

details: After hearing her father’s history, Pārvatī joyfully performs the Nabhas vow, makes and worships the instructed image, lives on milk alone and meditates on Gaṇeśa. Śiva’s mind becomes restless and he comes to her hermitage. At Gaṇeśa fourth and completion of the vow she sees bull-mounted Hara, rises, bows and worships him. She asks why he left and forgot her, compares a moment of separation with aeons, and explicitly attributes seeing him to her father-taught Varada vow and its favour.
outcome: Pārvatī’s previously promised encounter with Śiva is now actually narrated.

details: Himavat arrives and places the goddess’s hand in Śiva’s hand. Gods and Gandharvas worship Gaṇeśa and the couple, with divine drums, flowers and praise. Śiva also praises Gaṇeśa, places Pārvatī on his half-body, mounts the bull and returns to Kailāsa; others return to their stations. Brahmā explicitly closes the account Vyāsa asked about and introduces another story whose hearing is said to free all sins and fulfil wishes.
outcome: Hand-giving, half-body reunion and Kailāsa return close the frame’s personal goal.

details: Bhṛgu returns to the Somakānta frame, saying he will continue what Vyāsa heard from Brahmā. Somakānta and then Vyāsa request further Gaṇeśa stories. Brahmā introduces Śūrasena, king of Sahasra city in the middle country: wealthy, generous, sacrificing and protective, skilled in three powers, six political methods, four strategies and four army types, devoted to gods and Brahmins and ruler of the earth. His wife Puṇyaśālinī is righteous and beautiful; her fidelity is compared favourably with Arundhatī and her lack of envy with Anasūyā.
outcome: Outer narration and a new named royal household are introduced.

details: The king and court see a bright aerial vimāna with singing and send messengers to inspect it. The gaze of an unnamed leprous royal messenger, a vaiśya’s son, causes it to fall. Messengers report the crash as due to a harmful gaze. Śūrasena and his people go with music and find Indra with gods and meritorious people aboard. Bowing, the king praises the fortune of seeing Indra and asks why the vehicle fell and where he came from and was going.
outcome: The fallen vimāna’s cause prompts the king’s questions.

details: Indra repeats Nārada’s report of visiting Bhṛśuṇḍi, whose continuous Gaṇeśa meditation and japa have brought Gaṇeśa’s likeness. Nārada was honoured by the sage and came to tell Indra. Indra honoured and dismissed Nārada, then visited the Gaṇeśa-like sage by swift vimāna, exchanging honours. He was returning with his retinue to Amarāvatī when the messenger’s gaze caused the fall near Śūrasena’s city. The king asks which austerity produced the sage’s form.
outcome: Indra’s reported journey leads to a question about Bhṛśuṇḍi’s likeness.

details: Indra recounts the former life of the kaivarta Nāmā in Nandura of Daṇḍakāraṇya. A thief from childhood, adulterer in youth, false oath-taker, gambler and drinker, he is expelled from the village. Living with a female companion and child in a forest cave, he kills travellers and animals, grows wealthy, adorns the woman and her son, and sells stolen objects in another city. His ambush weapons include sword, shield, noose, bow, a staff with iron at both ends and full quivers.
outcome: Nāmā’s former life, household and robbery weapons are introduced.

cause: An unintended sacred bath is followed by the devotee encounter.
details: Chasing a traveller for a yojana, Nāmā falls, recovers and bathes at a Gaṇeśa tīrtha only to remove fatigue. On returning he sees Mudgala japping the deity’s name-mantra and raises an unsheathed sword to kill him, but even his fastened weapons fall and his mind changes through the devotee’s power. Mudgala laughs and asks why. Indra attributes Nāmā’s knowledge and dispassion to the bath and the sage’s sight. Nāmā confesses countless sins, renounces the weapons and asks rescue from transmigration, saying holy company benefits even wrongdoers.
outcome: The attack fails, the attacker changes and he explicitly seeks refuge.

details: Compassionate Mudgala remembers the fault of rejecting one seeking refuge. He says Nāmā is not entitled to prescribed gifts and other formal rites, yet offers all-siddhi name-japa. Nāmā bows; the sage teaches Gaṇeśāya namaḥ and plants his own staff before him. He commands one fixed seat, air diet and one-pointed japa until the sage’s return and the staff’s sprouting, with uninterrupted watering of its root morning and evening. A parenthetic line describes the protective hand placed on the disciple’s head.
outcome: Mudgala provides qualified name-japa and precise staff/ascetic instructions.

cause: Long japa, staff sprouting and the guru’s intervention lead to the described transformation.
details: Nāmā practices from a fixed seat beneath a tree, without food or desires and with controlled senses, japping the name. After a thousand years the staff sprouts; he continues waiting for the sage while anthill and vines cover him. Mudgala returns by chance, remembers the staff and disciple, sees the sprout and eyes-only ascetic, removes the anthill and sprinkles enchanted water. A divine Gaṇeśa-like body with two hands continues japa. On awakening, fire from the eyes rises to burn the three worlds, but Mudgala stops it. The guru’s return has no additional numerical interval.
outcome: The staff sprouts, divine likeness appears and the guru stops the threatening eye-fire.

details: The awakened disciple bows to and embraces his compassionate guru like a son embracing his father. Mudgala honours the anthill-reemerged one as son, names him Bhṛśuṇḍi and teaches the one-syllable mantra. Verse43 connects the name with a trunk through the raw clause bhūmadhyān nirgatā śuṇḍā; its exact anatomical meaning is unresolved, and eyebrow-middle is not silently substituted. Mudgala grants excellence among sages, worship by Indra, gods, Gandharvas and Siddhas, Gaṇeśa-like sin-destroying meditation and sight, fame, fruitful sight for visitors and a lifespan of a hundred thousand kalpas by his word. Gods and Nārada’s sages visit, praise the fruitfulness of their birth, learning, parents, tapas and fame, and call him Gaṇanātha. He honours and dismisses them.
outcome: Mudgala gives the new name, ritual-son honour, mantra, lifespan and visitor boons.

details: Bhṛśuṇḍi installs a Gaṇeśa image, sits in lotus posture, japs the one-syllable mantra and worships daily with sixteen services. His hermitage has pools, trees and vines, with predators, prey, mongooses and serpents free from mutual hostility. After another hundred years, Gaṇeśa is pleased and asks why his own likeness continues austerity. He promises sāyujya at life’s end, a site named by the raw expression nāmaleti, siddhis for practitioners, no rebirth through seeing the image, sons to the childless and knowledge to students. Indra concludes the origin account and asks Śūrasena’s next question.
outcome: Installation and further worship receive Gaṇeśa’s personal and site promises, closing the origin arc.

details: Śūrasena asks how Indra’s vimāna can fly and what he should do. Indra says properly transferred merit of one year from a Sankaṣṭa-caturthī-practicing Brahmin or kṣatriya in the city will restart it; ten thousand people cannot otherwise accomplish this. The king asks the vow’s merit, result, procedure, deity and earlier successful practitioner. Indra introduces a history of Kṛtavīrya and Nārada.
outcome: One-year merit transfer is prescribed; actual vimāna recovery remains pending.

cause: Persistent childlessness despite many rituals drives the couple’s forest tapas.
details: Kṛtavīrya is a brave, generous, sacrificing, sense-controlled king with moderate diet and devotion, ruling in the Sahyādri region with uncounted forces, gold vessels and beds, and twelve thousand Brahmins fed in rows. His wife Sugandhā is dutiful and devoted to gods, Brahmins and guests. They remain childless despite gifts, vows, austerities, sacrifices and pilgrimages because of former-birth sin. Entrusting realm, seal, treasury, people and districts to ministers, they practice in the forest wearing bark and skin, eating old leaves and air, becoming visible only by their eyes. Nārada sees them and tells the king’s unnamed father in Pitṛloka that his son may die tomorrow or the day after; an heir would sustain life, lineage and heaven.
outcome: Nārada alerts the father to his childless son’s predicted imminent death.

details: Nārada sees Bhṛśuṇḍi’s parents, sons, wife and daughter(s) upside down in blazing Kumbhīpāka, beaten by Yama’s servants. He tells the sage that Indra and other gods and Kapila’s sages seek his Gaṇeśa-like presence, yet his parents, wife, sons, daughters and servants suffer here through his fault. He calls for ancestral rescue. Bhṛśuṇḍi burns with distress. Verse 23 has dual putrau and verse 26 the broader plural roster; names and additional counts are not invented.
outcome: The explicit family roster and Nārada’s rebuke prompt a rescue.

cause: Bhṛśuṇḍi offers vow-merit through a conditional devotional prayer and water transfer.
details: Bhṛśuṇḍi considers a rescue, offers Sankaṣṭa-caturthī merit, views his absent kin through concentration, meditates on Gaṇeśa and holds water. He prays that, if his vow was performed devotionally, its power quickly rescue the ancestors, then casts the water into Gaṇeśa’s hand. Immediately divine favour gives them divine forms and vimānas. Served by Apsarases, praised by Cāraṇas and sung to by Gandharvas, they reach Gaṇeśa’s station. All other wrongdoers in Kumbhīpāka also go to Gaṇeśa’s abode. Indra attributes their actual good destination to one day’s merit.
outcome: Kin and other hell inmates actually reach Gaṇeśa’s abode through one day’s merit.

details: Indra says Śeṣa cannot count the merit of a lifelong devotional Sankaṣṭa vow, and that its power can restart his vimāna. This remains a prospective remedy in the Śūrasena frame; Bhṛśuṇḍi’s completed rescue is the supporting exemplum.
outcome: The narrative returns to the still-fallen vehicle’s prospective remedy.

details: Śūrasena asks what Kṛtavīrya’s father did after the hell-rescue account. Indra says the distressed father goes to Brahmaloka, bows to Brahmā and asks why his virtuous, generous, sacrificing, god-and-guest-devoted son remains childless despite many attempts. Having transferred the realm to his ministers, the son lives emaciated on air in the forest and may soon die. The father asks a remedy for former-birth sin which he can deliver to his son for lineage growth. Brahmā offers a past-birth account.
outcome: The father asks for a former-sin remedy to take to his son.

details: Brahmā describes Sāma, an antyaja wrongdoer whose sight destroys piety. For wealth he murders twelve peaceful Brahmins, leaves their bodies in a cave and takes their possessions. Returning home on Māgha dark fourth at moonrise, he calls his son Gaṇeśa twice and eats with him after taking no food or water. Verse 13 explicitly says tasyaputro’sau dies that night; verse 14’s saḥ reaches Vaināyaka through the unintentional vow, and verse 16’s remaining merit produces the present Kṛtavīrya. The Sāma-versus-son death and rebirth referent is unresolved. Brahmā predicts sonbirth when sins are destroyed; the father trembles and asks another remedy.
outcome: Unintentional-vow merit and royal rebirth are described with a fundamental referent gap.

details: Sāma murders and robs the twelve Brahmins and returns home at night. At moonrise on Māgha dark fourth, after taking no food or water, he calls his own son Gaṇeśa twice and shares a meal with him. This explicit son-name relationship is separated from the uncertain death and rebirth pronouns in the following verses.
outcome: The firm son-name relationship is extracted apart from the later uncertainty.

details: The father asks how the Brahmin-murder sin can end. Brahmā predicts that the royal son’s proper Sankaṣṭa vow will free him from sin. Asked its month and procedure, he prescribes Māgha dark fourth on Tuesday, with an auspicious muhūrta and Moon, tooth-cleaning, twenty-one baths and daily rites, japa, silence and no food. Slander, evil acts, betel, water drinking, harm and tale-bearing are prohibited. At day’s end bathe with sesame and āmalaka paste, use the one-letter, six-letter or Vedic mantra or Gaṇeśa’s name-japa, and meditate steadily.
outcome: Brahmā gives a prospective remedy and its constraints; no cure or sonbirth is yet enacted.

details: Perform sixteen-service Gaṇeśa worship with varied offerings: modaka, apūpa, śaṣkulī, laḍḍū, vaṭaka, pāyasa, rice, accompaniments, fruit, betel, fees, twenty-one dūrvā, lamps and flowers. At moonrise offer arghya first to the tithi, then Gaṇeśa, then Moon. Bow and request pardon; feed twenty-one Brahmins, or ten or twelve if unable, give fees, hear the story and eat silently. Spend the remaining night with music. A careful year of the vow is said to remove all sins and give an excellent son or another desired object.
outcome: Ordered worship, feeding alternatives and a year-long benefit promise are prescribed.

details: Further promises include removal of distress and hostile-army fear. Japa and fasting at a śamī root until moonrise give desired benefits even to blind, mute, intellectually limited and lame practitioners, and give wife, sons, wealth and kingdom. The annual food schedule is Śrāvaṇa: seven laḍḍū; Nabhasya: curd; Āśvin: fast; Kārtika: milk; Mārgaśīrṣa: no food; Pauṣa: cow urine; Māgha: sesame; Phālguna: ghee and sugar; Caitra: pañcagavya; Vaiśākha: the retained term śatapatrikā; Jyeṣṭha: ghee; Āṣāḍha: honey. The father asks why Aṅgāraka fourth is especially praised.
outcome: An annual food schedule and timed practice lead to the Aṅgāraka question.

details: Brahmā answers the father’s question about Aṅgāraka fourth. In Avantī, learned Bhāradvāja performs agnihotra, teaches pupils and observes rites on a riverbank. Seeing an unnamed Apsaras arouses desire; he falls, and emitted semen enters an earth-hole. A red, hibiscus-coloured boy arises, whom Earth lovingly raises. At seven years he asks his mother why he is red in a human body and who his father is. Earth explicitly says Bhāradvāja’s fallen semen met her, produced him, and she raised him.
outcome: Source-specific semen/earth origin and nurturing mother are explicit; no intercourse with Earth or the Apsaras is narrated.

details: The boy asks to see his father. Earth takes him to Bhāradvāja, bows and presents the son born of his semen and raised by her. With his permission she returns home; the sage rejoices, embraces and smells the boy’s head, places him on his lap, and performs upanayana at an auspicious time. He teaches Vedas/śāstras and a Gaṇeśa mantra, prescribing long observance and promising desired gifts when pleased. The boy sits in lotus posture on Narmadā’s bank, controls senses, meditates Heramba and japs on an air diet, becoming thin.
outcome: Explicit father’s acceptance, initiation and teacher/mantra role precede the boy’s austerity.

details: After one thousand years of severe tapas, Gaṇeśa appears at moonrise on Māgha dark fourth. His arms are described as digbhuja, with divine clothes, forehead moon, varied weapons, trunk/tusk/ears/earrings, many ornaments and immense solar radiance. The boy bows and hymns obstacle removal and creation, lordship of gods/asuras, transcendent attributes and world support/protection. Pleased by tapas, devotion, hymn and courage despite childhood, the deity invites desired boons.
outcome: Exact appearance time and boon invitation; digbhuja kept as the witness term, while later image explicitly has ten arms.

details: Bhauma praises the fruitful sight, birth, knowledge, lineage, Earth and tapas. He requests residence in heaven, drinking nectar with the gods, an auspicious name famous in the three worlds, and that the fourth on which he saw the deity always grant piety, remove all distress and give vow-practitioners their wishes through divine favour.
outcome: Personal heaven/nectar/name requests and distinct festival efficacy request are explicit.

details: Gaṇeśa promises nectar with gods and fame as Maṅgala; Aṅgāraka is explained by redness and Earth-son status. Aṅgāraka-fourth practitioners receive merit equal to a year of Sankaṣṭa observance and unobstructed tasks. The boy will become king in Avantī, and recounting the excellent vow gives all wishes. The deity grants and disappears.
outcome: Requests receive specific response, plus prospective kingship and festival benefit; actual transport follows.

details: Maṅgala devotionally installs a beautiful, trunk-faced ten-armed Gaṇeśa, builds a pleasing temple and names the deity Maṅgalamūrti. The site becomes wish-giving to everyone and liberation-giving through observance, worship and seeing.
outcome: Actual named image/temple installation and site efficacy.

details: Vināyaka sends his Gaṇas in a fine vimāna to bring Bhauma. They bring him in the same body to Gaṇeśa’s vicinity. Narrator states he obtained heaven and nectar with gods, giving Tuesday-associated caturthī its fame. Maṅgalamūrti also becomes called Cintāmaṇi for giving desired objects; the all-obstacle-removing deity is famous west of Pārinera city, now worshipped by Siddhas/Gandharvas at moonrise and granting desired gifts, sons/grandsons and prosperity.
outcome: Actual same-body transport and heaven/nectar attainment close the origin/site arc; named king accession remains only predicted.

details: Kaśyapa teaches the Vedas and initiates Vāmana with six syllables for restoring divine offices. After permission, the child practices one YEAR of fasting japa in Vidarbha. A ten-armed, peacock-mounted Gajānana appears with Siddhi and Buddhi.

Vāmana hymns the Lord. Reluctant to ask after receiving the vision, he nevertheless requests freedom from defeat and obstacles and success for the refuge-seeker’s purpose. The Lord grants all great and small tasks through remembrance.

Vāmana installs the four-armed, three-eyed Kashmir-stone image, builds its temple and endows a priest for worship three times daily. He reports to Kaśyapa and obtains permission to visit Bali’s sacrifice, where sages marvel at him.

Bali asks the visitor’s identity and desire. Vāmana performs an orphan claim and asks three steps of land for a hut. Śukra/Kāvya warns that he is Hari seeking the three worlds, but Bali chooses the infinite merit of the gift and formally grants it.

The printed Śakra water-stopper and śalākā episode remain under review. Water is given; Vāmana remembers Gaṇeśa and grows. The literal sequence gives heaven to his head, rodasī to one foot, nether regions to another and another placement on Bali’s head.
Ordered to Dharaṇītala, Bali asks how he could go without the Lord. Vāmana promises presence and later Indra’s office after the current holder’s tenure, while honoring Indra’s earlier refuge first.

Gods praise and celebrate, Vāmana vanishes and they return to their former places. His image becomes famous as a desire-giver. The Adosha and orientation clause is retained before the promised śamī explanation.
Brahmā reports the Lord’s śamī teaching to Priyavrata. Vyāsa asks the king’s identity; a nested Śiva–Pārvatī conversation opens his history.

Priyavrata’s wives and ministers are introduced. Prabhā wins his preference while Kīrti is rejected. Prabhā’s son receives rites, initiation and a princess’s marriage; the first wife is reduced to service and kicked down.
Kīrti despairs and considers Hari’s aid to Draupadī. Devala teaches Gajānana worship. She worships the Mandāra image with sixteen services and a hymn framed by five-deity non-difference.

Unable to obtain dūrvā, her friends bring śamī. At year’s end a dream gives unsolicited marital and son grants, predicts fourth-year poison death and Gṛtsamada’s revival, and promises hymn-reading fruits.

After completing her vow, Kīrti waits. Prabhā’s illness changes the king’s preference; Kīrti bears the promised son. Jealous Prabhā gives poison, physicians fail, she is expelled and the child dies as his mother takes him into the forest.

Gṛtsamada hears the grieving mother’s refuge request. He orders transfer of the śamī-worship merit into the child’s hand, and the boy rises. Kīrti reports the messengers’ battle and asks how the sage knew and why the leaf has this power.
Gṛtsamada describes the leaf’s superior devotional merit and introduces Nārada’s conversation with Indra before continuing the frame.
Nārada tells Indra about Aurava, Sumedhā and Śamikā. Their daughter marries Dhaumya’s son Mandāra, Śaunaka’s disciple, and later joins her husband after her father’s loving protection request.
The couple laugh at Bhṛśuṇḍī’s tapas-grown trunk. He curses them to shunned trees, adding release when the trunked Lord is pleased. They become Mandāra and thorny śamī.
After a month, the father and guru search and learn the curse through meditation. Seeking relief for daughter and disciple, they perform twelve YEARS of fasting, one-toe, six-syllable tapas.
A ten-armed, lion-mounted, noose-bearing Lord appears. The sages hymn him and receive an invitation to request boons, together with specific hymn-reading promises.

They request removal of treehood. Gaṇeśa refuses to annul his devotee’s word and gives permanent root-presence instead, with favored-offering substitutions and devotional benefits. He actually dwells at both roots.

Aurava’s tapas, heavenly departure and fire transformation are retained without an invented sequence. Śaunaka creates a Mandāra-root image, receives unspecified grants and returns to worship. Gṛtsamada explains why śamī became dear.
At Mahābala, the hurried sacrifice neglects Gaṇeśa and Sāvitrī and seats Gāyatrī. Sāvitrī’s curse becomes river forms at the petitioners’ request, including Śiva/Veṇyā and Kṛṣṇa/Kṛṣṇā.
Brahmā and the goddesses acknowledge the neglected worship and plan devotion. The women go to the Rāma-established Vakratunda image in Karnāṭaka; his victory is recalled briefly.
Varied austerities initially fail. Following a sky instruction, all offer śamī leaves and receive the four-armed, TWO-TUSK, mouse-mounted vision with Siddhi and Buddhi.
The goddess hymn requests original forms and constant remembrance. Gaṇeśa preserves Sāvitrī’s curse through river portions while restoring gods’ forms and offices. They apologize and worship.
Gods install the stone Heramba temple at Supattana; Indra takes the earlier Mandāra image. Divine offices and household joys return. Brahmā performs twelve YEARS of tapas and repeats the sacrifice.

Gṛtsamada applies the plant account to the child’s revival and asks to leave. Kīrti bows and dismisses him; devotional hearing and morning remembrance fruits close the account, before another question in38.

Because the child cannot recite six syllables, Kīrti asks for a simpler royal-success mantra. Gṛtsamada proposes the four-syllable Dhundhirāja name. Her origin questions introduce Skanda’s account to Agastya.
The account explains creation classes, merit and holy fields, Kāśī, Maṇikarṇikā and Bhāgīrathī, name and death efficacy and five-god unity. The birth-class numerical relation remains unresolved.
Bhasmāsura’s son receives Śukra’s five-syllable instruction and practices1000DIVINE YEARS. A ten-armed, five-faced Śiva appears, receives the hymn and invites rare wishes.

Durāsada requests broad protection, terror, kingdom and devotion. Śiva explicitly grants protection from gods with one Śakti exception, a radiance-born conqueror who keeps him alive under a foot, and renewed conquest if that foot is removed.
Armed with two ministers and a fourfold host, the demon takes earthly kingdoms and divine offices. Gods retreat, and he rules from Bhāsmaka/Mukundapura.

The flashback gives Bhasmāsura’s head-touch boon and pursuit of its donor. Mohinī’s dance imitation causes his own fatal head touch, after which the city is associated with Mukunda and her devotional favors.
Ministers direct Durāsada to still-unconquered Avimukta. Śiva withdraws to Kedāra, Jaigīṣavya remains, temples and worship are suppressed, and lost ritual nourishment leaves gods hungry.
Brahmā identifies the Śiva grant and the Śakti-radiance child as its exception. Gods and sages are directed first to Pārvatī, then to the cosmic Gaṇeśa.
Bhavānī accepts praise and directs a Gaṇeśa hymn. A sky voice assures the counter; petitioners seek explanation from Pārvatī while Śiva meditates.

Pārvatī’s mouth, nose and eyes emit radiance that becomes a ten-armed, ten-weapon Vināyaka. She worships, names him Vakratunda, gives her lion and requests the demon’s defeat and restored divine offices.
Vakratunda accepts his mother’s request and rides to Kāśī; he indicts Durāsada’s abuses and offers surrender before raising the axe.

Axe heart-strike leaves even a hair unmoved. Goad checks sword and axe breaks it into100pieces. Matching-growth wrestling continues many days; forehead punch leaves demon unconscious2muhūrtas, revived recognizing weakness.
Fire→rain counter; wind disperses rain→mountains counter; Raudra/Brahmā weapons collide and burn people/army; dual cessation agency unresolved. Demon leaves ministers to fight while he eats.
Lord’s56 varied mounted/armed forms dismantle host; surrender, flight and face-to-face death/heaven outcomes. Demon returns to dead host, recalls Śakti exception and flees.

Respecting fleeing-foe rule and Śiva nondeath boon, Virāṭa captures and holds demon by foot. Grants immovable gateway role, wicked suppression and continuing nearness; demon asks permanent foot, Lord assents.
Earth auspicious, gods/sages return offices, worshippers’ wishes fulfilled;56forms inKāśī and Eka-pāda inTuṇḍana after Virāṭa contraction; story phalas.

Praise restores ritual ways/office, Dhundhi/rāja name derived from search/function assignment; four-aim/progeny promise. Plant/food/gem worship,56Vināyakas/seven enclosures/five-faced doorway figure, cosmic duties resume. Divodāsa branch announced next.

Mudgala resumes Brahmā’s creation: Brahmins from mouth, Kṣatriyas arms, Vaiśyas thighs, Śūdras feet; renunciation from head, forest-stage heart, brahmacarya navel and household-state lower legs. Dharma chest and Adharma back set god/demon courses; gods/Gandharvas/Apsarases/Yakṣas/Asuras/Yātudhānas, snakes/birds/beasts/humans arise from his body. They act yet do not multiply. These are source-local cosmological body-emergences, not universal biological descent claims.

Mudgala classifies nine creations: first mahat, second tanmātra/bhūta, third vaikārika/indriya (three prākṛta); fourth stationary beings, fifth tiryak, sixth upward-flow gods, seventh downward-flow humans, eighth bhautika beings, ninth kaumāra (six vaikṛta). The first three are described as buddhi-pūrva, guiding creatures through principles. Brahmā is distressed that his diverse creatures do not multiply.

A couple emerges from Brahmā: Śatarūpā from left limb and Svāyambhuva Manu from right, first knowledgeable in Kṣatriya dharma. They ask orders; he directs sexual procreation through tapas. They bow, go to forest and practice intense Gaṇeśa meditation. Kardama emerges from Brahmā’s shadow, is ordered to create, then goes to forest desiring progeny and meditates on white-form Viṣṇu with prescribed tapas.

During this interval Madhu and Kaiṭabha arise from Viṣṇu’s ear dirt, conquer three worlds by arm strength and scatter terrified gods. They approach to eat Brahmā; Brahmā hymns Nidrā and she releases sleeping/unmanifest Viṣṇu, who rises. Viṣṇu wrestles them5000 years without defeating them; the powerful pair crushes him. He conceals himself, flees, takes Śaṅkara’s refuge, bows, narrates the battle and asks a victory method.

Śiva says Viṣṇu forgot Gaṇeśa and should worship for siddhi. He gives the six-syllable great Gaṇeśa mantra. Viṣṇu goes to Daṇḍakāraṇya, sits in lotus posture, meditates on Gaṇeśa and performs intense tapas by the six-syllable procedure1000 years. Gaṇeśa comes to grant; Viṣṇu joyfully bows, worships and begins hymn. The chapter does not explicitly label these1000 years divine.

Viṣṇu hymns Gaṇeśa as protector, Siddhi/Buddhi lord, remover of devotee obstacles and obstacle-giver to nondevotees, qualified/unqualified cosmic/acosmic Brahman, human-elephant form, cause/beyond cause, Jyeṣṭharāja, yoga giver in yogin hearts, māyā support and deluder of māyā-makers. He says grace gives intellect/praise, sight makes him Brahman-formed/yoga-giver; he dances with tears/raised hair. Gaṇeśa offers wishes pleased by tapas/devotion and promises hymn reciters/hearers all siddhis, four human aims and immediate desired ends through grace.

Viṣṇu requests rare unwavering devotion, incomparable knowledge, universal fame and varied strength, destruction-method for Madhu/Kaiṭabha and strength against other demons. Gaṇeśa assents, sends him to battle promising victory by strength. He reveals Brahmā, pleased by the pair’s tapas, kept their death very secret at boon-granting: when they themselves speak death, kill them by that stated mode. He says taking māyā and residing in their and Viṣṇu’s hearts he will bring them under Viṣṇu’s control; when Viṣṇu remembers him he will know the victory-method. The original demons’ request/tapas details and exact death words are not narrated here.

Gaṇeśa disappears. Viṣṇu establishes a great image with good Brahmins, worships richly; the place becomes Siddhikṣetra, renowned for siddhis through observance and served by siddhas. He resides/worships there devotedly with wife and entourage, then bows and hastens to battle. Meditating on Gaṇeśa he cuts the two powerful demons. No named cutting weapon, thighs/dry-place condition or final death dialogue is supplied in this chapter.
outcome: Viṣṇu cuts both demons while meditating on Gaṇeśa; narrator does not give detailed final duel or death speech.

details: Nine Brahmā sons perform1000 DIVINE years of heart-Gaṇeśa tapas by one-syllable procedure, daily worship and wind alone as food. Mouse-mounted Gaṇeśa comes, luminous yet gentle. Led by Dakṣa they hymn him as witness/self/yoga/peace, creation-preservation-destruction, all gods, beings/elements/food, cit/bodha/videha/asat/sat/sama/Svānanda/ayoga/yoga and Cintāmaṇi of mental activities. He offers boons and promises faithful hymn users all siddhis, progeny/spouse, infertility removal, wealth/grain/cattle, enjoyment/liberation/Brahman and desired ends. They request unwavering devotion destroying delusion, incomparable creation capacity and success in whatever they wish; he assents, vanishes, and they return to their places meditating on him.

Brahmā directs Dakṣa to worship Śakti so she becomes his daughter. After100 years Śakti appears; Dakṣa hymns her as māyā/delusion, mother/life-giver, Pārvatī/Gāyatrī/Sāvitrī/Prakṛti/Puruṣa and guṇa support, requesting daughterhood. She grants future daughterhood in many forms and filling the world through offspring, promises her hymn’s readers/hearers all wishes, and vanishes. Mudgala then addresses current Dakṣa: he abandoned Gaṇeśa name/mantra, scorned Satī who became ash, was made sorrowful by Vighneśa, but prior impressions restored memory. Kingship prosperity induces proud blindness/destroys knowledge, so sages avoid it; hear the present account devotedly.

Svāyambhuva Manu with wife goes to forest, performs intense tapas by eight-syllable procedure1000 DIVINE years and gains Gaṇeśa’s appearance. He bows, worships and hymns elephant/Human-elephant/Oṃ form, four arms, mouse vehicle, Svānanda, Siddhi/Buddhi and yoga, saying vision inspires praise and blesses father/tapas/knowledge/lineage/learning/vows. Gaṇeśa raises him, offers a boon and promises his hymn readers/hearers all ends, progeny/prosperity, sorrow removal, wealth/grain, four aims/Brahman and firm devotion.

Manu requests firm Gaṇeśa devotion eliminating delusion, capacity to create, excellent dharma maintenance, lasting protection of subjects, success in every wish and continual dwelling among Gaṇeśa devotees. Gaṇeśa assents to Manu, vanishes and goes to his own realm.

Manu and Śatarūpā bow to Brahmā and depart at his order; Manu rules dharmically, armed and fond of Gaṇapatyas. Through sexual union they produce sons Priyavrata/Uttānapāda and daughters Ākūti/Devahūti/Prasūti. He gives Prasūti to Dakṣa, Ākūti to Ruci and Devahūti to Kardama. Kardama’s100-year Viṣṇu tapas gains appearance; he asks Viṣṇu as son, receives grant, and Viṣṇu as Kapila becomes his son in Devahūti. Ruci’s mānasa twin Yajña/Dakṣiṇā is born in Ākūti; Yajña Viṣṇu fathers12 Yāma gods in Dakṣiṇā. With wife/sages he makes a jeweled four-armed Gaṇeśa image, constantly worships by yoga; Gaṇeśa gives marvelous yoga. Yajña becomes foremost Gaṇapatya yogin, chants Heramba and teaches disciples Gaṇapatya yoga.

Dakṣa fathers24 daughters in Prasūti, all Śakti portions/mothers. At Brahmā’s direction he gives13 to Dharma: Śraddhā,Lakṣmī,Dhṛti,Tuṣṭi,Puṣṭi,Medhā,Kriyā,Buddhi,Lajjā,Vapus,Śānti,Siddhi,Kīrti. Their Dharma sons respectively are Kāma,Artha,Niyama,Santoṣa,Lābha,Śama; Kriyā has Daṇḍa/Samaya; Buddhi Bodha/Apramāda; Lajjā Vinaya; Vapus Vyavasāya; Śānti Kṣema; Siddhi Siddha; Kīrti Yaśas. Kāma’s sons are Harṣa/Ānanda. These named daughter-personifications are retained in this Dharma lineage, without silently merging same-named Lakṣmī/Siddhi/Buddhi from other manifestation contexts.

Brahmā’s back yields couple Adharma/Hiṃsā. Their son Anṛta and daughter Nikṛti yield Bhaya/Naraka and daughters Māyā/Vedanā. Bhaya fathers all-removing Mṛtyu in Māyā; Naraka fathers worldly Duḥkha in Venā (27 raw spelling); equation with adjacent26 Vedanā is a contextual proposal, not verified identity. Mṛtyu yields Vyādhi/Jarā/Śoka/Tṛṣṇā/Krodha. These sorrow-producing Adharma descendants are said to have no further progeny and be ūrdhvaretas. Source-local personified genealogy is not merged with generic delusion/anger concepts.

The remaining11 Dakṣa daughters are married: Satī to Rudra, Khyāti/Bhṛgu, Sambhūti/Marīci, Smṛti/Aṅgiras, Prīti/Pulastya, Kṣamā/Pulaha, Santati/Kratu, Anasūyā/Atri, Ūrjā/Vasiṣṭha, Svāhā/Vahni, Svadhā/Pitṛs. Śaṅkara fathers Kārttikeya IN SATĪ here, appointed commander by Brahmā. Bhṛgu/Khyāti produce Lakṣmī beloved of Nārāyaṇa and Dhātṛ/Vidhātṛ, Meru’s sons-in-law. This source-local Satī motherhood is retained despite common accounts assigning another maternal form; no universal genealogy imposed.

Meru has daughters Ayati/Niyati; in them Dhātṛ/Vidhātṛ have two sons Mṛkaṇḍa/Prāṇa. Mārkaṇḍeya is Mṛkaṇḍa’s son; Vedaśiras is Prāṇa’s. The stanza supplies paired fathers/mothers and paired sons but the individual pair-to-son assignment is not separately explicit; this extraction preserves the joint family group rather than assigning a child four biological parents or forcing respectively order.

Marīci/Sambhūti have Pūrṇamāsa and four daughters Kṛṣi,Vṛṣṭi,Kṛṣṭi,Apaciti; Pūrṇamāsa sons Virajas/Parvata. Pulaha/Kṣamā have Karmaśreṣṭha,Varīyas,Sahiṣṇu and Vanakavīnāsa (digital name retained as printed). Atri/Anasūyā have Soma,Durvāsas and yoga-bearing Datta, three deities described as Brahmā/Bhava/Viṣṇu kalāṃśas; individual matching is not forced from this collective stanza alone.

Aṅgiras/Smṛti have daughters Sinīvālī,Kuhū,Rākā,Anumati. Pulastya/Prīti have son Ayoni;45 mentions Devabāhu and a daughter with exact name/gender referent unresolved;44 mentions Agastya and a former birth with exact identity-direction unresolved. Kratu/Santati have60000 ūrdhvaretas Vālakhilya sons. Vasiṣṭha/Ūrjā have seven named sons Citraketu,Surocaka,Virajas,Mitra,Ulbana,Vasubhṛt,Ghumān (घुमान् digital), and an unnamed lotus-eyed daughter;48 also mentions other seven beginning Śakti. Names/count overlap and Ayoni–Agastya identity are retained for review, without forced merger.

Vahni is described Rudra-natured and fathers Pāvaka,Pavamāna,Śuci in Svāhā. Each produces15 sons, giving49 fires in total including three and root Agni; all partake in yajñas. Pavamāna is friction-produced, Pāvaka lightning, Śuci the fire heating in Sun; each includes sons. Agni is everywhere/Rudra-natured and Brahmā’s son. This enumeration is not split into49 invented individual names.

Pitṛs include formless Agniṣvāttas and embodied Barhiṣads. Svadhā bears them daughters Menā/Dharaṇī, both knowers of Brahman. Menā bears Maināka/Krauñca and Gaṅgā/Pārvatī to Himavat; both goddesses gain Śaṅkara as husband. Himavat/Menā worship Satī by tapas and receive Pārvatī as daughter by boon. Dharaṇī is Meru’s wife and bears Ayati/Niyati already named. Mudgala closes this Dakṣa-daughter lineage account, whose reading/hearing grants all wishes.

Fathers individually teach Gaṇeśa worship and varied prescribed mantras to Dakṣa-daughter descendants. They go to forest, perform tapas/Heramba-japa and gain Gaṇeśa appearance after1000 years (no divine qualifier). They hymn Brahman/yoga/peace, protector/creator/preserver/destroyer, beyond māyā while its mover, infinite face/arms and witness, requesting firm devotion ending delusion, capacity in their respective tasks and all wishes fulfilled. Gaṇeśa grants successful intentions, happy devotion, task-capacity and firm fame. He promises hymn users siddhi by faithful hearing/reading and immediate desired fruit from21 readings for21 days; disappears. All men/women descendants return home happy, knowledgeable and successful in tasks.

Śaunaka requests detailed accounts of Atri’s deity-natured sons. Sūta says Candra arises as Brahmā portion, performs tapas and receives Gaṇeśa’s boon making him nectar-formed. His kalās nourish gods/people and rays increase food growth. Requested wording/duration are unstated.

Datta, Viṣṇu kalāṃśa, attains successive Brahman/yoga states such as inert/mad/piśāca/child-joy states. People of all varṇas/āśramas serve him, leaving no rest; distressed he submerges by yoga while they wait at shore. By siddhi he manifests Mokṣalakṣmī, rises holding her at left and wine-pot in right, drinks/enjoys with her. They judge him fallen and abandon him, allowing peaceful yoga. This is a narrated withdrawal stratagem; Mokṣalakṣmī is not silently identified with Viṣṇu’s ordinary spouse.

A nearby god/demon battle defeats gods, who flee and beg Datta’s protection.35 names a surā group arriving with bare/drawn weapons and gods fleeing; that arrival’s agency is separately flagged. Demons seize beautiful Mokṣalakṣmī, deludedly carry her on their heads; source says placing her at feet would instead have given victory. They lose radiance, are pressed by gods, flee to Pātāla; goddess vanishes into Brahman. No actual feet-placement victory is narrated.

Śaunaka asks why head contact with Mokṣalakṣmī harms demons. Sūta gives Vyāsa-derived explanation: these rajas/tamas demons seek enjoyment, steal/commit sexual misconduct, harm beings, drink and revile sages/gods/scriptures; they reject liberation and honor Bhogalakṣmī with heads. Sages/gods seek liberation, honor her at head. Demons’ yogin contact brings Mokṣalakṣmī, but without desire for liberation and while vicious/pleasure-attached she is angry and destroys them; taking unwanted liberation is treated as striking her with feet. Enjoyment-seekers should honor enjoyment goddess; liberation-seekers similarly reject enjoyment. Bhogalakṣmī is vāsanā-full, Mokṣalakṣmī without vāsanā. These are attributed yogic interpretations, not a universal physical head-contact rule.

Datta moves through varied avadhūta yoga conduct, sometimes eating/body behavior like cattle/beasts/birds. Reaching sahaja and inward-controller independence yet lacking peace despite manifest/unmanifest Brahman practice, he approaches father Atri, bows and is seated respectfully among yogins. He asks peace-yoga beyond qualified/unqualified/equanimity/turya/sahaja states he has practiced, troubled by independence still remaining. Atri promises eternal peace-yoga learned from Brahmā, says Gaṇapati is their and Śiva/gods’ family deity, origin/support of all; worship him to gain peace as other gods did.

Atri maps name/form to Śakti/asat, immortal self to Solar/sat, their unity to Viṣṇu/sadasat, distinct fourth/neti/nirmoha/independence to Śiva, and fourfold union to māyā-Svānanda Gaṇeśa. Karma yoga joins acts; knowledge yoga joins knowledge; their nonduality gives sama/ānanda; freely adopting/rejecting these is independent sahaja. Svānanda union joins worlds/Brahmans in nondifference; ayoga excludes union/entry and māyā, described as nirvṛtti. He distinguishes Svānanda-residing Gaṇeśa from mere Svānanda identity, play/union from playless yoga; dissolution of both saṃyoga/ayoga is Gaṇeśa’s peace/full yoga, where with/without māyā distinction is delusion. Terms remain this teacher’s doctrinal maps, not cross-school equivalences.

Atri calls Buddhi fivefold mind and Siddhi deluding accomplishment, distinguishing dharma/artha/kāma/mokṣa and Brahman-state siddhis. Reflections in five mental activities and five desired sovereignties are described as Gaṇarāja form and jīva respectively; desire circles in their wealth. With fivefold mind destroyed and sovereignties dissolved Datta will become Gaṇarāja in peace-yoga. Atri urges leaving prior avadhūta path to become chief avadhūta by casting off great mind/sovereignty, offers prescribed Gaṇeśa mantra and ritually gives one-syllable mantra to his son; Datta bows and leaves.

Datta, explicitly Viṣṇu-form, worships Gaṇeśa on Gaṅgā’s SOUTH bank, relinquishes previous grounds and practices heart meditation/peace. After ONE YEAR he attains peace and becomes Gaṇapatya. Gaṇeśa freely visits his hermitage; Datta rises/bows/hymns family deity as yoga-peace, Siddhi/Buddhi and fivefold mind, sovereignty/delusion-maker/destroyer, Svānanda/saṃyoga, Sāṃkhya/videha/bodha/deha-dehī, ahaṃkāra/mahat/bindu/nāda/Guṇeśa and creator/preserver/destroyer/Sun/Śakti/all beings. He says sight blesses body/parents/lineage/learning/yoga/tapas; dances with tears/raised hair. Gaṇeśa takes him by hand and embraces.

Gaṇeśa declares Datta a yogin through his grace, with full unwavering peace and no future distinction; to deepen love he will stay here. Atri’s Gaṇeśa knowledge becomes direct realization here, so he calls it Vijñānakṣetra and himself Vijñānagaṇapa; sight gives peace and devoted residents receive peace-yoga near Datta. Śiva formerly realized knowledge here and was named Vijñāneśvara by him; Datta’s practice near Śiva gives friendship through grace. Datta’s hymn gives users yoga-peace/Brahman, four aims, all siddhis and knowledge. No separate desired-boon request is narrated before this declaration.

Gaṇeśa vanishes; saddened Datta meditates and by grace offers self in yoga-nondifference. Devotee Datta/master Gaṇeśa separation ceases, with servant established in master-form: ātmānivedana devotion through peace-yoga. Vijñāneśvara Śiva appears, embraces his new friend, says he meditated on this same Gaṇeśa here. Placing Datta foremost, Śiva/Brahmins install Gaṇeśa on Gaṅgā south bank and sages name Vijñānagaṇarāja. The Vijñāna field gives travelers peace-yoga/all siddhis; installation is JYEṢṬHA bright Caturthī, annually celebrated then. Gods/yogins/Gandharvas/siddhas/nāgas/people serve; hearing/reading Datta account gives all siddhis.

Durvāsas, explicitly Śaṅkara’s portion, performs tapas and reaches neti-Brahman yet remains intensely angry/unpeaceful and seeks peace. Atri gives the same knowledge as Datta. He meditates on Gaṇeśa in Mayūreśa field and through devotion is made peace-yoga endowed by Gaṇeśa. From then he is anger-free, peaceful great yogin/Brahman-knower; Sūta closes Atri sons’ accounts as Mudgala told Dakṣa. No tapas duration or exact mantra separately specified here.

Sūta resumes Manu offspring at Śaunaka’s request; Dakṣa asks their deeds. Manu’s fully dharmic sons are Priyavrata/Uttānapāda; ELDER Priyavrata sees bodily transience and goes to forest. Distressed Manu asks visiting Nārada to instruct him. Priyavrata rises/bows at Nārada’s arrival. Nārada affirms transience but says human body owes three debts and sustains world through dharmic acts: gods by yajña, ancestors by śrāddha, human debt by progeny. He urges rule first, discharge debts, establish sons in kingdom, then go to forest for yoga. Affectionate son address is teacher speech, not replacing Manu parentage.

Priyavrata asks Nārada how one attains Brahman. Nārada teaches Gaṇeśa as yoga/lord of groups: outer/inner groups such as food are Brahman, their lord grants peace. He calls Gaṇeśa family deity, says ancestor Guṇeśa worshipped him to become Brahman; Brahmā/Viṣṇu/Śiva/Sun/Śakti are Guṇeśa sons who worshipped for peace; Brahmā’s sons including his speaking group became liberated/all-knowing yogins by worship. Priyavrata should worship too. He gives him one-syllable mantra and all Gaṇeśa worship instruction.
