Brahmā and Manu arrive, sons bow. Brahmā again instructs grandson Priyavrata, who returns with Manu to city. Manu establishes TWO sons in rule, goes to forest and worships Gaṇeśa by yoga. Beyond five mind-grounds, leaving mind he becomes Brahman, attains peace-yoga, goes to Brahmaloka and remains worshipping Gaṇeśa. Priyavrata rules earth dharmically with policy/dāna/renunciation, wins fame; varṇa/āśrama people are content, truthful and devoted to duties.

Priyavrata has10 powerful dharmic sons: Āgnīdhra,Idhmajihva,Yajñabāhu,Vīra,Hiraṇyaretas,Savana,Ghṛtapṛṣṭha,Medhātithi,Vītihotra,Kavi. Kavi/Savana/Vīra do not desire rule; he appoints seven others to Jambū/Plakṣa/Śālmala/Kuśa/Krauñca/Śāka/Puṣkara respectively. He then goes to forest, receives yoga from Nārada, becomes Gaṇapatya and finally Gaṇeśa-formed through yoga; source calls no comparable king past/future. Mother not specified here.

Vītihotra has sons Ramaṇa/Dhātaki in Puṣkara, with regions bearing their names. Ring-shaped Mānasā mountain stands between,10000 yojanas high; residents live10000 years and constantly worship resident Brahmā. Sweet-water ocean surrounds, described64-lakh yojanas; at its end Lokāloka mountain has inhabited/lit side and other uninhabited/dark side, beyond Sun/Moon light. Many pure sweet Mānasā rivers have water that removes disease; fatigue/sweat absent. Island width is not separately supplied in this passage, so ocean measure is not recast as island width.

Medhātithi’s Śāka sons are Purojava,Manojava,Pavamāna,Dhūmrānīka,Citrarepha,Bahurūpa,Jagaddhara. Seven regions are assigned: Purojava,Manojava,Pāvamāna,Dhaumrānīka,Caitrarepha,Bahurūpa,Vaiśvadhāra. Seven chief mountains;10000-year youthful defect-free people;32-lakh-yojana island enclosed in equal-size curd-whey ocean. They worship Vāyu.

Krauñca has16-lakh-yojana width, seven regions/rivers/mountains and other lesser rivers. Ghṛtapṛṣṭha has seven region-ruling sons with eponymous regions;31 raw compound/name segmentation withheld separately. People live11000 years and worship water-formed Nārāyaṇa; equal-size milk ocean surrounds, and island is also called Śvetadvīpa. No merger with similarly named external-source places.

Hiraṇyaretas’s seven Kuśa sons Vasu,Vasudāna,Dṛḍharuci,Satyavrata,Nābhigupta,Vivikta,Devaka have eponymous regions. Seven boundary mountains and fast good-water rivers relieving distress;10000-year life;8-lakh-yojana island and equal ghee ocean. They worship Havyavāha/Agni.

Yajñabāhu’s seven Śālmala sons Surocana,Saumanasya,Ramaṇa,Devavarṣa,Āpyāyana,Pāribhadra,Vijñāta have eponymous regions. Seven mountains/fast rivers;4-lakh-yojana width and equal surā ocean; people live8000 years. A specific worship-deity is not independently supplied here.

Idhmajihva’s seven Plakṣa sons Śiva,Yavayas,Kṣānta,Kṣema,Subhadra,Amṛta,Abhaya have eponymous regions. Seven mountains/rivers;5000-year life;2-lakh-yojana width with equal sugarcane-juice ocean. Dharma-following inhabitants worship radiant rain-giving Sun.47 digital lakṣadvīpa spelling retained as reference context, not a new eighth island.

From Plakṣa through Śāka people keep varṇa/āśrama duties; Puṣkara has one common varṇa/āśrama path and equal character. These islands have no changing yuga measure/dharma: time/duties remain same. People are without greed/envy, mutually helpful, meritorious and satisfied with own spouses, enjoying karma fruits like gods. Worshipping respective island deity grants happiness and four states beginning sālokya; other three are not named here. Jambū detail begins next chapter; outer-island account closes here.

Brahmā recounts going to Kailāsa and seeing Nārada present an extraordinary fruit to Śaṅkara. Gaṇeśa and Kumāra both ask for it. Śiva asks Brahmā which child should receive it; Brahmā recommends the young Kumāra. Śiva gives it to him, angering Gaṇeśa. Brahmā then returns home intending creation.
outcome: A specific fruit-allocation decision precedes Gaṇeśa’s anger; no race or other unprovided test is inserted.

cause: Moon mocks the fierce manifestation.
details: Gaṇeśa takes a fierce form, creates an extraordinary obstacle and frightens Brahmā. Seeing this fierce elephant-faced form and the bewildered Brahmā, Moon laughs with his retinue. Angered, Gaṇeśa curses Moon to become unfit to be seen in the three worlds: whoever sees him will become a great sinner. The deity then leaves for his own abode with Gaṇas.
outcome: An initially broad sight-curse is pronounced before the later request for mitigation.

details: Moon becomes discoloured, distressed and described by the unresolved cintāmaye hṛde clause, regretting his childish wrongdoing and loss of beautiful, honoured visibility. The gods hear the curse; Fire, Indra and others approach Gaṇeśa. Their hymn identifies him with creation, protection and destruction, transcendent and qualified forms. They seek refuge, explain that Moon’s invisibility distress affects the whole world, and ask favour so Moon, themselves and the world can gain happiness.
outcome: Moon regrets the mockery and the gods explicitly seek mitigation for the world’s distress.

details: Pleased by the gods’ praise, the four-goal-giving deity, here speaking as Vikaṭa, invites them to choose a great desired boon, promising even what is impossible in the three worlds.
outcome: Boon invitation only; the issued read-only fragment ends before their exact response.

details: The gods ask favour for Moon, saying his restoration benefits all. Gaṇeśa first proposes that Moon remain unseen for one year, its half or half of that, or that they request another boon. They prostrate again. Vikaṭa says his words cannot become false, even if cosmic order changes, but he cannot abandon those taking refuge. He narrows the harmful sight to Bhādra bright fourth: seeing Moon knowingly or unknowingly then brings abhiśāpa and great distress. The gods joyfully accept, shower flowers and leave with permission to speak to Moon.
outcome: The initial year/half/quarter-year proposal is distinct from the final annual date restriction.

details: The gods tell Moon his mockery of the universal teacher endangered all three worlds. They explain their difficult intercession, warn against Bhādrapada-fourth sight and command him to seek Gaṇeśa’s refuge for purified form and fame. Moon follows. Indra instructs the one-syllable sin-removing mantra; Moon practices severe tapas in deep concentration on the SOUTH bank of Gaṅgā. The duration is literally daśadvādaśavarṣāṇi; a definite ten, twelve or twenty-two years is not chosen without support. Gaṇeśa is pleased and appears.
outcome: Indra’s explicit instruction and southern-bank tapas lead to appearance; the numerical phrase remains unresolved.

details: Gaṇeśa appears four-armed, huge, wearing red garlands/clothes, red sandal and vermilion, illuminating worlds beyond many suns. Moon trembles, steadies himself, infers the deity has come to grant a boon, bows and hymns obstacle removal, the three worldly goals, cosmic functions, Veda/Brahman and intelligence. He asks pardon for an offence caused by ignorance and compassion rather than abandonment of one taking refuge.
outcome: Moon explicitly requests pardon after the overwhelming appearance and hymn.

details: Pleased by praise and prostration, Gaṇeśa grants Moon his former form again. Bhādra bright-fourth sight nevertheless retains abhiśāpa, sin, loss and foolishness. For the dark-fourth vow, Gaṇeśa is to be worshipped at Moon’s rising and Moon is also to be worshipped and deliberately seen; otherwise the vow is fruitless. He orders Moon to remain as a digit on his forehead and gives a monthly-second grant, retaining the printed nabhasyaśca qualifier without inventing a new audience or month rule. Having received the boons, Moon becomes as before.
outcome: Personal form restoration, forehead digit and ritual sight rules are distinct grants and conditions.

details: Moon installs a Varada image with gods and sages; they name it Bhālacandra. He builds a jeweled golden temple and worships with sixteen services. After worship, the gods and sages grant that this site become famous as a siddhi-field and give every siddhi to observance practitioners. They return to their places; the deity withdraws his body, and the joyful Moon, regaining his radiance, returns to his own abode.
outcome: Actual installation, naming and site grant close the narrated arc, while61.9/35 semantic gaps remain.

details: Kṛtavīrya’s father accepts the explanation of the dark-fourth meal at moonrise and asks why dūrvā is especially dear to Gaṇeśa. Brahmā introduces Sulabha of southern Jāmbā city, a wealthy, generous and self-controlled kṣatriya versed in Vedas/śāstras and devoted to Vikaṭa. Wife Sumudrā is beautiful, faithful, god/Brahmin/guest-devoted and follows her husband’s mind. Purified after bathing, they sit together to hear Purāṇa. Poor Brahmin Madhusūdana, continually contemplating the supreme deity, arrives for alms in worn clothes; Sulabha joyfully bows.
outcome: Named household and poor visitor introduced before reciprocal curses.

cause: Mockery and angry reciprocal curses.
details: Deluded, Sulabha suddenly laughs at the poor Brahmin. Angered, Madhusūdana curses him to become a suffering plough-pulling bull. Hearing her husband cursed, Sumudrā angrily curses the Brahmin to the printed cakrivān/feces-eating state; he curses her to become a poor, cruel caṇḍālī eating excrement and urine. Abandoning their rare human bodies, Sulabha becomes the endlessly labouring bull, Madhusūdana a donkey, and Sumudrā the violent, impoverished caṇḍālī. The subsequent actual donkey form is recorded without inventing another interpretation of cakrivān.
outcome: Three actual changed births/forms follow the curses; no numeric curse duration is given.

details: The wasted Sumudrā/caṇḍālī wanders south of the city and sees Gaṇeśa’s temple with trees, birds and observance practitioners seeking wishes, sons, liberation or wealth. On Bhādra fourth, a city-wide Gaṇeśa festival meets a torrential storm. Driven and beaten from houses, she enters the temple holding fire; some beat her there, but yogins restrain them. She lights grass to warm herself. Wind carries one dūrvā sprout onto Gaṇeśa’s head. The cold-fearing donkey enters, and the bull, released from the plough, also comes by providence.
outcome: Unintended grass-offering occurs during three cursed beings’ storm refuge.

details: The bull and donkey eat her grass and fight with hooves and horns near the deity while people sleep. Dūrvā falls from their mouths onto Gaṇeśa’s trunk and feet, pleasing him. She strikes them with a staff and eats the offerings. People awaken at hoof sounds, beat and expel her with staff, fist, elbow and stones. Fearing contact, they bathe the deity with enchanted tīrtha water and worship afresh. They also beat all three and close the temple doors, leaving the trio without escape.
outcome: Further inadvertent offerings and renewed worship arise amid violence.

cause: The deity counts their unintended offerings and movements as worship.
details: The cries and movements of the trapped trio move Vikaṭa. He considers that their presence caused renewed worship, their dūrvā reached him and they performed many circumambulations. He declares one dūrvā offering on Bhādra bright fourth and circumambulation make a person honoured and worthy of his regard. He decides to take the trio to his own abode and sends Gaṇeśa-shaped Gaṇas with a festive vimāna, Gandharvas and Apsarases. The Gaṇas give them divine bodies, place them aboard and swiftly bring them to Gaṇeśa’s abode before astonished onlookers.
outcome: The three cursed beings actually receive divine bodies and Gaṇeśa’s abode.

details: Onlookers conjecture that former merit caused the destination. Yogins leave meditation and ask the Gaṇas how these grave wrongdoers gained a rare blessed end despite no visible piety. They would abandon their own observance to do that method: after uncounted dispassionate, air-fed austerity they still have not seen the deity and ask when his abode will be theirs.
outcome: An explicit efficacy question opens the Gaṇas’ nested dūrvā explanation; the outer conversation continues.

details: The rescuing Gaṇas tell the yogins that even Śeṣa and four-faced Brahmā cannot fully describe Gaṇeśa, whom Brahmā and Śiva praise. Dūrvā’s greatness is not known even to sages/gods and cannot be attained by sacrifices, gifts, tapas, vows or homa. They introduce an earlier Indra–Nārada conversation: Indra honours the visiting sage, seats him and asks why dūrvā is especially dear to Gaṇeśa.
outcome: The Gaṇas’ explanation embeds Indra–Nārada, which next embeds Kauṇḍinya’s teaching.

details: Nārada describes the sage Kauṇḍinya in Sthāvara city, with a wooded hermitage south of the settlement and lotus lakes populated by birds and other creatures. He meditates and performs intense tapas before a happy, boon-giving four-armed Gaṇeśa image covered in dūrvā, japping the six-letter mantra. Wife Aśrayā asks why he offers loads of mere grass daily when nobody is ordinarily pleased with grass, and what merit it gives.
outcome: Explicit sage, wife, ritual image/mantra and efficacy question introduced; this sage is distinct from the earlier city named Kauṇḍinya.

details: Kauṇḍinya recounts a festival in Dharma’s city with gods, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Nāgas, sages, Yakṣas and Rākṣasas. Dancing Tilottamā’s covering falls; Yama sees her breasts and desires to embrace and kiss her. Ashamed, he leaves the assembly; his semen falls on the ground. From it arises a flame-garlanded, distorted-faced, cruel man with terrible sounds, burning earth and reaching the sky with his hair, terrifying the three worlds.
outcome: Explicit semen-origin of the later named fire-demon; no intercourse with Tilottamā is narrated.

details: The assembly goes to Viṣṇu, hymns him and seeks help for the world. Viṣṇu goes with them to Gaṇeśa, recognized as capable of destroying the threat. Gods and sages praise obstacle-making/removing, universal witness, world-origin/protection/destruction and wish-granting qualities, asking what other refuge could remove fear. They lament an untimely dissolution and ask why the deity neglects them when all face death.
outcome: The threat produces a collective refuge plea through Viṣṇu.

details: Gaṇeśa compassionately appears as a beautiful, strongly radiant child with two arms reaching the knees, fine limbs, ornaments and costly clothes. The gods/sages rise, acclaim and bow, ask his identity and purpose, and infer Brahman’s child-form has come to rescue those who abandoned rites through Analāsura fear. The smiling child confirms their understanding and says he voluntarily came to kill the harmful demon.
outcome: Two-armed child manifestation explicitly announces the rescue purpose.

details: The child announces a means of killing the demon and directs the gods to carry it out. The following strategy clause is preserved as sarvair bhavadbhis taṃ dṛṣṭvā nodanīyo balād aham; its exact intended action remains unresolved. He tells them to watch his and the demon’s remarkable encounter. They joyfully yet uncertainly discuss his capacity and bow. Analāsura approaches as dissolution-fire, burning ten directions and devouring humans. The people cry out and sages flee, warning the child to escape before the fire kills him, comparing it with a great predator. Gaṇeśa stands firm like Himavat; they retreat far away, leaving him there.
outcome: The appointed encounter begins; the child remains after the rescuers flee. The precise preceding strategy is withheld.

details: Aśrayā asks Kauṇḍinya what occurred between the steadfast child and the fire-demon. Through Nārada’s narration to Indra, Kauṇḍinya says the advancing demon shakes earth and mountains, roars like thunder, drops birds from branches, uproots trees and leaves the sea without water. The child seizes the fiery demon by māyā power and swallows him before everyone, like the jar-born sage swallowing the ocean.
outcome: The demon is actually captured and swallowed; subsequent danger is internal fire.

details: Gaṇeśa considers that the demon entering his belly could burn the three worlds seen inside. Indra gives Moon to calm the fire; gods and sages praise Bhālacandra, but the throat-fire persists. Brahmā gives his mentally created maidens Siddhi and Buddhi, described through cooling lotus/water/Moon imagery, and tells him to embrace them. The embrace calms the fire only slightly. Viṣṇu gives a tender lotus, bringing Padmapāṇi praise; Varuṇa pours cold water; Śiva gives a thousand-hooded serpent binding the belly, giving the name Vyālabaddhodara. The throat is still not cooled.
outcome: Named cooling attempts have specific donors and limited or failed outcomes, not a single successful counter.

details: Eighty-eight thousand sages arrive, each placing twenty-one nectar-like dūrvā sprouts on the deity’s head. The fire finally subsides and Gaṇeśa is pleased. Knowing this, gods and sages offer more dūrvā. He declares even great or small devoted worship fruitless without dūrvā, and none gains its worship-fruit without it. Devotional offering of one or twenty-one at dawn gives a fruit not attained even by hundreds of sacrifices, gifts, vow accumulations, severe tapas or rules earned over crores of births.
outcome: Exact eighty-eight-thousand/each-twenty-one cooling succeeds and prompts the dūrvā requirement.

details: The gods worship again with dūrvā. The joyful deity roars, grants many unspecified boons and withdraws his child form. They call him Kālānalapraśamana, install an image in a built temple and name it Vighnahara. Victory gives the city the name Vijaya; obstacles being removed explains Vighnahartṛ. Bathing, giving, tapas and observance there become inexhaustible through his favour. Kauṇḍinya closes the account to Aśrayā, promises all-sin removal by reading/hearing it, then introduces another old history.
outcome: Capture, successful cooling, named temple/site and actual withdrawal close the bounded fire-demon account.

details: Kauṇḍinya recounts Nārada visiting Gaṇeśa after many days. The sage bows, praises the fruitful sight and stands with joined hands. Gaṇeśa holds his hand and seats him. Nārada says he came to report an astonishing matter and would depart after bowing. Gaṇeśa asks him to describe everything before returning to his hermitage.
outcome: Nārada receives an explicit invitation to tell the report.

details: Nārada reports Janaka of Mithilā as proud, generous and learned in Vedas and Vedāṅgas: he continually feeds and honours Brahmins with ornaments, clothing and gifts, gives wealth to poor, blind and destitute people, and grants petitions. Nārada wonders whether Gaṇeśa’s satisfaction accounts for undiminished wealth. On visiting, Janaka mocks him through pride in Brahman knowledge. Nārada praises Gaṇeśa as giver of the king’s devotional desires, but Janaka claims to be lord, giver, enjoyer, protector, maker, cause and instrument, with none other in three worlds. Angered, Nārada says God alone makes the world, challenges the king’s apparent religious display, and promises evidence soon.
outcome: The king’s attributed claims and Nārada’s challenge motivate the later test.

details: Having heard the report, Gaṇeśa honours Nārada with arghya, ornaments, flowers and sandal. With permission Nārada goes to Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha. Gaṇeśa comes to Mithilā to test the king’s devotion, wearing a repulsive old Brahmin form with bleeding wounds, flies and missing teeth. He stumbles, faints and falls amid children; people cover their noses and spit. At the royal gate he asks to be announced as an old, hungry Brahmin guest desiring a meal. Janaka orders his admission, observes his filthy clothes, trembling, bleeding and exhaustion, suspects a divine test, and resolves to satisfy him if merit allows.
outcome: The narrator identifies the disguised deity; Janaka separately conjectures a divine guest.

details: The guest says he came after hearing Janaka’s fame and asks food until fully satisfied, promising the merit of one hundred sacrifices. Janaka takes him inside, honours him and serves tasty food. The guest consumes the entire portion in one mouthful, then a mountain-sized portion in one mouthful, then prepared food sufficient for ten thousand. Rice is put to cook in innumerable vessels and he eats every finished batch.
outcome: Successive immense servings fail to satisfy the guest.

details: Some advisers conjecture that the guest is a Rākṣasa and gifts to such beings give no merit; others say even the three worlds could not satisfy him and urge offering grain. All palace, city and village grain is gathered and consumed, still without satisfaction. Messengers report none remains; Janaka lowers his head. The guest departs house to house asking food. Residents explain their grain was collected by the king and already eaten by him. He questions how he can leave unsatisfied after hearing Janaka’s unparalleled giving fame. Amid silence he finds the Brahmin home of Virocanā and Triśiras, enters like its owner, and sees no equipment or metal vessels.
outcome: Janaka’s resources are exhausted; the test continues in a poor couple’s home.

details: The couple sits on bare earth, with sky as covering, avoiding contact with metals. They eat unasked food, use water for their rites and maintain purity. Amid flies and mosquitoes their Gaṇeśa image is worshipped with flowers and leaves in exclusive devotion. The disguised guest says Janaka did not satisfy him and ostentatious action cannot preserve sattva; he asks anything in their house that could satisfy him. The couple wonders how they, poor people, can feed one whom an emperor could not, comparing a drop with rivers unable to fill the ocean. He says even a small devotional gift greatly satisfies him; abundant gifts without devotion or given for display are fruitless.
outcome: The guest explains why devotional giving differs from abundance without devotion.

details: The couple swears nothing remains except one dūrvā sprout left from the morning Gaṇeśa worship. At the guest’s request Virocanā offers that single sprout with devotion, imagining rice, pāyasa, varied cooked dishes, accompaniments and lickable or suckable foods upon it. He joyfully eats it; his stomach-fire immediately subsides, he gains complete satisfaction and embraces Triśiras.
outcome: One actually offered sprout accompanied by imagined foods satisfies the guest whom abundant actual food did not satisfy.

details: Gaṇeśa abandons the repulsive disguise and appears four-armed, lotus-eyed and trunk-bearing, holding lotus, axe, rosary and tusk, wearing costly crown, earrings, divine clothing and scents. He invites the couple to choose their desired boon. They ask for firm devotion wherever they are born, or liberation from the difficult ocean of transmigration, wanting nothing else. He assents with tathā, joyfully embraces Triśiras again and vanishes.
outcome: The deity explicitly assents and withdraws; no later death or selected alternative is invented.

details: Kauṇḍinya tells Aśrayā that this is why he offers dūrvā: the deity who remained unsatisfied by innumerable foods gained full satisfaction through one sprout. He states that hearing the offering’s greatness gives all wishes; devoted hearing or telling brings sons, wealth and enjoyment here and hereafter, Gaṇeśa devotion, and liberation for a desireless person.
outcome: Kauṇḍinya applies the completed test account to his own practice.

details: The rescuing Gaṇas say Aśrayā still doubts. Knowing her heart, Kauṇḍinya instructs her to take one dūrvā to Indra and convey his blessing and request: obtain gold equal in weight to this sprout, neither less nor more, and bring it back. She accepts the instruction and takes the sprout to Indra.
outcome: An exact equal-weight request opens a second demonstration, distinct from a request for abundant wealth.

details: Aśrayā asks Indra for gold at her husband’s instruction. Indra says a message could have sufficed for him to send gold; she insists on exactly the sprout’s weight, neither less nor more. He sends a divine messenger with her to Kubera, requesting the exact measure. Kubera laughs at the sage, Indra and Aśrayā for seeking so little, and gives much gold. She refuses it from fear of her husband and doubt about unequal weight. A goldsmith’s scale and then a merchant’s scale fail to balance the dūrvā.
outcome: Offering abundant gold does not satisfy the stated equal-weight condition.

details: An oilman’s scale also fails. A pot is attached and gold placed on one side, while the dūrvā’s pan descends. Kubera adds more gold, then all treasury wealth like a mountain; it still does not equal the sprout. He asks his unnamed devoted wife to climb into the pot and proposes to follow if that fails. She enters; it remains unequal. He adds the entire city and himself. Hearing from the messenger, Indra comes on an elephant and enters with his wealth, yet the sprout does not rise. Troubled, he invokes Viṣṇu and Śiva, who arrive with their cities and mount the pot; still the sprout does not rise.
outcome: The mounting sequence adds gold, treasury, wife, city, Kubera, Indra with wealth, and Viṣṇu/Śiva with cities without raising the sprout.

details: Śiva, Viṣṇu and Kubera descend. With Varuṇa, Indra, Fire, Maruts, gods, divine sages, Siddhas, Vidyādharas and Uragas, they go to Kauṇḍinya at day’s end. They bow and say his sight removes sin and earlier merit promises future good; his wife has taken all their strength. They confess they do not know the sprout’s greatness: even three worlds did not equal one offered with devotion upon Gaṇeśa’s head; sacrifices, gifts, vows, tapas and study do not match it, nor can they fully know the sage’s exclusive devotion, japa and tapas. All worship Gaṇeśa and the sage with their wives, hymn, dance and sing. The hymn names Brahmā, Hari, Śiva, Indra, Maruts, Fire, Vivasvān, Yama, Śeṣa, Varuṇa, Moon, Aśvins, the lord of speech, Garuḍa, Yakṣa king and Aṅgiras as unable to fully know the deity. Having pleased him, they obtain the sage’s permission and return home.
outcome: The gods acknowledge the experiment’s failure, praise the devotion, worship and depart.

details: Aśrayā now knows dūrvā’s greatness, trusts her husband’s words, worships Vighneśvara with dūrvā and bows to Kauṇḍinya. She reproaches her own doubt, praises his knowledge and compassion and asks pardon while taking refuge. The couple rises at dawn, collects dūrvā, bathes and offers it with exclusive devotion. They worship morning and evening continuously, relinquishing sacrifice, vow and gifts. Knowing this, Gaṇeśa compassionately brings them to his own abode.
outcome: Doubt resolves, sustained joint worship follows, and the couple actually reaches Gaṇeśa’s abode.

details: The Gaṇas state no Śeṣa, Brahmā, Hari or Īśvara can exhaust dūrvā’s greatness. Verse40 says the three worlds became equal by its leaf on a scale, while the preceding trial and26 say they did not equal the sprout; these formulations are retained without reconciliation. Remembering dūrvā removes threefold sin because it also recalls Gaṇeśa. Hearing, recounting or meditating the Cintāmaṇi-site greatness brings enjoyment and liberation. They explain that this caused the rescue vimāna for the three: dūrvā fell from the bull/donkey mouths and the woman’s warming grass through strong wind onto Gaṇeśa. Pleased, he purified them and gave his own presence. Even its scent satisfies him, incidentally or with devotion, still more offering it upon his head.
outcome: The Gaṇas explicitly answer the yogins’ rescue question; the scale wording remains unresolved.

details: Brahmā says the king and sages hear the messenger’s unprecedented dūrvā account. After bathing, they and servants worship Vināyaka with sprouts. They obtain radiant divine bodies, hear divine music, board a fine vimāna in divine clothes and scents, and reach Vaināyaka’s abode, some bearing his form. Townspeople who come to the celebration each offer twenty-one dūrvā, enjoy their allotted pleasures and eventually reach Gaṇeśa’s place; the vimāna moves upward through this merit. The discourse instructs devotees to worship with dūrvā, condemns deliberate omission through caṇḍāla and hell language, says seeing a dūrvā worshipper purifies another sinner, and permits one sprout when many are unavailable, multiplying worship a crore-fold.
outcome: The yogins/king/servants actually gain divine bodies and abode; townspeople’s later destination is also narrated. Disparaging prescriptions are attributed to the source.

details: Brahmā closes the dūrvā history to the king, calling hearing it sin-destroying, forbidding its telling to someone of wicked understanding and prescribing communication to a beloved son. Indra says the father hears this excellent account from Brahmā, rejoices, bows and returns to his own place with permission and wonder.
outcome: The nested dūrvā teaching closes; the father returns before the next dream-delivery account.

details: Śūrasena asks Indra what Kṛtavīrya’s father did next. Indra says the son-seeking king anxiously considers childlessness after hearing the Sankaṣṭa and dūrvā accounts. Verse3 calls the dreamer Kārtavīrya, while the waking king is explicitly Kṛtavīrya in13; the name variation is retained. He dreams of his father. They embrace, unable to speak through emotion. The father takes his hand, seats him and says Nārada reported his efforts for a son, prompting the father’s visit to Brahmā. Brahmā prescribed Sankaṣṭa-caturthī and promised offspring to the royal son once the vow removes sin. The father says the book was written according to Brahmā’s instructions, gives it, and tells him to practice for a year so Siddhivināyaka will be pleased and a son will result.
outcome: The father delivers a book and prospective remedy in the dream; the printed dreamer name remains under review.

details: The father vanishes; the king, explicitly named Kṛtavīrya, awakens and sees the book in his hand. Recalling the dream, he weeps from sorrow at separation and joy at obtaining the book. His ministers gather, urge care and ask the cause, saying his grief affects them. He explains the father’s appearance, gift, immediate disappearance and instruction to practice for a son, and says wonder, joy and sorrow arise because the book remains in his hand after waking.
outcome: Actual waking possession of the book is narrated separately from the ministers’ interpretation.

details: The ministers infer that Gaṇeśa, father of all, came as the king’s father and gave the remedy, arguing the book and true dream otherwise lack an explanation. Indra says the king steadies himself, summons scholars and friends, and asks the book’s meaning. The Brahmins identify a Brahmā–Kṛtavīrya dialogue, Sankaṣṭa-caturthī, detailed moonrise worship, Aṅgāraka-fourth glory, arghya mantras for tithi, Gaṇeśa and Moon, feeding and honouring twenty-one Brahmins with gifts, and distinct ordinary/white-dūrvā benefits. They call it fortunate and beneficial, removing distress by hearing and remembering. King and public rejoice and he honours them.
outcome: The divine father-form remains an attributed ministerial inference; scholarly interpretation prepares the king’s actual practice.

details: Kṛtavīrya gives the scholars abundant clothing, ornaments, jewels, wealth and grain. He summons Atri, explicitly guru of his own family. At an auspicious time he properly honours Atri and Vināyaka and receives the one-syllable vidyā. Controlling senses, meditating Gaṇeśa and japping with exclusive devotion, he actually practices the Sankaṣṭa vow to please Gaṇanātha and obtain a son.
outcome: Family guru instruction and actual observance follow; no child is born in this chapter.

details: Śūrasena asks Indra how Brahmā taught Kṛtavīrya the successful Sankaṣṭa vow. Indra recounts the father approaching Brahmā in Satyaloka and asking what people in distress, anxiety, separation from friends, difficult undertakings, or seeking wealth, sons and good fortune should do. Brahmā prescribes the wish-accomplishing vow: daytime bathing with herbs and white sesame, proper intention and Gaṇeśa meditation, and devotional worship with Āgama mantras on dark fourth at night’s moonrise. The king asks the exact worship method.
outcome: Brahmā answers a general remedy request and specifies time, preparation and ritual authority.

details: After daily rites at moonrise, prepare a clean cow-dung-coated place with a pavilion and honour Gaṇeśa’s seat with kuṅkuma and rice. Set a kalaśa with five gems and a gold vessel; silver, copper or bamboo is permitted when unavailable, and cloth according to ability. Draw the Āgama-prescribed yantra and install a well-formed gold image. Meditate one-tusked, huge, molten-gold-coloured, large-bellied, wide-eyed Gaṇeśa with fire-like eyes, riding a mouse, fanned by Gaṇas, with Śeṣa as sacred thread. Invoke him to remove distress and remain present until the vow ends.
outcome: The image/mount/thread are meditation instructions; no actual travel or new birth is inferred.

details: The parenthetical ritual alternatives recite Puruṣa as thousand-headed, thousand-eyed and thousand-footed, embracing what has been and will be; Virāj arises, and Puruṣa arises from Virāj. Gods perform sacrifice with Puruṣa as offering, spring as ghee, summer as fuel and autumn as offering-material; gods, Sādhyas and sages worship the primordial sacrificial Puruṣa. From the sacrifice arise the curd-ghee mixture and aerial, forest and village animals, Ṛc/Sāman/metres/Yajus, horses, creatures with teeth on both sides, cattle, goats and sheep. The bodily social formula assigns mouth to Brahmins, arms to Rājanyas, thighs to Vaiśyas and feet to Śūdras. The cosmic formula gives Moon from mind, Sun from eye, wind/breath from ear, Fire from mouth, interspace from navel, heaven from head, earth from feet and directions from ears. The gods bind Puruṣa as sacrificial animal with seven enclosures and twenty-one fuel-sticks; the closing alternative praises ancient Sādhyas in heaven. These are prescribed Vedic recitations, without a new narrated Gaṇeśa birth or universal biological identity assertion.
outcome: All named cosmogonic formula roles remain source-attributed ritual assertions.

details: The prescribed offerings proceed through seat, foot-water, gem-and-fruit arghya, sipping water from Gaṅgā and other tīrthas, pañcāmṛta of milk/curd/ghee/sugar/honey, bathing with Narmadā, Candrabhāgā and Gaṅgā-confluence waters, two garments, sacred thread, sandal, ghee/kuṅkuma rice, campaka/mallikā/dūrvā and other flowers, and fragrant incense. The formulas repeatedly ask acceptance and distress-removal, addressing Gaṇeśa as Gaṇādhīśa, Umāputra, Modakapriya, Lambodara, Ibhavaktra, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Vināyaka, Paraśudhārin, Īśaputra, Mūṣakavāhana, Mahākāya and Dhūmraketu. Parenthetical Puruṣasūkta alternatives accompany many services.
outcome: The service formulas supply petitions and source-specific epithets; they are not new narrated biological scenes.

details: Continue with lamp, modaka/apūpa/laḍḍū/pāyasa with sugar and ghee-cooked food, coconut/grapes/mango/pomegranate, areca/cardamom/clove/betel leaves, gold dakṣiṇā, and twenty-one dūrvā with a twenty-one-name list. Offer camphor light and campaka/aśoka/bakula/pārijāta flower handfuls. The hymn attributes creation, protection, destruction and universal appearance to the elephant-faced deity; the bowing formula praises obstacle-removal, devotee relief, liberation, knowledge and Vedic foundation. Parenthetical Vedic alternatives include Puruṣa-body social and cosmic emanations.
outcome: Offerings, names and cosmic praise remain explicitly within prescribed recitation.

details: After the hymn bow repeatedly and make twenty-one circumambulations according to ability. The prayer says those seeking tasks without worship of Gaṇeśa are ruined. Offer vāyana to the Brahmin teacher and special arghya with fruit, flowers, rice, water and dakṣiṇā. Invoke Heramba for distress-removal and honour Indra and the surrounding world guardians. Prepare ghee-cooked modakas with cooked mung and sesame and other foods/betel as able, then offer twenty-one dūrvā separately using the verse names. This second sequence includes Abhayaprada, Amareśvara, Gajavakra and Sarvavidyāpradāyaka alongside names shared with the earlier list; the distinct printed forms are retained.
outcome: Circumambulation, teacher offering, guardian worship and separate sprout-name sequence extend the prescribed services.

details: Request satisfaction with the properly directed worship, fulfillment of inner wishes, removal of obstacles and present enemies, destruction of enemies’ intelligence and prosperity of friends. Bow repeatedly and perform one hundred eight homa offerings. For vow-completion prepare vāyana of modakas or laḍḍū/vaṭaka and other foods with twenty-one fruits, wrap in red cloth and give to the teacher. Hear the sacred story and offer arghya to the tithi, then Gaṇeśa, then Moon seven times. The Moon formula calls him milk-ocean-born, arising in Atri’s lineage, accompanied by Rohiṇī. Ask the deity’s pardon, feed Brahmins, eat their offered remainder silently in seven mouthfuls according to ability and comfort, and perform this procedure in all four months.
outcome: The detailed worship chapter ends with monthly repetition; the broader explanation and udyāpana continue.

details: The king asks who first practiced and disclosed the vow and what merit/results it gives. Brahmā says Pārvatī practiced at Śiva’s instruction for four months when Skanda was gone and saw Kārttikeya in the fifth. Agastya desiring to drink the ocean practiced and drank it through Vighneśa’s favour in three months. Damayantī searching for Nala practiced for six months and then saw him. These are brief source reports; no unprovided journeys or battle details are added.
outcome: Three retrospective exempla give specific practice intervals and actual reported outcomes.

details: Citralekhā had taken Pradyumna’s son away. Grieving and uncertain where or by whom he was taken, Pradyumna hears Rukmiṇī address him as her son. She recalls Śambara abducting him when he was six days old, many years of grief and comparisons with other women’s growing sons, then Lomaśa’s fortunate visit and instruction in Sankaṣṭa-caturthī. She practiced four times; through its favour Pradyumna returned after killing Śambara in battle. She urges him to practice the same vow so he will learn where his son is.
outcome: Rukmiṇī’s retrospective rescue experience becomes explicit mother-to-son instruction for a new search.

details: Brahmā says Pradyumna practices the pleasing vow and hears from Nārada that the son is detained in Bāṇāsura’s city. At Uddhava’s instruction Kṛṣṇa, fearing a battle with Īśvara, properly practices the vow once. He goes to Śoṇitapura, defeats Bāṇāsura in combat, and quickly brings Aniruddha with Uṣā.
outcome: Nārada locates the detained son; one vow, actual combat victory and retrieval follow. No weapons or marriage ceremony are supplied here.

details: Brahmā says he too performed the vow desiring creation and produced varied creation through its power. Gods, asuras, humans, sages, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Uragas and Rākṣasas also practiced to quell obstacles. He instructs practice during distress, hearing the story, silent eating with hands between knees while meditating Gaṇeśa, and sharing the Brahmins’ remainder with relatives. Tasks accomplish in few months. Teach neither non-devotees, atheists nor deceitful people, but a son, pupil or virtuous devotee. Calling the king dear, righteous and a worker for public good, Brahmā says to perform this before other vows; men and women should perform it before intended tasks.
outcome: Reported creation and wider practitioners support instructions, timing and transmission restrictions.

details: Sūta says the king hears and properly performs the vow for relief from all distress. Its power enables him to conquer enemies and enjoy an untroubled kingdom with sons. This closing statement reports the royal outcome concisely; the witness proceeds to a further completion procedure and fuller sonbirth account, so it is not treated as exhaustive closure of the larger Kṛtavīrya family history.
outcome: A source closing outcome is recorded separately from the following fuller family account.

details: The king asks Brahmā to explain udyāpana for public benefit. Brahmā prescribes vow-completion in the first, fifth or seventh month. Make a flower pavilion decorated with various fabrics and a multicoloured sarvatobhadra arrangement; worship on a kalaśa as before with sandal and flowers. Give coconut arghya to the tithi, Gaṇeśa and Moon. Their formulas ask distress-removal; the Moon formula again gives milk-ocean and Atri-lineage origin and Rohiṇī accompaniment. Offer edible, chewable, lickable, drinkable and suckable foods and many fruits.
outcome: Exact alternative completion months and separate recipient sequence are prescribed.

details: Choose a teacher and twenty-one officiants. Perform ten thousand homa offerings with Gaṇānāṃ tvā, or use the root mantra for one thousand, half that, or one hundred eight offerings; then give bali, full offering and vasordhārā. Finish homa and feed Brahmins. Give paired garments, kalaśas, dakṣiṇā and seats according to capacity without deceit about means. Honour the fed teacher with clothes/ornaments and give fruit-vāyana, a winnowing basket filled with pāyasa wrapped in red cloth, the gold Gaṇeśa image with dakṣiṇā, an āḍhaka of sesame, and an adorned kapilā cow with calf. Request the Brahmins’ pardon, praying Vighneśa be pleased. Completing udyāpana gives horse-sacrifice merit.
outcome: Completion protocol reaches its stated merit and closing pardon request.

details: Kṛtavīrya’s father says Brahmā gave him these instructions for public benefit and tells his son to practice carefully for offspring. Indra says the intelligent performer follows every paternal instruction; verse19 names him Kārtavīrya, retaining the same name issue flagged in68. Learned scholars explain the vow. A gold image with Siddhi and Buddhi is installed in a great pavilion amid Brahmin recitation, Purāṇa learning, singing, dance, heavenly-reaching instrument sounds and some debate with mediators. The king japs, offers homa, worships and feeds many Brahmins. Adorned himself, he gives ten thousand cows to adorned Brahmins, food and many gifts to poor, blind and destitute people, then receives the truthful ascetic Brahmins’ blessings for a son.
outcome: Actual observance, ten-thousand-cow giving and requested son-blessings follow; gold image companions are not a new marriage narrative.

details: Through the Brahmins’ blessings the royal wife becomes pregnant within a short time and gives birth at an auspicious moment to a son with marks. Delighted, the king gives many gifts, later performs the son’s vratabandha and marriage, and consecrates the knowledgeable son in the realm. Enjoying a good son and pleasures, he reaches the Lord’s state at the end. All officiants, scholars and onlookers reach Gaṇeśa’s abode through his merit. This is the chapter’s concise outcome; chapter72 begins a fuller account of that son and is not yet extracted.
outcome: Pregnancy, actual birth, later rites, succession and collective abode are reported. Exact royal actor variation and detailed72 chronology remain open.

details: Kīrti asks about simultaneous feet at Tuṇḍana and Kāśī; the sage answers by cosmic omnipresence, unlimited forms and divine will.
Divodāsa’s character, Brahmā kingdom grant and exclusion of gods; tapas/rain and righteous administration relieve drought. Wife’s naming remains under review.
Drought precedes Śiva’s visit to the ten-thousand-year ascetic; own form/realm granted. Gods inspect a faultless king and stay in Kāśī.
The kingdom’s duties, worship and crops remain faultless. Successive envoys cannot find or create a fault and settle in Kāśī.
Śiva asks a māyā strategy to reduce royal merit; Dhundhi promises, honors family/guru and adopts an astrologer disguise.
Thought/dream/palm knowledge and effective healing, progeny and three-day wealth grants win people’s attention.
Court women abandon household duties; king forgets his former deity. Astrologer declines material patronage and directs obedience to a visitor on the seventeenth day.
King vows obedience. Viṣṇu’s Bauddha and Kamalā roles draw people from ritual duties through source-attributed māyā teachings, producing wrong.
Visitor links royal merit to residence; four-armed revelations, reflection and recognition lead the king to refuge, liberation request and royal-seal surrender.
Viṣṇu reports the abandoned kingdom; Divodāsa gives up insignia, installs his liṅga and waits in tapas.
Dhundhi sends for Śiva; the bull-riding return favors the fasting sage and brings praise of cosmic functions and divine precedents.
Śiva asks continuing protection and states worship/name/hymn phalas, installs the Gaṇḍakī image and actually gives Divodāsa liberation. Sage closes the beneficial māyā account.
The sage departs. Mother and son go to the Kāśī festival, offer roadside leaves/flowers, remain fasting and receive the ten-armed vision and boon invitation.
After a hymn and revival recap, Kīrti asks her son’s devotion, fame, detached rule, long life, virtues, strength and victory.
All requests granted, with thousand-year life/thousand sacrifices, end-remembrance/form promise; own axe given and Parśubāhu name assigned.
Homecoming, parental embrace/report and coronation rites; father takes forest-dwelling initiation and son begins rule.
A thousand-year righteous reign, constant leaf worship, wives/sons and generosity; succession followed by heaven for many kalpas in Dhundhi’s form.
Mudgala predicts the child manifestation and royal-house visit, promises the devoted king access to Nijaloka, and leaves him waiting.
The narrator previews the child’s past acts and return. The king’s intense separation alarms ministers; Mudgala visits and restores his awareness.
The king requests bodily arrival and a long stay rather than wealth. Mudgala grants arrival without return and states earthly and cosmic-duration terms, whose relation remains unresolved.

Mudgala transmits Kapila’s account of grace-based access, cosmic/yogic form, supporting Śaktis, palaces, ocean, lotus bed, attendants and freedom from bodily suffering. He directs exclusive devotion and departs; the narrator previews five thousand years of rule and bodily departure.

The revived child cannot pronounce the six-syllable mantra already taught. Kīrti asks an easy, effective formula leading to rule. Gṛtsamada gives his own four-syllable Dhundhirāja name, explains śamī worship and its royal/enemy-destroying benefit, and answers her request for the deity’s identity and history by beginning Durāsada and Divodāsa accounts.
Daily gifts and requests for devotion culminate in the Māgha Tuesday fourth assembly; the king waits for the promised vehicle.
Pramoda and Āmoda arrive by divine command, receive worship and convey the Lord’s longing and urgent instruction to bring the king.
The king entrusts his son and subjects to two ministers, embraces everyone and boards bodily. His body shines like the Sun; the escorts carry him at wind speed.
The king sees suffering Bhūtas, Pretas and Piśācas and asks their identity.
Slander, malicious tale-bearing and theft lead to this suffering realm.
Terrifying inhabitants have upright hair, gaping mouths, lolling tongues and cloud-like voices. Abandonment of śrauta/smārta rites leads here.
Silver/gold palaces and jeweled floors host beautiful singers and dancers. Temple singers attain it through great merit.
Varied vows, gifts and accumulated merit lead to this great city.
A hundred aśvamedhas, gifts of gold, gems, cows, chariots, horses and elephants, and holy-water pilgrimage lead here. The king sees the palace he had heard of.
Agnihotra practitioners shine with Fire’s radiance.

Good deeds bring enjoyment; bad deeds bring hell suffering, including Kumbhīpāka cooking, Asipatraka cutting, iron hammers, thorns, Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra and a worm/pus pit. The king shuts his eyes and begs to move on.
Gem/gold palaces surpass Indra’s city; gem/gold gifts and many crore tulādānas secure this destination.
Holy-water and food gifts lead here; donors of water through wells, ponds and tanks reside happily in water, with bodies described as dry.
Summer gifts of fans and water with vetiver/camphor bring residence with free movement.
Five-fire austerity and Sun devotion bring fulfilled wishes, Sun-like radiance and untroubled residence.
Pearl/gold gifts and Soma sacrifice lead here through great merit.
The proper gift of a thousand cows to brāhmaṇas brings residence.

Truth, Vedic study, good conduct, śāstra/Purāṇa learning, food gifts, sacrifice, pilgrimage, nonaccepting brāhmaṇas, helping others, tapas and generosity lead here. It spans eight thousand gavyūtis each way. Sages, royal/divine sages, Dānavas, Gandharvas and Apsarases serve/praise Brahmā. The king expresses gratitude.

Viṣṇu devotion, sesame-food/cow gifts, Gītā study and helping beings lead here. The bathing terms ūrjasnāyī, jhaṣasnāyī and meṣasnāyī are preserved unnormalized. The realm spans five thousand yojanas, with Viśvakarman’s gem/gold/silver palaces excluding darkness; Viṣṇu resides with Lakṣmī.
On Meru’s peak, ten thousand yojanas broad, it has Sun/Moon-like palaces. Five-syllable and Rudrādhyāya recitation and other meritorious practices lead here.

Through darkness and deafening bees, the king faints at Bhrāmarikā and trembles at Ādhāra; the escorts reassure him and show Kāmadāyinī and the cosmic support. Some head-position wording remains unresolved.
The escorts show the radiant city, restorative water and gardens, then the party reaches the sugarcane-ocean shore and disembarks.
The party drinks sugarcane juice and sees Vināyaka’s lotus bed, divine ornaments, Siddhi/Buddhi and personified power/Śakti attendants.
The escorts report arrival. The king recognizes the two-armed child, weeps at his feet, and receives a fatherlike embrace and head-smelling; both rejoice.
Vināyaka explains past royal games, restoration of dharma, return to Kaśyapa and his own realm, and sending Mudgala because he missed the king.
The king praises feet, eyes and hands, cosmic guṇa functions, grace, protection and devotional liberation.
Invited to ask, the king acknowledges the fulfilled arrival and requests no future birth or death. Vināyaka assents and keeps him nearby for the raw stated cosmic duration.
Brahmā describes transmission through Nārada and Gautama to the sages and the hymn’s conditional benefits.
Vyāsa asks to resume the child’s actions after Śukla’s meal. Brahmā agrees; the narrative returns to an earlier chronology.

Mudgala says Jambū’s ruler has nine sons Nābhi, Kimpuruṣa, Hari, Ilāvṛta, Hiraṇmaya, Kuru, Ramya, Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla; he gives each an eponymous region. Father is called Jambū ruler here, not named; prior 10.4 identifies him as Āgnīdhra. The SEVEN Priyavrata sons, distinct from these nine grandsons, then enter forest, perform tapas, become Gaṇapatyas/Brahman-knowers and at the end attain Gaṇeśa’s abode without return through yoga-nondifference.
Jambū has one-lakh-yojana extent and a surrounding salt ocean. In its middle is golden Meru, with varied minerals/herbs, good-water rivers, caves and creatures.

Meru stands above/below earth’s middle, lotus-shaped, with surrounding mineral-rich lotus-petal-like mountains. Gods, Guhyakas, birds, yogins, Rākṣasas, siddhas, Nāga chiefs, sages, Gandharvas, Piśācas/Bhūtas dwell there; gardens for gods and waters remove age/sorrow. Eight chief mountains beginning Kailāsa stand in directions with Rudra and direction-lords; central great forest is Brahmā’s place. Nine Jambū regions: three south, three north, two east/west, one central; Himācala and other mountains bound them.

Regions have varied mountains/rivers and happy inhabitants. Eight regions excluding Ajanābha have stable natural siddhi, eternally youthful beautiful men/women enjoying like gods, good qualities/mutual attachment, equal time/enjoyment, varṇa/āśrama dharma and compassion; no changing yuga-dharma or heat/cold suffering.

Nābhi’s region Ajanābha lies near Himācala and is karma-ground. Actions there send people to other islands/regions/Pātāla/heavens to enjoy fruit; after enjoyment they return here for acts. Sin sends men/women to hell, then back. Yoga there makes yogin and devotion gives Gaṇapatya nature, so this region called Himalayan is esteemed highest/all-giving, though relatively little pleasure, heat/cold and many diseases. Four varṇas and mixed/different dharmas, yuga measures/duties and diverse self-interested dispositions occur here.

Vindhya, Sahyādri and many mountains arise with rivers from them. Sweet river waters give merit by mere bathing; inhabitants act with threefold conduct. Divine tīrthas/Brahmin places give greater act-born fruits to servants. This Ajanābha region is called Bhārata because it bears karma. Mudgala closes the brief earth-circle account; hearing/reading removes sins. This etymology does not assert a king Bhārata ancestry not narrated here.

Mudgala describes seven cosmic-egg worlds Bhūr, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapo, Satya. Bhūr is the walking-accessible seven-island region illuminated by Sun/Moon; Bhuvar runs from Bhūr to Sun, Svar from Sun to Dhruva with corresponding Bhūr extent. Eight Vāyu divisions are Āvaha, Pravaha, Annavaha, Saṃvaha, Vivaha, Parāvaha, Parivaha, Vaha. Distance sequence in yojanas: Earth→Sun 100000, Sun→Moon 100000, Moon→stars 100000, stars→planet zone 200000, planet zone→ṛṣi zone 100000, ṛṣi zone→Dhruva 100000. Dhruva is axis of luminary wheel, holding wind-rays and moving stars. These are source cosmography, not modern astronomical measurements.

Sun maṇḍala extent 10000 and Moon 12000 yojanas; Rāhu 10000 below Sun, maṇḍala 13000. Darkness-formed Rāhu moves at parvan and rapidly covers Sun/Moon with shadow; called eclipse. Bhārgava’s maṇḍala is 1/16 Moon; Bṛhaspati 1/4 less than Bhārgava; Bhauma/Saura 1/4 less than Bṛhaspati; Saumya 1/4 less than those. Star/nakṣatra maṇḍalas successively 500/400/300/200, smallest star 1 ½ yojanas. Fractions preserved as stated, without calculated replacements.

Three distant slow planets named Saura, Aṅgirā, Bhauma lie above four fast planets Sun, Moon, Budha, Bhārgava. Ordering upward: Sun, Moon, stars, Kavi/Bhārgava, Budha, Bhauma, Bṛhaspati, Śanaiścara, seven ṛṣis, Dhruva. Sun travels two ayanas and governs planets. Bhauma is above Soma’s son, referring to Budha; only this explicit patronymic is normalized as parenthood, not an invented Bhārgava/Bṛhaspati family.

Sun chariot 9000 yojanas and shaft twice that; axle one lakh anchored at Dhruva, second axle’s wheel on Mānasā mountain. Wheel is zodiac/twelve-spoked; seven horses are metres led by Gāyatrī. Southward ayana is fast, northward slow. On Mānasā are east Indra’s Amarāvatī, south Dharmarāja’s Saṃyamanī, west Varuṇa’s Sukhā, north Kubera’s Vibhā. Sun dawn at Indra city, midday Yama, evening Varuṇa, midnight Kubera; potter-wheel-like movement gives direction-dependent perceived times.

Sun rays sustain people and fill three worlds, making day/night. Water, earth and sky and whole god/demon/human world arise, are supported and end in Sun. Enumerated deities, stars, fire, plants, Brahmins/water draw their radiance from him; he distributes all brilliance for play. Prabhākara is all-self/lord, Gaṇeśa portion, root of three worlds and karma-formed deity. This is source cosmological praise/support, not a universal biological genealogy.

Twelve other Bhānus arise as Sun kalāṃśas and shine from chariot in 12 months/seasonal order beginning spring: Dhātā, Aryamā, Mitra, Varuṇa, Śakra, Vivasvān, Pūṣā, Parjanya, Aṃśu, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu. Their source-qualified solar manifestation roles are distinguished from same-name gods/lineages; no biological parentage inferred.

Twelve sages praise Sun with metres: Pulastya, Pulaha, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Kaśyapa, Kratu, Jamadagni, Kauśika. Grāmaṇī rein-holders: Rathakṛt, Rathaujas, Rathacitra, Svabāhuka, Rathasvana, Varuṇa, Suṣeṇa, Senajit, Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, Rathajit, Satyajit. Same-name Grāmaṇī Varuṇa is not silently identified with water-lord/solar portion.

Twelve Rākṣasa leaders advance before Sun: Heti, Praheti, Pauruṣeya, Vadha, Sarpa, Vyāghra, Vyādha, Vāta, Vidyut, Divākara, Brahmopeta, Yajñopeta. Nāgas carrying Sun across 12 months: Vāsuki, Kaṅkanīra, Takṣaka, Elāpatra, Śaṅkhapāla, Airāvata, Dhanañjaya, Mahāpadma, Karkoṭaka, Kambala, Aśvatara. Eleven Nāga names actually present; no twelfth filled from another text. Serpent Airāvata/Rākṣasa Divākara are not merged with same-name elephant/Sun.

Twelve singing Gandharvas: Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, Hūhū, Viśvāvasu, Ugrasena, Vasuruci, Avīvasu, Citrasena, Ūrṇāyu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūryavarcā. Twelve dancing Apsarases: Ghanastanī, Rambhā, Puñjikasthalī, Menakā, Sahajanyā, Pramlocā, Anumlocā, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Urvaśī, Pūrvacitti, Tilottamā; they delight Sun in seasonal order. Nārada retains issued source-local identity with this attributed singing role, no biological status change.

Sages hymn, Gandharvas/Apsarases sing/dance, Grāmaṇī Yakṣa-like beings hold reins, serpents carry and Yātudhānas advance. Vālakhilyas escort Sun rising→setting. Attendants heat/rain/shine/blow/create, remove evil acts when recounted, travel in wind-speed wish-moving vimāna, nourish/protect at yuga end. Sun assumes their forms, makes day/night, nourishes Pitṛs/gods/humans and is Gaṇeśa portion/time-self. Other 8 planets bind to Dhruva by wind-rays and receive Sun nourishment.

Moon three-wheel chariot has 10 jasmine-white horses left/right; star pathways and Dhruva support with waxing/waning. Sun Suṣumna ray replenishes Moon nectar drunk by gods in sequence over half-month. With little fifteenth-part remaining, Pitṛs attend in afternoon and drink for 2 LAVAS; remaining kalā is svadhā nectar issued through rays at amāvāsyā, giving monthly satisfaction. Moon does not perish from nectar drinking; Sun causes waxing/waning. No lava-to-modern-time conversion.

Budha/Soma-son chariot 4 wind-speed LIONS; Bhārgava golden 8 horses; Bhauma 8 RAMS; Bṛhaspati golden 8 REDhorses; Manda iron 8 BLUEvultures; Svarbhānu/Rāhu black lions and Ketu doves, counts unspecified. All 9 planet/star stations bind Dhruva by wind-rays; he revolves and moves them in every direction. No remembered horse substitutions.

Successive higher worlds each one-KOṬI-yojana apart: Dhruva→Mahar (kalpa-authorized enjoyers), Mahar→Jana (Sanaka-led sages in trasareṇu vimānas), Jana→Tapo (fearless Vairāja gods), Tapo→Satya (returnless Brahmā residence). Brahmā/yogins drink yoga nectar there; renouncers, constant brahmacārins, vow/tapas/siddha/sacrifice practitioners dwell. It is flaming gate for yogins going to supreme Gaṇeśa; beyond is unsupported/world-form-free. Cosmic-egg Virāṭ form extends through Satya.

Śakti world 2 koṭiyojanas beyond Brahmā world, unsupported luminous Mahāmāyā setting, 10000-yojana extent. Desireless Śakti devotees/yogins attain it. Resident Śaktis create same-form men by own brilliance and play with them in female form. This is cosmic manifestation/play, not ordinary biological procreation.

Solar world 4 koṭiyojanas beyond Śakti world, unsupported/eternal/luminous, extent equal to Śakti world. Sun-residents by śuklagati and desireless Sun devotees arrive, as radiant as Sun. Male-form Sun creates karma-māyā Saṃjñā from LEFT LIMB and continually plays with her. This solar-world origin is recorded alongside earlier 1.17’s Śakti-heart origin, without a single biological-birth claim or chronology harmonization.

Viṣṇu/Vikuṇṭha world 8 koṭiyojanas beyond Solar world, 10000-yojana extent, unsupported/eternal/luminous. Desireless devoted Vaiṣṇavas attain perpetual happiness and freely moving women/men reside. Viṣṇu creates Bhogalakṣmī from LEFT and Muktilakṣmī from RIGHT and plays in twofold māyā. Mukti form not automatically identified with Datta’s specifically manifested Mokṣalakṣmī.

Śaṅkara/Kailāsa world 16 koṭiyojanas beyond Viṣṇu world, 10000 extent, unsupported, luminous, delusion-free/happy. Desireless Śiva devotees arrive. Śiva plays by yoga: left is Prakṛti, right Puruṣa, their union ānanda; Nārāyaṇa-mayī Śakti and half-female/half-male Śiva. He separates that Śakti into THREE forms, unnamed here, and continually plays, delusion-free yet māyā-supporting. No three remembered goddess names or new biological spousal genealogy imported.

Beyond that Mahī lies Svānanda Brahman, described as supreme state in this teaching. Self-experienced Brahman is fourfold: Śiva unmanifest/neti/nirmoha, Viṣṇu sama, Sun self, Śakti asat; their nondifference/union is Svānanda. Every principle has its own Svānanda, with varied Brahmans such as space supporting successive hierarchy. Full Gaṇapati Svānanda is all-union samādhi; Gaṇeśa abides in each own-bliss as kalāṃśa for play and all siddhis. Hearing the briefly told higher worlds gives all wishes; no exact beyond-Mahī distance supplied.

Seven nether regions descending: Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Pātāla. Atala dusky, 10000 yojanas below Earth and 100000 extent; unnamed Maya-son, Namuci and Nāgas inhabit. Vitala white, 10000 below, inhabited by Nāga/Asuras Kambala, Śaṅkukarṇa, Hayagrīva, Jumbhaka. Sutala yellow similarly below, with Vainateya-led birds, Bali, Kālanemi and other fearless Nāga/demons. Vainateya patronymic retained for Garuḍa without an unstated father.

Talātala gravelly with Mayāsura, Bāṇa, Andhaka, Kālakeya and Nivātakavaca groups and carefree Nāgas. Mahātala black with Takṣaka/Nāgas and thousands of Hiraṇyapura-based demons fearless of gods. Rasātala stone-made, below, with Vāsuki-led Nāgas/demons, luminous sharp poisonous inhabitants. Pātāla blue, Śeṣa’s purposeful station; demons/gods/Nāgas worship the Nāga lord devotedly.

Śeṣa stands 30000 yojanas below Pātāla, Gaṇeśa devotee/portion, Viṣṇu kalāvatāra and called Kālarudra. Thousand-faced, powerful, poison-born flame burns entire world; deathless hence Ananta, he dissolves at Brahmā-day’s end and remains. Vāsuki-led Nāga kings, Prahlāda-led demons and Nāga women serve him; women worship for many desired successes, not a narrated grant of all requests.

1000 yojanas below Śeṣa is Viṣṇu’s tortoise/Kūrma station, served by Varuṇa and others; 1000 further below is Viṣṇu’s Varāha, served by Earth and others, giving fearlessness to devotees. Whole structure rests on Śeṣa; Śeṣa rests on Kūrma, Kūrma on Varāha. Unsupported Varāha remembers Gaṇeśa in heart and by that power supports all. No battle or Earth-lifting episode supplied here.

Below Varāha are purifying/punishing hells Raurava, Tāmisra, Mahāraurava, Andhatāmisra, Sūcīmukha, Lohadaṇḍa, Taptavāluka, Khaḍgapatraka, Lālāsya, Kṛmibhakṣya and many others, where sinners are cooked. Mudgala says the cosmic sphere cannot be fully expanded here; Dakṣa’s curse-delusion will end by Gaṇeśa worship and he will know truly. All cosmic eggs alike have 8 envelopes and Guṇeśa support; this is Gaṇapati’s egg-form briefly told. Devoted hearing/reading gives all, siddhis, enjoyment/liberation and sin-cover destruction.

Āgnīdhra is Priyavrata’s son, Nābhi his son. From Nābhi’s sacrifice arises a son described as Viṣṇu embodied in sacrificial kalā form, dwelling as his son; 16.8 supplies Ṛṣabha name. No mother named here.

Ṛṣabha has 100 sons with Bharata first; 81 become Brahmins through tapas; nine other Gaṇapatya yogins named Kavi, Hari, Antarikṣa, Prabuddha, Pippalāyana, Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa, Karabhājana are body-free, ūrdhvaretas and roam worlds. Nine rulers in Jambū’s regions have eldest Bharata chief; 8 calls him emperor of nine brothers. Ṛṣabha divides kingdom and goes forest. Counts 100/81/9/9 and emperor-of-nine-brothers are retained literally; total/category membership not reconciled.

Forest Ṛṣabha performs various tapas and yoga, becomes avadhūta, passes jada/unmatta/piśāca and sahaja states. He follows fourth, unmanifest, neti, delusion-free, independent Śaṅkara Brahman and teaches Śiva wherever he goes. Yoga reveals independence as defect, since Brahman neither depends nor is independent; loses peace, visits Śiva’s abode, receives honor, and is astonished by Gaṇapatya yogins who are Śiva disciples. No austerity duration stated.

Ṛṣabha hymns Śiva as yoga/world-support/Brahman lord, asks full peace-giving śāntiyoga, declares servant and disciple. He explains that sahaja was highest he knew but independence took peace away. Śiva joyfully teaches that Gaṇeśa is peace-yoga, origin/support/end of all, and promises peace through a secret he ATTRIBUTES to Sāmaveda. This witness’s Sāmaveda attribution is not independent quotation verification.

Śiva teaches ga as all visible/invisible mind-and-speech forms, ṇa as mind/speech-free saṃyoga/ayoga; their Brahmans are principles and nirodha. Both letters are Brahman-forms in Gaṇapati name, and Gaṇeśa their lord. Contemplate mind/speech and their beyond as Gaṇeśa and māyā. He illumines five mind-grounds, hence Cintāmaṇi; worship him as yoga and relinquish grounds for peace. Gaṇeśa transcends saṃyoga/ayoga; abandon māyā-born delusion for happiness. All statements are attributed instruction.

Śiva stops teaching; Ṛṣabha bows and returns forest. Practicing taught yoga he gradually attains peace. He still never abandons Gaṇapati, so Gaṇeśa comes near him. Ṛṣabha prostrates in joy, with tears/gooseflesh and folded hands, hymns. Actual peace precedes divine appearance and later devotion boon.
outcome: Ṛṣabha attains peace BEFORE Gaṇeśa appears.

details: Ṛṣabha hymns Gaṇeśa as Brahman beyond difference/nondifference, formless eternal world-form, infinite, beyond beginning/middle/end, Guṇeśa creator/preserver/destroyer, many-avatar protector of devotees, god/demon forms and worshipped by them, yoga-giver and lord of yogas/Brahmans, all-origin and final survivor, Heramba in nijānanda, Siddhi/Buddhi lord, giver of four aims and Brahman attainment. Vedas and Śiva-led gods cannot fully praise him. Hymn ontology is attributed to Ṛṣabha.

Ṛṣabha requests firm unwavering devotion, falls holding Gaṇeśa’s foot and is respectfully raised. Narrator calls him Śiva disciple/Śiva-wise and eternal Viṣṇu. Gaṇeśa promises immovable devotion and peace-giving hymn; whatever wished he grants through reciting/hearing it. God disappears; Ṛṣabha remains peaceful yogin and actually attains Gāṇeśatā. No extra immortality/wife/power request, or substitution of Gāṇeśatā for requested devotion.
outcome: Immovable devotion granted; Gaṇeśa disappears; Ṛṣabha attains Gāṇeśatā.

details: Devoted hearing/reading of Ṛṣabha’s account gives all, Brahman attainment and peace for peaceful minds. Account phala kept separate from hymn grant.

Mudgala polemically distinguishes Ṛṣabha’s renunciant conduct from its adoption by householders. An unnamed king sees/adopts it and abandons karmamārga; the account labels resultant path Jaina, says Bharata suppresses it and forecasts Kali-age adoption. Raw arhadgṛhe location/person wording at 1 not securely identified; no remembered Arhat king name supplied. These are this witness’s sectarian claims, not a universal historical account.

Ṛṣabha’s eldest son Bharata rules righteously, pleasing subjects, then entrusts kingdom to unnamed son and goes forest. At Śālagrāma āśrama he performs fierce tapas, weakens body gradually and meditates on Viṣṇu. No son-name or fixed duration stated.

While Bharata makes Pitṛ offerings at river, a lion’s sudden roar frightens a pregnant doe. She leaps into river fleeing; fetus falls into water and she dies farther away from distress. Bharata compassionately rescues and carefully raises fawn; fondling/playing becomes attachment and his tapas-related acts gradually depart, as he fails to see attachment fault.

Fawn goes with other deer into unknown forest. Bharata searches forest after forest, laments and dies in continued grief; at death he sees deer nearby. Because of attachment fault he is born as deer. Earlier tapas grants previous-birth memory, so he fears attachment, abandons deer company, returns former āśrama, practices nonviolence/turns from dualities, eats dry grass, remembers Viṣṇu, bathes in tīrthas and desires saintly company. This is narrated rebirth/memory mechanism, not a deity boon scene.
outcome: Deer rebirth with former-life memory; avoids attachment.

details: Wandering in forest by earlier merit, deer-bodied Bharata sees Pulaha āśrama. Sages there perform tapas and Gaṇeśa worship; he joyfully dwells near them, devoted to saintly company.

Brahmā visits Pulaha āśrama; Pulaha and sages bow, honor/worship him and Pulaha massages his feet. Pulaha hymns and asks how suffering beings attain enjoyments, liberation and Brahman. He addresses father; narrator/Brahmā call him son. Brahmā promises sin-destroying, peace-path teaching. Father/son retained in established cosmic creation context, not ordinary biological generation.

Brahmā says disregard for Vighnarāja brings fear/suffering/obstacles. Suffering is obstacle; hells yield wrongful-act fruits; karma yields heaven’s enjoyments, yet heaven contains duality, male/female delusion, demons’ danger and final dissolution death fear. Cosmic egg is born/destroyed and guṇa-afflicted. Akarma gives liberation, yet liberation also has obstacles: embodied self bound by delusion in four bodies gains freedom by practice, and delusion’s presence/absence remains obstacle. Body/self Brahman imagined in yoga is divided by vikalpa; nirvikalpa own-glory still retains the distinction of with/without vikalpa. All claims are Brahmā’s teaching.

Brahmā’s Sāṅkhya/Brahman discussion uses svātmaniṣṭha/asvātmaniṣṭha, aparotthāna and seed/seedless contrasts. Clear thrust criticizes persistence of obstacle/seed of arising; precise relation of asvātmaniṣṭha generation/non-making at 42–43 is not normalized into English causal ontology. Raw source clause retained.

Svānanda Brahman/samādhi has own-union and nondifference; Brahmā says its arising/return by yoga carries anvaya flaw/obstacle. Beyond it ayoga remains distinct/no union, but separateness/vyatireka flaw also obstructs peace. Abandon both saṃyoga and ayoga for obstacle-free peace; relinquish five mind-grounds for yoga-nondifference. Fivefold mind is Buddhi/māyā; fivefold sovereignty-delusion is Siddhi. Gaṇeśa reflection falls there in yoga-form, a twofold māyā-reflection to relinquish. This is source teaching, not universal physical mechanics.

Brahmā recalls earlier teaching their family deity Gaṇeśa and Pulaha’s respectful worship, making him fit for yoga-peace. Now he teaches full peace and instructs continual prescribed śāntiyoga worship, with future Gaṇeśa state promised. Brahmā disappears; Pulaha stays in tapas/practices yoga. Earlier teaching not separately dated here.
outcome: Brahmā disappears; Pulaha practices yoga/tapas.

details: Pulaha gradually attains yoga-peace, daily devotedly worships Gaṇeśa image and meditates only on him. After unspecified time Gaṇeśa comes, but absorbed sage does not notice. Gaṇeśa makes heart-resident Dhuṇḍhi disappear; Pulaha cannot see inner form, looks as if bewildered and sees Gaṇeśa outside. He rises, bows, worships by rule and hymns with joy/gooseflesh. Divine removal of meditation-form, not destruction of the god or killing event.

Pulaha hymns Vighnarāja as removing devotee obstacles/giving nondevotee obstacles, Brahman/formless/witness/eternal/beyond argument, Vakratunda/Heramba/Svānanda dweller, devotee protector, yoga/peace giver, many-avatar/world support, god/demon lord, all-origin/many-middle/single-end, beyond beginning/middle/end, creator/preserver/end-maker, Lambodara/elephant-face/ears, four-armed, four-aim/Brahman embodiment, mouse-banner/mouse-mounted and holding noose/goad. Vedas, yogins and Śiva/Viṣṇu-led gods cannot praise completely; he bows and asks lasting favor. Source hymn attribution, not universal physical assertion.

Pulaha requests firm unwavering devotion; overwhelmed by love he dances. Gaṇeśa grants firm unwavering joy-giving devotion, and promises appearance near him whenever he remembers. Hymn gives devotion, enjoyment/liberation and peace-yoga; human reciters/hearers gain all happiness and become like Pulaha. God disappears; Pulaha remains and worships. No fixed appearance-duration or immortality request.
outcome: Gaṇeśa disappears; Pulaha remains worshipping.

details: Deer-bodied Bharata dwelling there hears full knowledge, holds Brahmā’s instruction to Pulaha continually in heart, and joyfully meditates on Gaṇeśa while staying there. Narrator says full knowledge; this records reception, not independent resolution of 17.42–43 dense teaching grammar.

Bharata reflects that after leaving kingdom and remembering Hari, attachment to deer nevertheless made him deer-bodied. He attributes victory over difficult obstacles by Śiva/Viṣṇu-led gods/all beings to Vighnarāja grace. He praises earlier Vaiṣṇava devotion for saṃskāra leading to excellent knowledge, and fortunate meeting Gaṇapatya yogin Pulaha/ongoing saint company, now worshipping Gaṇeśa without obstruction. In time, devoted to Gaṇeśa and meditating on him, he abandons deer body. No new birth narrated within 18 and no express new liberation grant.
outcome: Meditating on Gaṇeśa, Bharata abandons deer body; next life outside bounded arc.

details: Śūrasena asks Indra for the detailed birth of the couple’s son after the vow. Indra says that through pleased Gaṇeśa’s favour the queen conceives and in the ninth month sees a son with two shoulders, beautiful face, nose and lotus eyes but no arms/hands, thighs/knees, lower legs or feet. She laments the gift, says remaining barren would have been better, questions removal of prior sin, the deity’s favour and Brahmin assurances, and repeatedly strikes her breast and forehead. The women weep; the king, ministers and townspeople hear and join the grief.
outcome: Actual sonbirth and the detailed absence of limbs are narrated before the remedy; no normal-limbed birth is substituted.

details: The king questions Gaṇeśa’s compassion and declares his japa, tapas, remembrance, gifts, worship, Brahmin feeding, observance and homa apparently wasted. He says fate is stronger and effort fruitless, comparing the son with a mouse gained by breaking a mountain. Ministers urge him to cease grief because what must occur cannot be changed: they cite Rāma following the deer and Dharmarāja entering forbidden dice and then forest exile despite knowledge. Crying will not make the child beautiful; good unseen merit could allow his later improvement and kingship with time, as trees bear flowers and fruit. The king steadies himself and tells his wife to rise without grief. The king’s first verse is printed1 before the numbering resumes12; this span follows its sequential position.
outcome: Attributed fatalist complaint is answered by ministerial counsel and an explicitly prospective possible improvement.

details: The king calls Brahmins, performs Gaṇeśa worship, svastivācana and auspicious śrāddha, and gives garlands, ornaments, clothes, cows and jewels. He gives clothes and appropriate gifts to friends, relatives, servants, musicians, bards, Cāraṇas and poor, blind and destitute people, distributing betel and sugar house to house. On the eleventh day he names the son Kārtavīrya and feeds the city with enthusiasm. Twelve years of the son’s life pass; Dattātreya voluntarily comes to his house.
outcome: The boy receives an explicit name on day11 and reaches age12 before the voluntary sage visit.

details: The king explicitly named Kṛtavīrya bows with his head at Dattātreya’s feet. The sage rises and embraces him. The king seats and honours him with seat, foot-water, arghya, a cow, clothes, sacred thread, incense, lamp, offerings, varied fruit, rubbing powder, betel, jewels, gold dakṣiṇā and foot-massage. When the sage is pleased and comfortably seated the king addresses him; the read-only fragment stops before the request.
outcome: The visitor is welcomed before the exact request and explanation; the next primary unread verse is31.

details: Kṛtavīrya says many births’ merit now bears fruit in seeing Dattātreya and predicts future good from his favour, since wrongdoers do not see such sages. Dattātreya explicitly says he came to see the king’s extraordinary son. The king again laments his apparently fruitless practices and describes the son as a thorn in his heart. He brings the boy; the sage covers his eyes, then knows the relevant action through meditation. He predicts this very son will conquer all and diagnoses the king’s failure to perform ācamana after yawning during the Sankaṣṭa vigil as dishonouring the distress-removing vow. The son was born without limbs but can become complete through a remedy. The king accepts the diagnosis and asks what method will restore his son through the sage’s favour.
outcome: Meditative diagnosis identifies one exact ritual omission; the father asks a remedy, without a new unnamed sin being invented.

details: Compassionate Dattātreya teaches the CHILD the one-syllable mantra with its auxiliaries and prescribes devotional Gaṇeśa worship with it, fasting and one-meal rules. He predicts that after twelve years Gaṇeśa will give the child sight of himself and the deity’s mere glance will produce a divine body. Taking leave of the king, the sage disappears.
outcome: Actual guru instruction is distinguished from the future appearance-and-glance prediction.

details: After Dattātreya leaves, the footless son asks Kṛtavīrya to take him to a deep forest so he can practice for Gaṇeśa’s favour. Both parents weep at his request. The father sends him to a fine forest in a human-carried conveyance; servants place him in a leaf hut and return to the city. The boy remains there, firmly resolved on tapas.
outcome: Actual relocation with servants and a leaf hut prepares the child’s separate twelve-year practice.

details: The boy regularly japs the guru’s mantra, meditates Gaṇeśa with firm dedication, and lives on air without food like earth-clod or stone. Twelve years pass. Verse3 describes his condition with the printed nirvāṇam, retained without interpreting it as death or selecting another precise state. Pleased by his dedication and devotion, coral-formed Gaṇeśa rises from the pond and faces him. He notes the twelve years in the deserted forest frequented by lions and tigers and offers a boon according to the boy’s wish. Hearing him, the boy resumes bodily awareness.
outcome: Twelve-year air-fed practice leads to an actual coral-form appearance and boon invitation; the exact nirvāṇam condition remains under review.

details: The explicitly named son of Kṛtavīrya bows and speaks before many sages in vimānas. He requests continual nondeviating devotion to the deity’s feet, saying he has no enthusiasm to ask anything else. Nevertheless, to satisfy his parents, he also asks beauty of body pleasing to all.
outcome: The two requested benefits and the parents’ happiness motive are explicit; no demand for a thousand arms is put in the child’s mouth.

details: Hearing the requests, māyā-bearing Gaṇeśa adopts aṇimā and enters the boy’s belly. With this entry Kṛtavīrya’s son gains a divine body with one thousand arms and two straight legs, standing like a mountain. Gods and divine sages shower flowers and praise both boy and deity with music.
