Kārtavīrya roars thunderously; the figure called Samavartin is greatly frightened and all earthly kings tremble, anticipating that he could shoot five hundred arrows in combat.
outcome: Actual aṇimā entry restores a divine thousand-armed/two-legged body. Five hundred combat arrows are an anticipated capacity, not an enacted battle.

details: Brahmā and the other deities descend from their vimānas and give the boy varied boons. They say deities will regain lost objects through remembrance of him; he will remove the heart-resident ā maya of all worlds. They call him an actual Viṣṇu form with the name Sahasrārjuna, promise fame in three worlds for a kalpa, protection of good people and those taking refuge, victory over all enemies and sovereignty of the earth. The deity group then disappears.
outcome: These later grants have a collective divine grantor; they are separated from Gaṇeśa’s earlier physical response.

details: All kings bring elephants, horses, human conveyances, parasols, fly-whisks, lamps, chariots and other gifts. With Brahmins leading, Kārtavīrya installs a coral Gaṇeśa image in a great temple. Brahmins name it Pravālagaṇapa. He gives villages to the Brahmins appointed for its worship.
outcome: An actual installed coral image and endowed worship establish the site after the transformation.

details: The place becomes famous as wish-accomplishing Pravāla-kṣetra. In a separate earlier account Śeṣa practices there desiring to bear earth and obtains many boons from Gaṇeśa: earth-bearing strength, omniscience, one thousand heads and supremacy among nine Nāga clans. With delighted mind he earlier installs the deity, bringing the second name Dharaṇīdhara, granting all wished fruits to those who remember or hear it.
outcome: A source flashback explains the second site-name; Śeṣa’s boons are not assigned to Kārtavīrya.

details: Sahasrabāhu honours the Brahmins and takes leave of the kings, then returns to his city to see his mother and father. Both parents and the city rejoice at his restored form. His parents give varied gifts to eminent Brahmins.
outcome: The son actually returns to both parents and receives their joy; the birth/remedy/reunion sequence has a bounded ending.

details: Indra closes the Sankaṣṭa glory, saying it became known in the mortal world through Kṛtavīrya’s son and was experienced by gods and kings such as Candraseṇa. Remembrance alone gives accomplishment. Briefly, Rāvaṇa received the printed akhilājñatā and the Pāṇḍavas obtained their kingdom through its favour. Indra says his stalled vimāna will move to Amarāvatī if this vow’s merit is given into his hand. Brahmā says Śūrasena hears joyfully, bows to Indra, praises his own earlier merit for hearing such a vow and begins practicing. No merit transfer or actual departure occurs here.
outcome: The exemplum returns to the stalled-vimāna frame with a conditional merit request; Śūrasena starts a vow, while the vehicle remains unresolved.

details: Vyāsa asks Brahmā what Śūrasena did after hearing Indra. Brahmā says the king sends his messengers to bring a Sankaṣṭa practitioner. Searching house to house they find a fine vimāna and a severely diseased caṇḍālī with draining mouth, sores, insects, stench, wasted body and unclean appearance, whom Gaṇeśa’s messengers have come to take. Astonished, royal messengers bow to her and ask the divine servants who she was formerly, how she became like this and what merit accounts for her ascent.
outcome: The royal search encounters a rescue already ordered by Gaṇeśa and elicits a past-life account.

details: Divine messengers identify her as daughter of the Bengal kṣatriya Śāraṅgadhara, called Sundarā/Sundarī in the verse. They praise her voice, face and beauty through comparisons with Rati and renowned nāyikās and describe men’s sexual agitation on seeing her. She pursues adulterous encounters, costly clothing, ornaments and sensual pleasures, openly known in Bengal like a prostitute, repeatedly deceiving her husband Citra and spending her father’s amassed wealth.
outcome: Her father and husband are distinct named men; beauty comparisons do not establish identity with Rati or another woman.

details: One midnight she leaves her sleeping husband, dressed attractively; Citra catches her hand in anger and rebukes her habitual adultery.17 says her anger becomes quiet, then describes intoxication and strength from forbidden food. In darkness she takes a dagger in her right hand, cuts Citra’s belly and goes to the intended lover. An awake neighbour learns what happened and informs the king. Royal messengers wait, seize her on return, bring her to the king and execute her outside at his command. Yama’s messengers take her to terrible hell, where she suffers upside down, bitten by worms and recalling former deeds. At a kalpa’s end she is born an unfortunate caṇḍālī in the mortal world. The source prints5 for the verse in position15.
outcome: Husband-killing, report, royal execution, hell suffering and kalpa-end rebirth are narrated in order.

details: In that rebirth she drinks liquor and sleeps during the day. Waking hungry in night’s first watch, she begs at a vow-practitioner’s home, receives food and eats at moonrise. By chance and of her own will she utters Gaṇeśa’s name; immediately Gaṇanātha sends the fine vimāna. The verse in position25 is printed5. Her conduct is not a deliberately undertaken proper vow.
outcome: Daytime drunken sleep, moonrise food and voluntary name utterance precede actual divine rescue, without a fabricated conscious complete observance.

details: Royal messengers recount their mission: Indra rode to see Gṛtsamāda, came to Bhṛśuṇḍi with gods, bowed and worshipped, received permission and worship, and headed home. In Śūrasena’s city his vehicle fell through the gaze of a leprous Vaiśya son. Indra told the king that Sankaṣṭa merit would restart it, prompting the search. They propose taking this woman to the king so she can transfer vow merit, afterward gain twice the merit and resume her ascent while Indra’s vehicle returns home. Gaṇeśa’s servants refuse, saying they have no order from him to give her to someone else.
outcome: Merit transfer and doubling are only a royal-emissary proposal; divine messengers refuse without Gaṇeśa’s authorization.

details: The servants place her on the vimāna; she immediately gains divine radiance, clothing and ornaments and is taken toward Gaṇeśa amid divine music. The royal messengers return to Śūrasena and report. Her shining vehicle passes, her gaze falls on Indra’s craft, and contact with her craft’s air raises it while people and divine sages watch astonished. Indra actually goes to Amarāvatī and all return to their places; she, with divine body and freed from sin through Sankaṣṭa merit, reaches Vaināyaka’s abode. Properly hearing or carefully telling this story gives all desired objects and removes distress.
outcome: Actual divine-body rescue and abode, plus gaze/vehicle-air contact restarting Indra’s craft, occur without the rejected merit-transfer transaction.

details: As Śūrasena’s emissaries report, Sundarī’s radiant divine vehicle passes. Her gaze falls on Indra’s craft; contact with her vehicle’s air raises it before amazed onlookers and divine sages. Indra actually reaches Amarāvatī and the others return to their places. This is the enacted ending of the earlier fallen-vimāna question, not the refused proposal to transfer her merit.
outcome: Indra’s craft actually flies and he returns to Amarāvatī; the earlier frame’s missing flight remedy/return is now present.

details: Having heard and seen the vow’s greatness, Śūrasena asks Vasiṣṭha for a suitable time to practice a vow giving immediate assurance. The sage prescribes Māgha dark fourth on Tuesday. The devoted king and unnamed wife assemble supplies. On that day he bathes, finishes daily rites, worships Gaṇeśa and honours Brahmins and Vasiṣṭha with permission. He concentrates on Gaṇeśa and japs the name, standing on one big toe until sunset. He bathes again, observes evening worship and starts proper pūjā with Vasiṣṭha.
outcome: Actual timed observance and guru-guided services follow the earlier exemplary rescue.

details: The king prepares a great banana-pillared pavilion with clothing, ornaments, parasols, fly-whisks, mirrors, flowers, gems and lamps. A beautiful, well-proportioned gold Gaṇeśa image stands on a gold kalaśa. Amid Brahmin recitation, song, dance and instruments he performs Vedic and Purāṇic sixteen-service worship with pañcāmṛta, modaka/apūpa/laḍḍū/pāyasa and sugar, varied dishes, scented water, fruits, areca/betel, jewels and gold dakṣiṇā, dūrvā, light and mantra-flowers. He gives arghya to tithi, Gaṇeśa and Moon, honours and feeds Brahmins and gives ten thousand cows, clothes, ornaments and fees. He eats with friends and kin and keeps night vigil with song, instruments and stories. At dawn he bathes and worships again, then gives the image, furnishings and dakṣiṇā to Vasiṣṭha. Pleased, Gaṇeśa sends a prosperous vimāna.
outcome: Complete actual ritual and donations precede the deity’s sent vehicle; the exact ten-thousand-cow gift is retained.

details: The messengers place the king, bearing Gaṇeśa’s form, aboard while people rejoice. They say pleased Vināyaka sent them, eager to see him. The king weeps with joy and says the unfathomable, unmanifest Lord beyond speech and mind, praised by Vedas, śāstras and deities, has no need to see him; his being remembered is great fortune. The messengers admit devotees make the formless deity assume form. The king expresses a great wish: how can he leave his city for Gaṇeśa when he has not even consumed Hālāhala apart from its people? He cannot enjoy highest happiness without them. They agree his wish should be fulfilled, fearing Gaṇeśa’s anger if they refuse.
outcome: The king requests collective inclusion; messengers promise accommodation before the later actual lift attempt.

details: The messengers immediately put all the city’s beings aboard, explicitly all caturākaraja creatures, with divine clothes and ornaments. Some wonder how they gained this without their own merit; others attribute rescue to the king’s merit, comparing metal becoming gold through a treasure and sinners attaining perfection through saintly speech. The attendants attempt upward movement, but the craft remains inert on earth. Some spot a leprous man and urge discarding him, saying the craft will rise when he descends. Śūrasena instead offers to exclude himself and carry all others, or asks the man’s former birth, sin and a compassionate remedy. The messengers reassure him and undertake to explain. Numbering prints15 at position35 and4 at41.
outcome: All classes are accommodated, but lift actually fails. The king refuses the proposed abandonment and explicitly seeks remedy or his own exclusion.

details: The messengers describe a learned ascetic Brahmin devoted to gods and Brahmins in Gauḍa city. His son’s mother is Śākinī; the son’s faithful wife is Sāvitrī. An only-child affection leads to adornments, great beauty compared with Rati’s husband, and parents unwilling to endure separation. In youth he abandons his wife for adultery, slander and disregard for paternal counsel. When an unnamed captivating prostitute comes, he puts away his ornaments before his parents, then steals them and gives them to her. He lives absorbed in her amid scents and pleasures, compared in dedication with a Brahman-focused yogin.
outcome: The source introduces distinct mother and wife before the son’s abandonment and theft; the unnamed prostitute is not merged with Sundarī74.

details: The distressed father searches every house for his son without eating or drinking, but cannot see him. At midnight he tells his wife their home is empty without Budha and asks when life-preserving sight will return. Śākinī says hunger, thirst, anxiety and grief exhaust her and only seeing the boy will sustain her. Dūrva takes his staff and searches again. An elderly man of lowest caste named Bhīma tells him Budha is playing in the prostitute’s home, passion-bound and disregarding parentage, and says his grief is wasted. Dūrva asks how his son could become absorbed there and goes to that house.
outcome: Source explicitly names the father Dūrva and son Budha and gives Bhīma’s information; no Pāṇḍava or planetary identity is inferred.

details: The father seizes the intoxicated, red-eyed son’s hand and rebukes him, preferring a thorn-tree or stone to such a son and questioning his life. Budha strikes the father’s face, insults him for obstructing his pleasure and kicks him to death.24 reports Hareśvara with so’vadat at the father’s death; its speaker is not assigned without support. The son rejoices, binds the father’s foot, throws the body away, drinks and returns to the prostitute. Next morning Śākinī joyfully embraces him, with milk flowing through affection, asks where he was, says both parents waited without food/water, and repeatedly urges him to find his searching father. Angered, he hits her head with dry wood, knows her unconscious, ties and throws her outside and returns to the prostitute. Good people cremate both parents with their wood. The king does not punish him because he is a Brahmin.21 is printed2.
outcome: Both parents are killed and cremated, and royal nonpunishment is explicitly explained. The single death-utterance speaker remains unresolved.

details: When Budha returns, wife Sāvitrī gently urges virtuous conduct suited to his respected birth: act now for future-world happiness, in youth for old age, during eight months for the rains and by day for the night. She says the king excuses him through affection for his father and his Brahmin status, asks why he abandoned his faithful, beautiful and compliant lawful wife for a prostitute, and describes public condemnation, fear of speaking to him and her shame. She proposes marital companionship rather than public wrongdoing, urges him to leave the prostitute and abandon ignorant or negligent deeds, and says continuing otherwise loses both this world and the next. Her words pierce Budha deeply.
outcome: A detailed wife-to-husband corrective conversation precedes his threat and her death; no new woman or mother identity is substituted.

details: Enraged, Budha insults Sāvitrī and threatens her with his parents’ fate. She says one who did not respect his educating parents cannot protect her, and regards death at her husband’s hand as better for a virtuous wife. He seizes her hair and beats her with wood, clods, fists and stones. Through prior merit she remembers Rāma in husband-form and dies from his blows to vital parts. She goes to heaven with divine body and enjoys highest happiness. He drags her by the foot and throws her far away at night, then tells the prostitute he destroyed everyone for her and resumes pleasure.
outcome: Wife-killing and her actual heavenly/divine-body destination are narrated; her remembrance does not establish identity with the Rāma born in the next chapter.

details: After much time Budha visits sage Kalabha’s house while the sage bathes, seizes his beautiful wife by the hair, embraces, kisses and rapes her. Sulabhā says her parents’ given name has made her easy to him, condemns the assault in her husband’s absence and curses him to become a leper in another birth whose very name people will avoid. He flees frightened to the prostitute but resumes drink and pleasure. Brahmā declines further wrongdoings, saying telling others’ faults diminishes merit. Budha eventually dies; Yama orders messengers to throw him into hell until the elemental dissolution. Having endured that, he is born in a Vaiśya home, severely leprous through the sage’s wife’s curse. The discourse condemns his deeds, prescribes clothed bathing after touching him and avoidance of his name, and says removing him will raise the craft.
outcome: The curse specifies a later birth; actual hell and Vaiśya-leper rebirth are narrated, ending the past-life explanation before the king requests mercy.

details: Hearing the messengers’ account, Śūrasena trembles, says he did not know these acts, rises and bows anxiously. He asks compassionately for a way to remove all the wrongdoer’s defects. They tell him to rise and listen: Gaṇeśa has a famous FOUR-syllable name; japa it into the man’s ear and all faults will cease like darkness at sunrise. They say he is not qualified for other remedies, so the name alone should be japped.
outcome: The king seeks restoration, and the servants prescribe an auditory name remedy with an explicit limitation.

details: At the messengers’ direction Śūrasena japs the four-syllable name into the Vaiśya’s ear THREE times, with jayapūrvam prefix wording retained. Merely hearing Gajānana, the man gains a divine body shining like the dawn sun. All sin ends through hearing the name alone; he boards the craft. By Vighnarāja’s command, the messengers immediately bring that vehicle with all its beings to Vaināyaka’s abode. Brahmā closes the answers and praises Sankaṣṭa-caturthī as righteous, fame- and life-giving, granting accomplishment by hearing, quelling suffering and obstacles, and the power of dūrvā and the name.
outcome: Actual hearing removes sin, gives divine body and permits collective final transport; the previously proposed exclusion is not enacted.

details: Vyāsa asks who else practiced the vow. Brahmā says Jāmadagnya Rāma practiced it and gained fame, victory, knowledge and long life. Vyāsa requests the full origin account: how Rāma was born, of which father and mother.
outcome: A brief retrospective vow result introduces a new parentage narrative, not a completed revenge sequence here.

details: In Śvetadvīpa Jamadagni is a great sage, knowing three times and performing creation/destruction, restraint/favour through mind, frightening gods. His wife is explicitly Reṇukā, whose beauty exceeds Kāma’s wife.6 says she became famed as Rati; this source’s Reṇukā/Rati description is kept distinct from automatically identifying Kāma’s wife. Poetic comparisons describe creatures seeking her eye-beauty and Moon serving Īśvara for her face-beauty. She is praised as beginningless/endless goddess, root nature and ruler. Rāma is born to her from Jamadagni, here praised as an actual Īśvara form; the son is compared with Viṣṇu the yoga lord. He is beautiful, strong, obedient to parents, devoted to gods/Brahmins/gurus/wise people/cows/bodhi, learned in Vedas/Vedāṅgas/śāstras/smṛtis, eloquent as Bṛhaspati, forbearing as earth and deep as ocean.
outcome: Direct father/mother/spouse relationships and attributed divine/poetic descriptions are distinguished from universal biography.

details: With his parents’ permission Rāma goes to the forest printed Nimeṣāraṇya, firmly intending study of many disciplines. After his departure mighty King Kārtavīrya appears. The source attributes earth-subjection, steady Lakṣmī as a Viṣṇu portion, five-hundred-arrow volleys and formidable strength to him. His innumerable elephants, chariots, horses and infantry cover earth when he moves; his conch frightens enemies, and five hundred hand-claps shake the cosmic egg. In blue clothes with blue parasol and similarly dressed four-part troops, he wanders forests, rivers, forts and mountains and kills some game. On a Sahyādri summit he sees an excellent hermitage and asks servants whose it is.
outcome: Rāma leaves before Kārtavīrya’s hunting visit; the printed place name is not silently changed to Naimiṣa.

details: The king’s servant identifies Jamadagni as a sage like a second Sun, capable of curse and favour, whose sight removes crores of sins, and advises a visit. Kārtavīrya holds back his full army, takes selected companions and goes to the sage sitting on kuśa with fire-like radiance. All bow; troops sit in large halls and groves while the king, with four attendants, sits on the sage’s appointed seat. Jamadagni and pupils honour them with foot-water, arghya, seats and cows. Hunt-worn troops bathe in clean cold lakes and hear pupils reciting Vedas and śāstras and debating.
outcome: A respectful actual visit and sage hospitality precede the later dispute; full army restraint is stated.

details: The king praises his parents, birth, knowledge, tapas, fortune, lineage and fame as fruitful through seeing Jamadagni and calls him Para-Brahman, satisfied by hospitality. Though knowing him, the sage asks identity, name and purpose. The king explicitly says he is Kṛtavīrya’s son called Kārtavīrya, with no purpose beyond beneficial sage sight, and asks leave to return. Jamadagni reciprocally praises the visit and insists he eat before departing. The king says he cannot even drink apart from innumerable troops and doubts all can be fed. The sage assures a four-kind meal for the whole army, invites even the home forces and asks him to rest briefly by the river while food is prepared.
outcome: Explicit self-identification supports the local father-child line; the king’s concern for troops produces a promise to feed all.

details: Astonished, the king goes to the riverbank. Jamadagni calls his wife, tells her what happened, and the couple summons and worships Kāmadhenu. They ask her to preserve their honour and truth by instantly feeding the invited king’s innumerable forces according to taste, otherwise their promise would fail and ill fame follow. At their prayer she creates by her own power a great city with beautiful houses, gem-pillared halls, gardens, flags, music, vessel rows, four-kind food, gates and moat, male/female attendants and abundant prepared meals. Guards prevent unauthorized entry under Jamadagni’s rule. Varied soups, pāyasa, cooked dishes, pañcāmṛta, edible/lickable/suckable/drinkable foods, fruits and seasoned dishes are prepared in innumerable bright vessels. Through Kāmadhenu’s satisfaction, the sage summons pupils to invite Kṛtavīrya’s son and troops to eat.
outcome: The sage-wife prayer is answered by Kāmadhenu’s own actual city/food creation; no new Gaṇeśa boon dialogue is invented.

details: Jamadagni urgently sends pupils to invite the riverbank king, with blessed greetings and prepared innumerable six-taste dishes. Kārtavīrya and the army bathe and come to a house and gateway he has neither seen nor heard of in three worlds. Staff-bearing guards initially stop him, seeking the sage’s signal, but pupils overrule them and bring him into the hall. The king inwardly wonders at wealth exceeding even Hari, Hara and Brahmā. The sage comes forward and seats guests at their vessels.
outcome: The vast feast is actually presented, with an initial authorization barrier removed by pupils.

details: With the king’s permission guests and troops, including outside diners, are seated in rows; the king is seated after everyone. They eat amid music, question unfamiliar tasty dishes, roots and fruits and marvel at preparation within one watch. Pupils give washing-water and tooth-cleaning sticks and leftovers to elephants, horses and bulls. In another large prepared hall people eat sugarcane, grapes, mango, jackfruit and pomegranate and receive cardamom, clove, camphor, khadira/areca and betel. Jamadagni gives everyone suitable clothes and ornaments and especially costly gifts to the king. He modestly asks what a forest sage could provide a king already fulfilling all wishes and praised as a Viṣṇu form; by following his invitation the king has made his fame and the sage’s successful hospitality known, as a great man obeying a smaller man gains saintly reputation.
outcome: Actual feeding of people and animals and subsequent gifts fulfill the invitation before the king’s new demand.9 is printed1.

details: Astonished, the king asks whether the previously unseen marvel arose through māyā or tapas. Jamadagni says he has never uttered falsehood, even in jest, and truthfully identifies Kāmadhenu as the agent of everything. Brahmā remarks on adverse fate and approaching ill fortune. Though fully fed, the king decides to take the cow. He argues peaceful, desireless, sense-controlled forest sages living on roots, fruit or air, studying Vedas/śāstras and seeking liberation have no need for such riches; a great object belongs with great work and a forest dweller is not suited to the jewel. He demands a willing gift of Kāmadhenu and says she will still be the sage’s when kept with him, then threatens what powerful kings with armies cannot seize at home or abroad.
outcome: The agent explanation is Kāmadhenu, not a new Gaṇeśa grant; the king turns hospitality into a coercive gift demand.

details: Hearing Kārtavīrya’s words, Jamadagni burns with anger like Fire fed ghee and rebukes him with red eyes. He says he invited what he thought a good, pure, great king but did not know hidden crookedness, using heron and cuckoo/crow comparisons. He condemns his own error in seeking royal friendship, a friendship neither seen, heard nor experienced in the world.
outcome: Jamadagni rejects the demand and diagnoses deceit in the guest; the dispute remains active into battle.

details: Jamadagni says the king seeks Kāmadhenu while courting self-destruction, desires the unattainable and risks the sin of destroying three worlds. The king erupts with anger and says only the sage’s Brahmin status made him endure harsh words. He rises and orders messengers to release the cow from her tether and bring her. They surround her, but her foṭkāra blast kills some; her anger-fire burns others. The force of her breath blows other warriors into the sky, covering the Sun and making the scene obscure.
outcome: Actual coercive seizure attempt triggers three distinct cow counters: fatal foṭkāra, anger-fire and sky-lifting breath.

details: Darkness, earth-shaking and falling trees accompany the assault. Troops flee in ten directions. Someone whips the cow from a distance; she leaps and chases the army like lion against elephants or Garuḍa against serpents. Kārtavīrya tells frightened troops he will blow his conch and make her flee, but the mighty world-filling blast does not frighten her. Servants then strike her with staffs and iron. From every struck body location emerge armed, equipped warriors. Śakas and Barbaras arise from her hair; Paṭaccaras from her foot region, with varied Yavana peoples and other warriors also arising. Cavalry, elephants and powerful charioteers join combat against the king’s troops.
outcome: The conch counter fails; body strikes produce the cow’s armies with exact stated hair/foot origins.

details: Cow-generated fighters strike down royal troops; more converge and hundreds die through mutual blows. Weapons smash weapons, then wrestling continues amid dust, noise, obscured Sun and inability to distinguish one’s own side. Horses, elephants, chariot wheels, drums, flutes and war cries fill the battle, frightening spirits/Rākṣasas and warriors’ wives while benefiting scavengers. Knees and heads are broken; swords, shields, bhallas, arrows, bows, warriors and chariots fall beyond count. Remaining royal soldiers flee. Cow troops pursue laughing but DO NOT kill the fugitives, rebuking them for attacking a sage who harmed them in no way. The narrator attributes the king’s bad judgment to former fault.
outcome: The royal army is routed; pursuit is explicit but killing of fleeing troops is expressly withheld.

details: With his army broken, Kṛtavīrya’s son rises, takes FIVE HUNDRED ARROWS and bows, places his left knee on earth, draws the bows and shoots an arrow-net at the cow army. The number grammatically accompanies arrows; no exact five-hundred-bow count is asserted. The volley is fruitless. Repeated equal volleys break not even one cow warrior. The king despairs at his lost strength. The cow army says one should not strike a distressed opponent and goes to heaven; Kāmadhenu questions combat with the lesser opponent.30 is printed00.
outcome: Repeated royal volleys actually fail; the opposing force withdraws while refusing to strike the distressed king.

details: After Kāmadhenu leaves, Kārtavīrya goes to Jamadagni in anger, claims to know his deceit and says a deceitful man should not count as a Brahmin. The KING HIMSELF takes one arrow and pierces the sage; the arrow lodges in his heart and Jamadagni gives up life. Reṇukā protests needless Brahmin-killing. The red-eyed king tells her to be silent or he will kill her too and strikes her with TWENTY-ONE arrows. She remembers Jamadagni and remains alive to ask why he struck innocent parents and predict certain destruction of his arms. Hearing her, the king departs to his city with a small remaining army, anxious, grieving soldiers, reproaching himself and without enthusiasm. This chapter describes a continuous visit sequence;80.21’s later recollection gives a different home-and-return chronology.
outcome: The king directly kills Jamadagni, wounds Reṇukā who still speaks, and then returns home; no imported sons kill the sage.

details: After the king leaves, the arrow-covered Reṇukā grieves, asking where her sons are and especially her angry beloved Rāma, and says seeing him will precede her departure to the gods’ abode. At her remembrance Rāma comes, sees her arrows and his father dead from Kārtavīrya’s heart-arrow, faints like a wind-felled tree and weeps. He compares the fatherless hermitage with earth lacking Meru, Amarāvatī without Indra and the world without Gaṅgā, laments the parents’ great tapas and mother’s world-burning capacity, and removes her arrows with her head on his lap. Recalling her milk, food, clothing, fruit and attentive care, he condemns life without his parents. The plural sons are unnamed; no names or counts of brothers are imported.
outcome: Rāma actually returns and tends his living, wounded mother before her final instructions and death.

details: Reṇukā wipes her son’s tears, says she will remain near him and tells the earlier events: Kṛtavīrya’s son arrived at noon with troops, was honoured and fed through Kāmadhenu, then demanded the cow. When the sage was silent he angrily released her; at contact she generated a powerful four-part army. Royal troops fled and the king repeatedly loosed five hundred arrows but was defeated. She explicitly says he WENT HOME, the cow went to heaven, and he RETURNED to kill the father with one chest-arrow and wound her without offence with twenty-one. This direct mother’s recollection differs from79.35–43’s continuous visit sequence; both are retained.
outcome: Her alternate chronology is recorded as a recollection, without silently inserting a return into79.

details: Reṇukā commands prompt destruction of the wicked king and making earth without kṣatriyas TWENTY-ONE times because twenty-one arrows were put in her body. She gives another instruction: perform the parents’ funeral rites where no one has ever been cremated, summon all-Veda-knowing Dattātreya, and perform subsequent rites through thirteen days so both attain their destination; no other teacher is equivalent. After speaking she actually abandons her body and reaches a difficult-to-attain abode. The narrator adds that Rāma did all she commanded. That concise fulfillment summary is retained without inventing the unexamined detailed funeral or repeated revenge episodes.
outcome: Mother’s commands and actual death close the parent-loss episode; the narrator’s broad summary is distinct from later detailed enacted events.

details: Prepared-meal invitations and disparagement of Śukla bring citizens to the sleeping child. He declares the small devotional meal satisfying and refuses another mouthful.

The one Lord becomes many, visiting every home with the king, accepting elaborate hospitality, playing/teaching and fulfilling wishes. Drums and flowers mark the event; the king cannot explain simultaneous visits.
Inspecting two or three homes, the king sees himself and the child after each meal.
Sanaka/Sanandana find the deity everywhere, cannot find a pure meal place and leave hungry. Meditation reveals Vināyaka within, around and in each other.
The ten-armed lion-mounted vision appears. The pair bow and praise, saying their wish is already fulfilled; no fresh personal grant is spoken.
After disappearance, the relieved pair install the as-seen image and name the shrine and lake. Visitors worship and depart; the sages return, followed by conditional account-hearing benefits.
The king’s exhausted house search ends at Śukla’s. His reproach meets the child’s reply and citizens’ testimony; he recognizes the deluding māyā.
Meditation brings Vināyaka-form; māyā restores royal distinction. The child is carried toward the palace in a palanquin.
Seeing the devoted couple follow, the child mentally grants extraordinary wealth without a new spoken request.
The returning couple fear offense and the missing hut, then discover servants, ornaments, palatial dwelling and food. Śukla recognizes unobtrusive grace and teaches the value of devotion.
Hidden lightning-form envoys attack. Bearers flee; the child seizes and whirls the pair, compassionately stops and questions them.
They confess Narāntaka’s mission and praise their rescuer through the five illustrative father roles.
Citizens warn of future harm. The Lord preserves his earlier fearlessness promise and releases the pair; king and child reach home.
The envoys return to Raudrapura and introduce their report with the duty to tell good and bad truthfully.
They recount the earlier demons’ forms, counters and deaths, followed by their own attack and release. Differently printed recap identities remain unresolved.
They report Śukla’s meal and simultaneous royal/deity household visits, then counsel careful self-interest and admit the child’s unmatched power.
Narāntaka rejects caution, threatens child/king and orders the four-division host to arm for Kāśī.
The equipped divisions march with frightening dust and noise; an unnamed minister rides a jeweled chariot. Gods flee to a cave as Narāntaka approaches.
The king arms, seeks counsel and hears conditional surrender/delivery advice, which is not implemented.
Demons burn the city and capture/assault fleeing inhabitants. The king chooses fighting rather than tolerating abduction.
After initial success, the king and two ministers’ sons are captured alive. Narāntaka boasts that the child must now be defeated and marches home.
Ambā faints and laments her captured husband; widowhood language remains her despairing speech.
The child roars at the grief and Siddhi creates the terrifying host in response to his war purpose.
The leader asks food; the Lord orders consumption of the army and bringing Narāntaka’s head, promising more food if needed.
Kālapuruṣa consumes all divisions, counters arrows/astras and exhausts the demon’s weapons, then pursues him through the worlds.
Seized by the hair, the living demon is forcibly brought before Vināyaka with refuge advice; no actual surrender is narrated.
The leader asks rest and the demon’s liberation. The explicit answer grants rest in the mouth; the leader enters and is reabsorbed. Demon liberation remains ungranted in this speech.
Brahmā explains the leader through Vināyaka’s universal creative power, retaining Siddhi’s proximate agency.
The captives see worlds/universes in the belly, seek mental refuge and leave by the child-shown hair-pore route.
The king recalls capture and rescue and asks its causes. A head touch gives divine knowledge; after his hymn the Lord again veils it through māyā.
The king reunites with his unnamed mother and then wife Ambā; the companion label shifts to ministers without secure identity allocation. The population is restored and families celebrate.
Expecting enjoyment/liberation but choosing combat, Narāntaka boasts. The child counters the boast and the king warns him to leave. The demon breaks the king’s bow and fells him.
Axe blow, hurled mountains, matched māyā forms, weapon/astrā counters and wrestling continue. The king falsely believes the child dead and withdraws.
Unattributed Piṇāka/arrows appear. Both arms are severed to the demon’s and father’s doors, yet other arms remain and tree attacks resume.
Arrows sever legs and a head, landing at the brother’s and father’s homes. Māyā restores legs and another head appears; day-and-night combat continues.
Repeated axe decapitations fail. The Lord deludes the boon-proud enemy’s time/state/person perception; he recalls Śiva’s boons and expects death.
Virāṭ appears and crushes Narāntaka with the great-toe nail tip, the actual final killing act.
Gods celebrate; Earth says half the burden is gone and asks complete relief. The king worships the victor and praises the sight.
Citizens request devotion/nonseparation without explicit assent; gifts and wishes for future victory conclude the Narāntaka death account.
The head appears at the parents’ courtyard. They recognize, faint, lament and praise the lost son, without a narrated liberation claim.
They carry the head to the elder Devāntaka. He recalls shared life/tapas, mourns his younger brother and is consoled into revenge resolve.
The parents explain the Kāśī marriage visit, the father’s brother Dhūmrākṣa’s death, reprisal forces, Narāntaka’s expedition and the head arrival.

Devāntaka threatens sacrifice of the child, gathers demons in divine offices and flies to encircle Kāśī. Citizens panic before two or three days have elapsed; exact54 sent/slain referents remain unresolved.
The king requests rescue again. Vināyaka assumes a vast lion-mounted armed form and flies out to face the host.
Ordered to make a varied army, Siddhi remembers the eight named powers; they arrive with an armed four-division host.
After the enemy’s victory blessing, eight demon commanders attack eight arrays. The summoned Laghimā versus formation Prathimnā discrepancy remains open.
General slaughter and obscuring dust lead to anxiety when Śukra revives dead demons through unnamed vidyā.
Īśitā’s anger produces kṛtyā, commanded by her glance to take Bhārgava in her bhaga, disappear and abandon him in Bārbāra. Gods rejoice; no Śukra death is stated.
Demons flee or seek refuge; fortunes alternate and general battle gives way to duels. Final Devāntaka outcome remains beyond this scope.

An unnamed Brahmin sage of the Āṅgirasa family has Bharata as son. Fearful of attachment even in this birth, Bharata meditates on Gaṇeśa near the sage. Hearing Vedic and other Gaṇeśa praise strengthens previous knowledge. He conceals all cleverness, displaying dull childlike conduct out of fear of marriage and attachment. The father is an unnamed Āṅgirasa descendant, not the creator sage Aṅgiras himself.

Father gives Bharata sacred thread and teaches sandhyā, cleanliness and Vedic acts including ācamana. Bharata does not accept instruction, acts differently even when struck, performs acts when physically guided but later appears unable to recall them. People call him Jaḍa and doubt his knowledge; he disregards honor, insult, blame and praise. Father does not arrange marriage because of apparent dullness, which pleases Bharata.

Father dies in time; unnamed virtuous mother follows him (sahagā). Nine brothers born to his mother’s co-wife take control over Bharata: these are half-brothers in this later birth, not Ṛṣabha’s earlier sons. Their arrogant wives give leftovers, spoiled or burnt food and husks without affection. Brothers dishonor him with words/clothes and call him family disgrace. He eats rejected food as nectar wearing rags; when women withhold even that, he eats only once within two or three days. This is deprivation, not a fasting vow.

Hungry Bharata wanders house to house seeking food and accepts work. Pleased people give food/clothes; his brothers see him, bring him back and make him their worker. Their wives still give bad food/husks, which he eats as nectar. Brothers station him to guard ripe grain fields day and night for food; understanding bodily life, he remains equal in pleasure and pain.

Robber chief praises Bhadrakālī and promises a human victim if he obtains abundant wealth. Wealth is then actually obtained; source does not explicitly narrate a deity boon or identify its grantor. He sends robbers at night; they happen upon Bharata, seize him by force and take him to their station. Bharata understands bodily prārabdha. Chief honors and feeds him tasty food, then takes him with music to the goddess.

After Mahākālī worship the chief draws a naked sword to kill Bharata. Seeing possible bodily death, Bharata is unshaken and remembers Gaṇapati, accepting whether body falls today or lives long. Angry Gaṇapatya Mahākālī emerges from the image, takes the chief’s sword from his hand, beheads him with it and drinks blood. Other robbers are killed with that sword. Goddess plays with her own gaṇas while intent on Gaṇeśa praise. Bharata bows and leaves, wandering freely for alms while remembering Gaṇapati. No actual liberation narrated.
outcome: Chief and robbers killed; Bharata bows and resumes alms-wandering/Gaṇeśa remembrance.

details: Sindhu ruler Rahūgaṇa is inwardly inclined through prior saṃskāra but cannot gain peace despite effort. He goes toward Kapila’s āśrama near Gaṅgā, said by a Brahmin to be on Gautamī’s south bank. His palanquin bearers tire; attendants recruit replacements, finding the Āṅgirasa sage Bharata. Accepting bodily prārabdha he carries without distress. To avoid injuring creatures he steps only where none are present, slowing bearers and rocking the palanquin, distressing king. Gaṅgā/Gautamī labels preserved as this witness’s setting, not mapped to modern geography.

Angry Rahūgaṇa orders steady carrying; fearful bearers blame newcomer as moving like drunk. King rebukes him as wicked/mad. Knowing king desires yoga and is qualified, Bharata replies that all is māyā/delusion/untrue, questions king/people division, says he has abandoned duality/equality and king cannot discipline him into abandoning yoga. He resumes silently carrying and worshipping Gaṇapati. Hearing yogic speech, frightened king jumps to ground, sees ragged Brahmin with sacred thread/Brahman radiance, prostrates and addresses him respectfully.

Rahūgaṇa asks pardon for ignorant offense, sees apparent avadhūta with sacred thread, and asks whether he is Kapila, Nārada, Aṅgirā, Pulaha, Kratu, Datta or Yājñavalkya. These are queried identities, not actual identifications of Bharata or onstage visits by those sages.

Rahūgaṇa explains fear of offending Brahmins: he praises them as Supreme Lord’s bodies, supports of acts/knowledge/Brahman, the printed 25 mouth/hearing/gods-stomach clause is separately unresolved; gifts yield imperishable state, mantras/gods depend on them and mantra-less acts are fruitless. He calls devoted act/tapas/knowledge/yoga Brahmins liberators/teachers/Brahman. He attributes divine falls to slighting/curses, restoration to Brahmins and all attainment to service. He fears them more than Viṣṇu/Śiva. Taking Bharata’s feet, bowing with head there, he cries; compassionate Bharata raises him and begins reply. These claims are king’s praise, not universal physical/social facts or new narrated curses.
outcome: King cries at Bharata’s feet; compassionate sage raises him.

details: Bharata identifies himself as Āṅgirasa, called Jaḍa Bharata, formerly Svāyambhuva Bharata and now Jaḍa. He assures Rahūgaṇa that ignorant insult to his body will not produce sin, he need not fear and may go; Bharata will go freely under prārabdha. This is forgiveness of this offense, not a generic future immunity. Rahūgaṇa praises meeting, identifies Sindhu kingship, says he left royal matters to seek peace from Kapila at Gautamī, and asks Bharata to accept him as disciple and teach peace. Compassionate Bharata begins difficult Vedic-secret yoga-peace instruction.

Bharata teaches fourfold body and fourfold embodied self appear different through delusion despite unity. Body-Brahman is bindu, embodied-self Brahman soham; union is bodha/self-arising Brahman varied by vikalpa. When bodha ceases, Sāṅkhya Brahman enjoys only own happiness; he questions own happiness without other happiness and describes other-arising and its seed. Beyond self/other arising, Svānanda is union/nondifference. No remembered four-body names supplied.

18 states fivefold Svānanda and names satya/asatya/sama/neti fourth; 19–20 relate self/other arising, experience and varied Brahmans/worlds.21 names name/form as asatya/Śākta Brahman; 22 gives divided name/form and immortal solar self/all-illumining Brahman. Precise reference/allocation of experience in 19 and name/form versus solar self in 22 withheld; literal distinctions retained without remembered philosophical repair.

Bharata teaches Viṣṇu as bliss/nondifference/equality of two and being/nonbeing; Śiva fourth, neti, unmanifest, delusion-free independent Brahman. Fourfold union is own-form māyā-associated Vināyaka; ayoga destroys union and is māyā-free Gaṇeśa. Ayoga brings withdrawal/beyond own distinction; yoga-peace does not perceive either union or ayoga. Māyā-associated versus free distinctions are delusion to abandon. Mind fivefold and sovereignty constitute twofold delusion; relinquish them to become peaceful. All statements remain attributed teaching.
Bharata stops; king bows, abandons kingdom and goes forest. Practicing prescribed means, Rahūgaṇa actually gains peace and becomes Gaṇapatya. No new apparition or deity boon scene in these verses.
outcome: Rahūgaṇa actually attains peace and becomes Gaṇapatya.

details: Āṅgirasa Bharata wanders Earth, arrives by fate at Mayūreśa field, recognizes previous Gaṇeśa manifestation and stays meditating in one place as if dull. After one year Gaṇeśa actually comes to see him, mounted on mouse and accompanied by Siddhi/Buddhi. Bharata bows and hymns with tears/gooseflesh and devotion. The one-year interval belongs to this field arrival/meditation, not all prior lives.

Bharata hymns peace-form/giver, Vighneśa/Heramba, Siddhi/Buddhi lord and giver, devotee-fear remover, devotion-loving/yoga-peace Gaṇeśa, mouse-mounted/four-armed/Svānanda/Vakratunda, infinite forms/play. He is fulfilled by sight inaccessible even in Vedic reach, says devotion alone drew deity to him, and asks what gift can please the source of all portions. Four arms and Vakratunda here are hymn attributes, distinct from narrator’s actual mouse/Siddhi/Buddhi appearance.

Bharata offers his body, bows and requests ONLY firm unwavering devotion to deity’s feet. Repeatedly bowing, he dances with love. Gaṇeśa grants firm unwavering devotion; hymn will give yoga-peace and please him. Whatever a reciter desires he will give, and hearers obtain likewise. God disappears; Bharata remains devoted there. Neither requested liberation nor a new bodily transformation boon is added.
outcome: Firm devotion granted; deity disappears and Bharata remains there.

details: At the end Bharata actually becomes Gaṇeśa-form. Narrator locates the famous sage’s cave/place north of Gaṇeśa and facing him at one krośa. People who see that place attain permanent liberation. Devoted hearers/readers of Bharata account obtain enjoyment/liberation. Mudgala closes Priyavrata-family righteous kings devoted to various gods. Site not assigned a modern location; site-view benefit not retroactively substituted for king’s actual outcome.
outcome: Bharata becomes Gaṇeśa-form; site position and separate audience benefits stated.

details: Svāyambhuva Manu’s son Uttānapāda righteously rules Madhyadeśa. Wives are Sunīti and Suruci; Dhruva is Sunīti’s son, Uttama Suruci’s son. King is controlled/deluded by Suruci and disregards Sunīti. Dhruva approaches to sit on royal lap, is dishonored with Suruci’s malicious involvement, and goes angrily to forest. He meets/bows to Nārada, who learns events and gives Viṣṇu’s twelve-syllable mantra. At Mathurā he meditates and performs severe tapas for ONE THOUSAND YEARS. Pleased Viṣṇu comes and gives undivided earthly kingship and, at end, heavenly kingship/Viṣṇu’s Dhruva-form abode. No recalled six-month duration or exact bīja imported.

Dhruva returns and bows to parents; king honors his radiance, later makes him king and goes forest for tapas. Gaṇeśa-devoted Nārada teaches him to worship Gaṇeśa beyond difference/nondifference, as gods, sages/yogins and earlier kings do, for peace. Nārada gives SIX-SYLLABLE mantra; its power makes Uttānapāda Gaṇapatya. Remembering Gaṇanātha at death, he actually attains Gaṇanātha sāyujya. This six-syllable initiation belongs to father, distinct from Dhruva’s later one-syllable Gaṇeśa mantra.
outcome: Father’s actual Gaṇeśa sāyujya; Dhruva rules.

details: Nārada visits ruling Dhruva, who honors his guru. He says Viṣṇu sent him from Vikuṇṭha to direct prescribed Mayūreśa pilgrimage for lasting abode, otherwise obstacle/fall. First-person madīyakam in 23 belongs to relayed Viṣṇu promise, not Nārada’s own new abode grant. Viṣṇu also instructs one-syllable Gaṇeśa japa:when Dhruva abode dissolves at Brahmā-day end, Dhruva will attain peace/Brahman; without it yoga-peace cannot come. Nārada properly gives ONE-SYLLABLE mantra; Dhruva becomes siddha, goes Mayūreśa and performs pilgrimage with gateway marks. Prediction of end-stage kept separate from actual ending 32–33.

With mantra-knowing Brahmins Dhruva installs Gaṇeśa, builds extensive costly temple with golden pinnacle and worships devotedly. He names deity Dhruvavināyaka.29 gives half-krośa distance from Gaṇeśa but printed nāpūrvadvārasamīpagam direction clause unresolved.31 residence duration varṣamāsaṃ also not securely normalized.

Dhruva returns city, rules, and at end goes heavenly Dhruva abode supporting luminaries. Meditating on Gaṇapati there, when Dhruva station perishes he actually goes straight to Svānanda. Humans seeing Dhruvavināyaka there or hearing this Dhruva account gain enjoyment and firm liberation. Actual station/Svānanda ending is distinct from earlier Viṣṇu promise.
outcome: Dhruva actually attains Svānanda after luminary-station destruction.

details: Aṅga, a descendant in Dhruva’s line, righteously protects people like father. His wife is Mṛtyu’s UNNAMED daughter; their son Vena is cruel. Exhausted by failed instruction, Aṅga abandons kingdom and goes forest sorrowfully. Robbers plunder rulerless land; frightened people seek Brahmins, who enthrone Vena in paternal realm. He kills robbers but abandons proper conduct, hurting varṇa/āśrama practitioners. Sages restrain him; he claims everyone should worship him as protector. Angry Brahmins kill him by curse.

Sages churn Vena’s LEFT aṅga/body-part seeking king; cruel sin-formed man arises, short, dusky, bearded and tawny-eyed. They say niṣīda; he becomes named Niṣāda, receives forest station and Niṣādas descend from him. They then churn RIGHT aṅga; an energetic COUPLE emerges, both Viṣṇu-kalā-associated. Couple bows to Brahmins; male is consecrated king and named Pṛthu, upholding royal dharma/prosperity. Neither left thigh/right arm specificity nor partner name Arci is supplied.

After time people lack food and seek Pṛthu. Earth swallowed resources under Vena’s adharma and cannot return them under righteous king. Angry Pṛthu draws bow/arrow to kill Earth; she flees in cow form and he pursues like Yama. Finding no refuge, she seeks Pṛthu with folded hands, asks him not to kill woman/cow/Earth and protect surrendered one. He threatens death unless she manifests varied food always. Earth says plants already consumed cannot be directly returned; asks first leveling, then calf and milker so cow-form yields all plants as milk. Killing would be futile without these arrangements.

Pṛthu crushes mountains with bow-tip, levels Earth and arranges towns/villages; source says this starts their arrangement. He makes Earth his DAUGHTER by adoption/putrītva, so she is called Pṛthvī. With Manu as CALF, Pṛthu himself MILKS six-taste food-milk. Beings of three worlds then obtain their own food-milk. Adoption and calf-role are not biological parentage.

Milking roles: Veda-form Brahmā CALF/Bṛhaspati MILKER takes milk; 36 does not separately name its substance. Rudra CALF/Kālāgnirudra MILKER yields flesh-form Hara-life milk. Viṣṇu CALF/Yajamāna MILKER yields act-born sacrifice-support milk. Sun CALF/Dhruva MILKER yields luminaries’ life. Śeṣa CALF/Vāsuki MILKER yields serpent food. Śiva CALF/Nandikeśvara MILKER yields knowledge/vidyā milk. These are source-specific cosmic milking roles, not parents/children; Rudra and Śiva labels retained separately in this table.

Mobile/immobile beings and lords milk Pṛthu-prepared Earth. He honors and joyfully protects her as daughter; she remains happy. He rules Earth as emperor and undertakes hundred horse sacrifices with great dakṣiṇā. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Indra-led gods, Gandharvas, Kaśyapa-led sages, Śeṣa-led Nāgas and varied people with wives come. Hundred opening count is kept distinct from final NINETY-NINE completion at 52.

As last sacrifice begins, worried Indra in matted hair/rags steals horse. Pṛthu’s UNNAMED son sees him but lets him go as ascetic; Indra leaves horse and disappears afraid. Next he uses bone-bearing/ash-smeared disguise and son does not strike him. Altogether Indra steals horse SIX TIMES. Pṛthu prepares to kill him; Brahmā consoles/restrains him, and Indra is not killed. Pṛthu completes NINETY-NINE sacrifices. Urged by Brahmā, Indra bows; Pṛthu renounces enmity and embraces him. Honored gods/guests depart; Pṛthu resumes righteous protection.
outcome: 99 sacrifices; Indra survives, bows and is embraced; Pṛthu resumes rule.

details: Pṛthu teaches dharma and rules happily, described as Viṣṇu-form/equal prowess. Four Sanaka-led sons of Brahmā, ever child-aged, radiant and delusion-free, visit. Pṛthu rises, prostrates head at feet, worships with footwater/arghya/seats and massages their feet. He praises land/city/home/lineage/parents/learning/tapas as fortunate through visit, attributes sight to earlier merit, and asks their instructions. No guessed new parental genealogy from his praise.

Pleased by humility, Kumāras say they desire no task and are naked, have come because they heard king’s fame in heaven, and ask permission to return Brahmaloka. Pṛthu says he has enjoyed kingdom/varied pleasures and now asks yoga for peace. Recognizing qualification/disenchantment, they teach that full Gaṇeśa yoga-peace is to be worshipped with great devotion for peace. This is teacher exchange, not a direct new Gaṇeśa appearance.

Kumāras recount earlier visiting Śiva seated meditating beneath banyan at his abode. They bow and awaken him with hymns; ending meditation he says salutation to Gaṇeśa. Astonished, they ask who Gaṇādhipa is and why supposedly independent sahaja Śiva bows. Śiva joyfully explains primordial Gaṇapatya peace-knowledge. These are recollection inside Pṛthu teaching, not simultaneous Śiva visit to king.

In recollection Śiva questions independent sahaja versus dependent threefold categories in Veda-described Brahman, and calls varied karma/yoga/knowledge forms māyā-associated. Union of actions is action-Brahman, similarly knowledge-Brahman. Gaṇa means group, union of external/internal differences; food/prāṇa and other Brahman-denoting words are gaṇas and Gaṇeśvara their lord. He is yoga of union/ayoga and all yogas; Śiva and others are his yoga-form gaṇas and bow. Māyā is obstacle/reflection-delusion, overcome by Vighnarāja service; Gaṇapatya yogins become Brahman. Śiva declares Gaṇeśa-form identity and difference as māyā. Claims attributed to recalled Śiva speech.

Śiva identifies fivefold mind as varied Buddhi, and sovereignty there as Siddhi. Gaṇeśa reflection amid two māyās is deluded; abandon reflected state/fivefold mind through Gaṇeśa service to become Cintāmaṇi. He questions operation of union and yoga in Gaṇeśa-identity, affirms nondifference and yoga-peace/Brahman attainment, and calls this his secret meditation, why he is Gaṇeśa’s servant and bows. Kumāras say doubt ended; they now wander Earth/heavens/nether hollows as Gaṇapatya yogins. Buddhi/Siddhi here are philosophical personifications, not new biological spouses or marriage scene.

Kumāras continue recollection:desiring Gaṇeśa sight, they learn deity has become Kaśyapa’s son and gone to devoted unnamed Kāśī king’s house for his work. They go Kāśī and see brahmacārin child-form Gaṇeśa among children, bow and hymn. This is source-local child manifestation; not merged with other-source two-sage Kāśī episodes or Divodāsa story.

Kumāras hymn Vināyaka as Kaśyapa beloved son, BORN FROM ADITI’S WOMB/brahmacārin, māyā-support/transcendent, devotion-bound/Heramba, eternal Brahman/lord of Brahmans playing yoga/ayoga, beginning/middle/end, Prakṛti/Puruṣa, nāda/anāda/subtle/gross, god/demon/human/Nāga/water/land forms and beyond māyā. Vedas/Śambhu cannot fully praise him; they are fortunate to see their yogin-family deity. Hymn womb-parentage attributed precisely to incarnation, not generic universal biological descent of Gaṇeśa.

Kumāras fall silent/prostrate; devotion-bound child Vināyaka says hymn gives yoga-peace to readers/hearers and he will give the desired object while himself moved by the hymn; Kumāras will become Gaṇapatyas like Śiva. No request words or Pṛthu-directed boon here. Child then plays with children like ordinary child. Kumāras visit Kāśī king, are honored, eat and return to their place. They conclude Pṛthu should worship Gaṇeśa as full peace-knowledge.

Kumāras return Brahmā’s world. Pṛthu divides kingdom among UNNAMED SONS(plural) and goes forest. Following yoga progression he becomes Gaṇapatya; at end humble king WITH WIFE merges in Gaṇeśa. The wife is unnamed, not remembered Arci. Hearing/reading Pṛthu account gives all. Actual merger is distinct from embedded Vināyaka promise to Kumāras.
outcome: Pṛthu and wife actually merge in Gaṇeśa after forest practice.

details: Barhis arises in Pṛthu’s lineage, righteous/armed protector devoted to karmamārga. He performs varied sacrifices, covering Earth with east-pointing kuśa. Hunting in forest, he marries UNNAMED daughter of Samudra; TEN sons are born, alike in appearance, conduct and mind, collectively named Pracetas. Seeking progeny, they perform tapas near ocean at Nārāyaṇa-named lake, worshipping Viṣṇu. No individual son names, duration, Śiva hymn or next-generation spouse imported. Compassionate Nārada comes to Prācīnabarhis engaged in acts at home; king welcomes him.

Nārada asks what karma will give, calling action binding and king’s sacrifices violent through animal slaughter. He says slain animals angrily await chance to kill king; this is Nārada’s warning, not actual attack or fulfilled curse. Now old, king should leave acts for knowledge that burns karma shoots. Astonished Prācīnabarhis says he knows karma-centered mode and asks knowledge cutting karma roots/to cross existence-ocean. Seeing him purified by acts yet karma-oriented, Nārada teaches.

Nārada says knowledge is nondifference-yoga/Brahman attainment; Gaṇapati reflection is deluded jīva within heart. He names five citta states and defines them: kṣipta where person casts mind and knows through heart; mūḍha fails to understand directed mind/knows otherwise; vikṣipta liberation/Brahman-longing, neither immersed in worldly joy nor yet united with Brahman; ekāgra self-form in all states, seen inwardly through yoga; nirodhikā/nirodha beyond body/self, giving repose through yoga at union/ayoga limit. No remembered standard four-body names or different Yoga Sūtra gloss substituted.

Fivefold mind is Buddhi playing with Gaṇapa in heart. Sovereignty-delusion is Siddhi, described fivefold as dharma/artha/kāma/mokṣa/Brahman and playing with Gaṇapa. Buddhi is knowledge, Siddhi sovereignty; Gaṇeśa reflection amid them is deluded jīva, māyā-bound/desiring māyā joy. It illumines five mind states, hence Cintāmaṇi name. Precise 24–30 doctrine is attributed; 25 own-state/sovereignty compound separately unresolved. No literal new marriage or biological wifehood from these personifications.

Nārada names four bodies gross(sthūla), subtle(sūkṣma), sama and nāda, with bindu their ultimate state. Embodied self is fourfold through delusion despite unity, its Brahman soham. Union/self-arising/other-arising and fivefold self-experienced Brahman follow; 33 precise satya/other-arising assignment is separately uncertain.34 names satya/asatya/sama/neti differences, 35 eternal nondifference-union/samādhi happiness Svānanda, 36 ayoga repose and peace-yoga through ending union/ayoga. Gaṇeśa lord of Brahman-groups illumines Buddhi; king should worship heart-resident peaceful deity. Sthūla/sūkṣma/sama/nāda preserved exactly rather than remembered causal-body lists.

Nārada stops; king bows and says he is saved by teaching his nearby Brahmins do not know. Nārada disappears, wander-singing with vīṇā and Gaṇapa remembrance. Prācīnabarhis promptly entrusts kingdom to MINISTERS, goes forest and meditates Gaṇeśa. Following Nārada’s knowledge progressively, he becomes Gāṇeśaka; at end actually merges in Brahman-form Gaṇeśa and is called Brahman-attained. Hearing/reading account destroys sin and gives all. No entrusting kingdom to sons, no actual animal retaliation and no new deity boon scene.
outcome: Prācīnabarhis actually merges in Gaṇeśa at end.
